the commission is aware of the fact that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the application of the competition rules to the various categories of undertakings. this joint debate is living proof of that, mr president. we have heard profound and at the same time philosophical remarks on economic policy and the importance of institutional order. our common intention is to modernise and strengthen competition policy, a pillar of the social and market economy and of european integration. the main thrust of the reform of competition policy, which we will have the opportunity to deal with together, is to ensure effective protection of competition, to reduce the bureaucratic burden on companies and to bring decision-making processes closer to citizens. i would like to personally and sincerely thank mr von wogau for his commitment to the white paper and for the quality of his report. i would like to group the comments made during the debate on the von wogau report into four points, which i do not regard as criticisms of the commission but rather as fundamental contributions, because there are still legitimate concerns which we want to overcome together: efficiency, the risk of renationalisation, consistency in enforcement and legal certainty. i'll be back in a moment to examine them one by one. the efficiency. i am convinced that this reform will strengthen, not weaken, the protection of competition in the single market. the present notification system, ladies and gentlemen, no longer achieves this objective because it does not ensure that the commission is informed of the most important restrictions - i would remind you that in thirty-five years only nine prohibition decisions have been taken following a notification and in the absence of any denunciation - and it does not guarantee transparency and does not provide real legal security for companies which, in most cases, receive a simple administrative letter of classification. the proposed system will improve competition protection, in particular because the commission will be able to concentrate its action on the most serious restrictions, and will therefore involve the national authorities and those responsible for competition more closely in the repression of infringements, and because it will enable the victims of such infringements to apply directly to the national courts whose task is to protect subjective rights. the renationalisation. first of all, although this is superfluous, i would like to remind and emphasize, three times if possible, that the white paper does not touch on mergers and state aid - we do not think of devolution in these areas - but, as regards regulation 17, there is a risk of renationalization. we have considered this problem, do you think! we have considered and screened it with great care, particularly because of the concerns you have expressed. i do not think that these fears are justified, frankly. the commission proposal gives it a central role in determining the direction of competition policy. the reform does not imply any reduction in the work of the commission but rather a refocusing of it on the more important dossiers. it will lead to a gradual development of the european culture of competition - i would like to emphasize this because the expression used by president randzio-plath, which i fully agree with, struck me very strongly. the reform will therefore lead to a transplantation, to a rooting, in the soil of the european culture of competition, where today thrive various small plants, which are not uniform, of the different national cultures in terms of competition. the 15 national laws will be gradually abandoned to make way for a wider use of community law which can be applied by a greater number of actors. i would like to emphasize that this is a communitization and not a renationalization of competition law. consistency in application. the risk of inconsistent application of the competition rules must be borne in mind, but i do not think it should be exaggerated. like many other provisions of the treaty, articles 81 (1) and 82 have after all been applied for decades by national authorities and courts and i do not think that this has created any major problems. in a legal exceptional system, the maintenance of consistency will depend first of all on the clarity of the substantive rules. the commission will endeavour to refine the legislative framework, both through acts of general application and through its decision-making practice. effective conflict prevention mechanisms will also need to be established and the white paper contains information and consultation mechanisms. in this connection, i should like to say a few words about the idea, which i think is excellent, put forward by mrs riis-jørgensen and mr huhne, namely the idea of monitoring the application.

in writing. - (it) although the content of article 158 of the ec treaty is intended to promote the harmonious development of all the communities, it must be said that the total elimination of disparities is still a long way off. in some cases, such as the italian objective 1 regions, these disparities even increase paradoxically, mainly because of the still weak capacity of the structural apparatus to approach community procedures and because of the persistent fragmentation of procedures. despite the normative measures, the community structures still need to be made more flexible. without administrative simplification, the community's objectives of efficiency and concentration will be difficult to achieve. in this respect, the commission document is lacking in any recommendation to the member states to simplify national procedures and legislation in relation to the submission and examination of projects by the national authorities, as well as in relation to financing, implementation and control. smes, micro-enterprises and craftsmen in particular are still 'weak subjects' because for them the legislative and administrative constraints imposed by certain member states, including italy, are major obstacles to access to the structural funds. a major handicap is the inability and impossibility for the regions and other subjects to plan in time. the commission, which should have consulted parliament in time, under the decision on guidelines 97/99 (howitt report), therefore found a kind of easy alibi in the constitution of the reduced programming phase within the member states and published the guidelines in july 1999, well before the newly elected parliament began its legislative activities, thus preventing it from acting on the current range of guidelines. the interim evaluation of article 42 of regulation 1260/99 will therefore be of considerable importance. the current guidelines do not generally have the merit of being clear and transparent. they only touch on one important issue, however: the possibility of measuring progress against verifiable objectives and in full harmony with the strategies of community policies, and do not properly address the implications of enlargement, especially since they do not contain specific provisions or clarifications in this area, neither for the regional and national authorities nor for the candidate countries. however, the different organization of the guidelines, which, leaving aside geographical objectives, are intended for sectoral policies, can be assessed positively. if, in theory, this can satisfy the requirements of concentration and thus of the effectiveness of assistance, a question arises of itself, namely whether the present situation of the objective 1 regions actually allows a policy of integrated assistance, which requires an operational instrument for coordinating the sums allocated. we could then in principle even respond positively to the commission's request to create a management centre for structural promotion in the member states to coordinate the implementation and management of structural assistance on the ground, provided that this centre does not become a supranational centralising instrument and ensures that effective attention is paid to those regions which - i repeat once again - due to a whole series of convergent negative factors have not yet reached the correct levels of use of the structural funds, so that the replacement of the geographical objective by sectoral policies could lead to a negative intervention in fact. the guidelines, as approved by the commission, are very limited because, instead of meeting the objective of indicating directions, they provide a catalogue of possible provisions, a catalogue which, in the absence of a progressive definition of priorities, could plainly mislead the member states by orienting them towards a range of proposals contrary to the concentration sought. it could be said that, as things stand, we have again lost the opportunity to effectively strengthen sustainable urban development by containing the growing phenomenon of urbanisation and the associated degradation of the landscape. the importance of the instrument of the global grant, which could prove very useful for the rebalancing of urban and rural areas by giving, moreover, the dignity that is required of local bodies which, by their autonomy, could define conditions for territorial development with shorter deadlines, thus contributing to the efforts to reform the structural funds and to the objectives of efficiency, concentration and administrative flexibility, has not been properly assessed. rural areas must be seen as a resource in which more and more investment is needed, encouraging young people to stay in rural areas to avoid economic and social destruction. it is now known that to achieve this goal, jobs in rural areas will have to be created not in agriculture as traditionally conceived - which is nevertheless an essential instrument for safeguarding the environment and biodiversity - but in sectors such as rural tourism, sport, culture, the environment, small and mediumsized enterprises and services. the guidelines show a real gap due to the lack of concrete guidelines to ensure coordination between the esf and the employment strategies, a coordination which, since it is being applied for the first time for the 2000-2006 programming period, presupposes that the member states need 'guidelines'. it should also be stressed that once again the commission is in fact avoiding the problem of concrete action in the field of equal opportunities. in conclusion, we have a document which is not particularly satisfactory and, in some respects, disappointing.

commission. - (sv) thank you very much, mr schörling. these are two important questions. i'm glad i have the opportunity to clarify them. no, we should not start with a cost-benefit analysis, but rather with an assessment of what we know, what science can teach us and how we should view it in relation to the risks we believe exist for the environment or for human and animal health. on the other hand, when a measure has been decided on, it must be a cost-effective measure, so as not to adopt measures which are completely absurd from the point of view of efficiency. so we should not start with a cost-benefit analysis. the other question concerns the reversal of the burden of proof. it is quite true that we need to apply it in some cases. i have taken the case of the chemicals strategy as a good example of where it is needed. this is the area in question, but it can be said that this communication on the precautionary principle is horizontal; it covers all the specific policy areas. that is why it is not specifically about reversing the burden of proof in this respect or what the burden of proof will look like, but rather about political decision-making and the basis for it. it is absolutely true, however, that we must, for example, in the case of chemicals, ensure that the burden of proof is reversed.
- (it) mr president, i think that in order to work, the precautionary principle should be quite radical, otherwise we are constantly lost in the tortuous tangles of interpretations. let us take one example: it has been shown that an anti-cryptogaming product causes blind children to be born. so it is teratogenic. all right, this is an anti-cryptogamic, an anti-fungal. it is a british laboratory that has proven the teratogenic effect, perhaps the only one, however, to have done tests. well, in my view, since the threat to health is so serious, the precautionary principle requires that the product be withdrawn immediately, as new zealand has done, for example. i would therefore like to ask the following question: when human health is at stake, or when serious effects on human health are possible, should we analyse costs and benefits? a blind child is too high a price to pay, in my opinion, and no amount of profit could ever make up for it. i would like to know whether, in the final analysis, the precautionary principle, as you understand it, madam commissioner, would presuppose in this case that the product be withdrawn from sale until other laboratories have proved otherwise.

the rapporteur. - (it) madam president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioners, the conference on rural development, held in cork from 7 to 9 november 1996, identified rural development as one of the priorities of the european union, since it is essential for agriculture, for sustaining existence and continuous development, for providing farmers with an environment with the necessary infrastructure and services, for better respect for the environment and a better quality of life, and for diversification and job creation. this is why an integrated development policy for all rural areas in the union is needed, with the following elements: an integrated and multisectoral approach, simplification of administrative procedures, improved partnership between the european institutions and local national actors and environmental protection. in the 1998 agenda 2000 programme, the commission identified two key principles on which rural development policy should be based: the recognition of the multifunctional role of agriculture and the need for an integrated strategy for rural areas in development. the first principle is intended to create a new pact between the farmer and society, making the farmer the administrator of the countryside and ensuring that society is willing to pay for the environmental services needed to maintain the recreational value of rural space. the second principle is based on the fact that today most employment opportunities in rural areas are not in the traditional agricultural sector, which requires the establishment of a comprehensive development programme that integrates rural development policies with sectoral agricultural policies: rural development thus becomes a pillar of the same common agricultural policy. the leader community initiative was launched in 1991 with the aim of promoting a new bottom-up approach to rural development and diversifying interventions, adapting them to local needs. the objectives were to improve the development potential of rural areas by using local initiative, to promote the acquisition of knowledge in the rural development sector and to disseminate it to other rural areas. leader i was aimed at rural areas covered by objectives 1 and 5b of the structural funds. 217 local action groups participated in the project, with funding equivalent to eur 1155 million. leader ii, a programme covering the period 1994 to 1999 - for which, unfortunately, we do not yet have an overall evaluation - has had a greater impact than leader i. it should have had more than 800 beneficiaries phases in that this time all rural areas will be able to benefit from it; it is also more ambitious and better adapted to the challenges that rural areas will face. the main changes are: all rural areas will be eligible for leader +; the criteria for selecting local actions will be more rigorous; integrated local development plans, the use of information technology, the improvement of the quality of life and the promotion of local products will be the priority themes. i therefore support the continuation of the initiative because, as i said, it puts forward innovative development commission. - (sv) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking the committee on the environment, and especially the rapporteur, mrs lienemann, for the ambitious and of agreement which is reflected in the amendments which have been tabled in parliament. many of them are in addition to the many constructive and informal discussions which parliament and the council have had on the margins of the first reading. most of the amendments proposed by parliament help to improve the text and make it more ambitious. the commission can approve 72 of the 108 amendments, in whole, in part or in principle. many of the amendments tabled by parliament show that an agreement will be necessary. i therefore call on parliament to vote for an ambitious position in the forthcoming negotiations. i would like to start by quoting some of my most important arguments. today we have the opportunity to fulfil the commitments we have made under the ospar convention. rather than making these objectives legally binding, we must consider their political nature. this is also reflected in several amendments tabled by parliament. as far as water charges are concerned, this directive will determine europe's water policy for the next three decades. it is our duty to ensure that this directive now offers the real motivations, the real driving forces for an effective tariff structure and price formation that improves our environment with good cost-effectiveness. it would be nice if water was a human right and could be free. but water is not free - nor are housing or food free. first, with effective management tools we can have better water treatment and management. i would also like to add that i am in favour of a tighter timetable and of clarifying the objectives and is also stated in recital 14. let me also say to mr bowe and to my scottish colleague that he can continue in good conscience to drink a glass of scotch whisky now and then. we have not considered it into our water supply must be one of the main objectives. i am glad to see that some of parliament's amendments have focused on this. the commission fully supports the proposal to incorporate the provisions of the ospar convention into the text. but we must be careful to grasp their meaning and their precise meaning. as i said, the objective and timing of the ospar are above all a political commitment. the introduction of a legally binding timetable would be in contradiction to the timetable. however, it must be ensured that the member states and the community can be compelled to take measures to achieve these objectives and to respect the timetable. i therefore support amendments nos 6, 10, 14, 24, 58, 60 and 88. the commission cannot accept amendment no 19, which defines timetable is necessary for the commission proposal to limit the discharges of priority substances. amendment no 59 introduces requests for a review of the list of priority substances. it would create legal uncertainty as to the status of the list and cannot therefore be accepted. the request of amendments nos 60 and 93 for a specific list and a list of substances for which data are insufficient cannot be approved. such lists would have an unclear legal status and would not be consistent with the procedures for adopting the list of priority substances. in this connection, i would like to stress that the ospar convention does not in any way alter the existing community legislation on nitrates in the agricultural sector. the nitrates directive should therefore not be affected by this framework directive. i appreciate the flexibility of parliament in the many sensitive and difficult issues relating to the solution of the problem of charges for water services. i can wholeheartedly support the demand that the price of water be set at a level which encourages the sustainable use of water resources. i also support the call for an appropriate contribution from each sector to cover - doc. a5-0033/2000 by mr andersson, on behalf of the committee on employment and social affairs, on the communication from the commission on a concerted strategy to modernise social protection (com (1999) 347 - c5-0253/1999 - 1999/2182 (cos))
- (it) mr president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the objective of developing a concerted strategy to modernise social protection in the european union is certainly a good thing, as was the launch, with the luxembourg summit, of the european convergence strategy for employment and employment policies. the labour market and social protection are in fact two sides of the same coin, which require that policies and regulations be brought into line. if the labour market is efficient in terms of employment levels, flexibility and wage efficiency, the welfare state and social protection cannot fail to be so, and vice versa. previously, the european countries had each defined the rules for the operation and financing of the two markets on their own, in a quasi-autarky manner. fiscal and exchange rate policies were in place to ensure internal and external balance. with maastricht and the single currency, fiscal policies have been severely restricted and it is no longer possible to resort to devaluation, to seek lost margins of competition. the structural and cyclical differences between countries can therefore no longer be made up by deficit and exchange rate. in the absence of full employment mobility within the union and a redistributive fiscal policy at the federal level, the only degree of flexibility is left for labour and social protection markets to correct both structural and cyclical imbalances, so-called asymmetric exogenous shocks. and that's where the paradox is. the convergence of political and monetary europe inevitably leads to the convergence of the rules of the game on labour markets and social protection. at the same time, however, the single currency, combined with the lack of employment mobility and a redistributive tax policy, forces us to non-convergence of wages and social protection to compensate for productivity differences between countries and regions. it is not hypocrisy and fancy words such as convergence, benchmarking, modernisation and concertation that will bring us out of these contradictions. either the european union becomes a genuine federal state, with genuine redistributive taxation, genuine employment mobility and hence, and only from now on, with common rules on employment and social protection, or it is better not to make vain promises and not to have illusions about the impossible paths to convergence, a principle which sounds good but which is harmful, especially to the poorest. we should all be aware of this.
commission. - (el) mr president, i would like to thank mr andersson for the really excellent work he has done and which has resulted in very broad agreement, and i would also like to thank the members for their contribution. i will make a few comments on what has been said. first, i would point out that the debate on social protection issues has been going on for several years among the european institutions, and that in 1995 the first communication entitled 'the future of social protection' was issued, and that, as far as the european parliament is concerned, there were the communications by mrs weiler and mr pronk. today we have the communication from mr andersson. i think we have made important progress, since we are now talking about the modernisation of social protection. secondly, we must take account of the legal basis on which the european commission can operate. you know very well that there is no legal basis in the treaty for policies at european level, but there is the agreement that emerged at the last european council, there is an agreement to start coordination actions and the exchange of experiences, the exchange of successful programmes between the member states. thirdly, there is a horizontal approach to the women's issue in the four areas around which the communication is centred, namely paid work, the sustainability of pension schemes, social integration and, finally, the quality of health care, because in each of these areas - accepts the ratification by this parliament. i would like to stress the importance of these two treaties. the wipo copyright treaty and the wipo performances and phonograms treaty are both progress in the international protection of copyright and related rights and a major improvement over the berne convention and the treaty of rome. these two treaties contribute to a high level of protection of works and other aspects, all of which provide public access to content via electronic networks. both treaties explicitly allow the community to become a signatory party and to play an important role in the management of this area. the ratification of the treaties by the community is therefore of great significance, since it would show that it attaches great importance to intellectual property rights. ratification would also lead to greater international recognition of the role of the european union in copyright matters. at international level, there is enormous support for the accelerated entry into force of the treaties. these have now been ratified by twelve or thirteen member states of wipo, including the united states. this entry into force depends largely on the european union, as thirty acts of ratification are needed and those of the european union and the member states and associated countries are of paramount importance to reach this number. many developing countries also expect the european union to ratify these treaties quickly, as this would send a strong signal to the world. in this context, parliament has already played a key role in the discussions on the draft directive on copyright in the information society which led to the adoption of the barzanti report in february 1999. this directive is the necessary complement to the proposed decision and contains essentially the basic principles of the wipo treaties. the european parliament must once again follow the exceptional assent procedure referred to in article 300 (3). it is essential to send the appropriate signal to the outside world in the form of this recommendation. in short, to repeat the commission's conclusions: it supports the draft recommendation and hopes that it will have important significance for the whole world interested in intellectual property.

in writing. - (it) we await with interest and hope a concrete strategy for modernising social protection systems in europe which is not, however, alien to similar processes of cohesion. modernisation, but also cohesion, are highlighted in the report, which we welcome. many policies have already ventured, sometimes with difficulty, along this latter path, but many others will have to do so before europe, even at the level of subsidiarity, is a large house welcoming not only the citizens of the member states but also those of the candidate countries. the european social security systems have always played a positive role in the processes of civil and democratic development of each people. if these systems are to continue to play this role today in the face of economic upheavals, changes in the world of work and changing social requirements, it is obvious that they must be modernised. there are three main points to be emphasized. the first concerns the close interdependence which must exist between economic, employment and social security policies in directly proportional terms. the second concerns the management of social security systems and the bodies which implement them. the work done today is increasingly based on complementary provisioning frameworks and is becoming more and more efficient. but in our view, the role of the public body cannot be diluted, both from the point of view of the universality and - we hope - the quality of basic social protection benefits. it is, in essence, a principle of justice which affects health, pension systems, but also assistance for which strategic coordination, even if renewed, by the public body remains unavoidable. the third aspect concerns the principle of subsidiarity on which europe is based. we still lack a common strategy for social protection and security, and the systems in force are essentially based on the action and internal solidarity of each member state. a process of modernising these systems cannot ignore the differences in economic, employment and social protection between member and candidate countries. modernisation, which is closely linked to a process of cohesion, although based on different bases, must therefore be able to bring about an upward evolution and not the other way round. it is, moreover, a question of civilization, progress and the common dignity of the present european union and the european union as it will be after enlargement.

should like to comment very briefly on other points in the draft resolution. we accept that the agreement should, to some extent, serve as a model for other agreements, although of course we will also concerned about it. i shall look at the matter again, although i must stress that the fact that we have two phare programmes in progress is a real risk of confusion. however, i would like to stress the rapporteur. - (it) mr president, the adoption of this agreement between the european parliament and the commission on the detailed rules for implementing the council decision on comitology marks the end of an episode of about two years in the life of this parliament and of the few representatives of the various institutions of the union who are passionate about this issue, and who some do not hesitate to call masochists. since 1993, the way in which the commission exercises its implementing powers, in particular the mysterious and even suspicious practice of committees, has led to conflicts and a climate of mistrust between the institutions, with the risk of serious consequences for the legislative process. this is why, following declaration no 31 annexed to the treaty of amsterdam, the union institutions embarked on a complex process of negotiation and consultation which culminated in the new council decision. it is a fairly thorough overhaul of the old regime, although in our view it is totally inadequate. in particular, the decision introduces a principle of parliament's power of control: i am talking about the possibility of sounding the alarm in the event that the commission, by taking an implementing measure pursuant to a legislative act resulting from codecision, exceeds its powers as an executive organ. it was decided, during the long interinstitutional negotiations in which parliament took an active part through its rapporteur, mrs adelaide aglietta, that the european parliament and the commission would conclude an interinstitutional agreement on the detailed rules for the application of several aspects of the new decision, on the one hand, to clarify certain points which the council did not intend to take up in its decision and, on the other hand, to organise more precisely the information and control system in relation to implementing measures. at the trilogue meeting in strasbourg on 6 october 1999, the president of the european parliament and the president of the commission endorsed the principle of the rapid conclusion of such an agreement. we believe that we have fulfilled this commitment, which was not too difficult for us in view of the climate of mutual trust and respect which prevailed in the negotiations with the commission. the agreement is essentially two-fold. first, the european parliament must be informed, which is the sine qua non for the effective exercise of its right to intervene within the meaning of article 8 of the decision. until now, information has been received in the form of paper documents; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the information will now be sent to us electronically, thanks to the system known as circa, to which parliament will have access and which is a real innovation, not only for us but also - i am sure - for the commission. secondly, article 8 of the council decision does not specify the manner in which or the time limits within which the european parliament must sound the alarm, that is, exercise its modest power of control. paragraphs 6 and 7 of the agreement lay down the following procedure: the european parliament adopts its full reasoned resolution in plenary and has one month to assert its right to intervene before the commission adopts its draft implementing measure. however, it is not always possible to wait a month before implementing an enforcement measure: we are all aware of this. the agreement therefore provides for an emergency procedure to speed up the work of the committee responsible. in conclusion, i would say that before we can know whether it is a good agreement or a bad one, we must wait until we see it work in practice. the european parliament will have to acquire the necessary means, which it does not currently have, to ensure effective monitoring and control of the executive process, while the commission will have to accept the reorganization of some of its practices to enable parliament to exercise its control and to inform it properly. finally, and in any event, it should be remembered that in the european parliament's view the real solution to the problems of comitology is still the revision of the procedure provided for in the treaties for the implementation of standards and the gradual abolition of committees, the existence of which is an anomaly which seriously impedes the commission's executive power and which risks prejudicing the legislative powers of the european parliament.

commission - (nl) mr president, first of all, on behalf of the commission, i should like to express my warm thanks to the rapporteur, mr olle schmidt, and to the members of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, on the substance of the matter, and to the rapporteur, mr brian crowley, and to the members of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, whom i would like to thank for their detailed and important work on refining and extending the proposals. since the adoption of directive 85/611 the investment fund sector has undergone a long evolution and it is now important to modernise the rules. the new proposals aim at a maximum level of investor protection, which is an essential condition for the integration of markets resulting from the introduction of the euro. since the average european family puts its savings in investment funds, the proposals contain provisions for prudent management - and i want to emphasize this point - prudent management in terms of investment policy and risk distribution. the two proposals form a coherent whole. the first proposal extends the number of instruments in which a 'collective investment vehicle' - a ucits - can invest. as has already been pointed out in this house, ucits are among the major players in modern capital markets. their presence offers a large number of traditional investors the opportunity to participate in these markets, taking into account the principle of risk-sharing with adequate control. as diversified forms of investment are permitted, individual investors can also enjoy all the advantages of the new investment techniques. the second proposal extends the role that these important intermediary institutions can play in the capital markets of the european union with regard to the development of the investment fund sector. if we allow the establishment of branches and the establishment of certain services across borders, these institutions will finally be able to make use of the freedoms granted by the treaty of rome which they have been deprived of for all these years. the commission welcomes many of the clarifications proposed by the committee on economic and monetary affairs and will be taking up many of its ideas. the commission will take up the amendments - and i am using the numbering in its most recent form - 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9, 13, 19 and 21 to the first proposal and 23, 28 and 32 to the second proposal, as they are very useful clarifications and improvements. i also welcome the ideas put forward in amendments nos 1, 10, 11, 14, 18 and 20, if they are properly worded. i also support the idea behind amendments nos 17, 36 and 45, which envisage a general maximum percentage of counterparty risk. i can also accept the idea proposed in the second paragraph of amendment no 47. all the amendments i have just mentioned relate to the first proposal. as regards the second proposal, the ideas put forward in amendments nos 24, 25, 29, 30, 41 and parts of amendment no 27, which contain reasonable suggestions, can be taken up, again with an adaptation of the wording. the commission proposes to take up the contents of the directive by making certain changes to its wording. i also note the request of the committee on economic and monetary affairs to codify the whole text once it has been approved - amendments 7 to the first proposal and 22 to the second. the commission is in favour of codification and will, within a reasonable time after the approval of the proposals and subject to its right of initiative, work on a codified version. i cannot, however, take up the wording of the recital in its entirety. the commission also considers that a number of the amendments proposed by the committee on economic and monetary affairs would fundamentally alter the content of the first proposal. the commission therefore regrets that it cannot accept the following amendments to the first proposal. amendment no 8 because the proposal to make a general reference to investments 'referred to in this directive' instead of the more precise indication of investments 'referred to in article 19 of the directive' would complicate the application. in addition, this amendment could lead to different interpretations in the member states which would probably seek the instruments considered in other articles of the directive. amendment 16 threatens investor protection because the prohibition of a security from the custodian is a contradiction in terms. similarly, securities lending operations via clearing houses and approved exchanges - as opposed to the sale or purchase of securities - are not automatically covered by these institutions. that is why we cannot accept the proposed amendment. amendment no 42 concerns a provision which is not modified by the proposal and which has not caused any problems since the directive was implemented. i therefore see no reason to delete article 22 (3) and therefore reject this amendment. amendment no 44 cannot be accepted because if it is provided that non-harmonised funds must follow the rules 'set out in the directive' in respect of borrowing, lending and short selling and depository, this would effectively lead to a situation in which only a few funds, for example swiss funds, would be eligible for investment. this is contrary to the commission's intention to widen the spectrum of investment and the wording chosen could be contrary to the gats agreements. amendment no 47 is unacceptable as regards the proposed amendments to the first paragraph of article 22a because this proposal is in total contradiction with the allocation rules of article 22, especially if ucits are required to indicate a reference point in their prospectuses, as has been discussed in the council. the main point of contention with regard to the first proposal is, however, the amendment by which parliament intends to authorize the use of over-the-counter instruments for general investment purposes. the commission notes that under the law in force in some member states, the use of otc derivatives for general investment purposes is already permitted. the commission also reserves its judgment in view of the inherently high risks of such investments compared to more traditional financial instruments. i believe that otc instruments could cause problems because they are not liquid, their price is difficult to assess and they carry counterparty risks that are not covered. it seems inconsistent to take a very cautious approach to investments in non-harmonised funds or bank deposits and at the same time to allow investments in otc instruments, which are undoubtedly riskier, without reservations. in rejecting amendment no 39 put forward by the rapporteur, the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy has agreed with the council. the consequence of this amendment by parliament would be that funds would theoretically be allowed to invest in otc instruments and to trade the participation rights in their funds throughout the internal market. in practice, access to other eu markets for these theoretically harmonised funds investing in otc instruments could be blocked through the application of different national laws and safeguards against otc investments, which would run counter to the fact that eu legislation is still provided for all funds investing in these instruments. in view of this potential negative impact on the internal market and the inherent risks of otc instruments, the commission cannot accept amendments nos 12, 15, 37, 38, 39, 43, 46 and 48 and the parts of amendments nos 17, 36 and 45 that relate to otc instruments. as regards the second proposal, i have just indicated that the commission will take account of a number of amendments. however, there are certain amendments which the commission cannot accept: amendment no 26, which does not seem to correspond to the order in which authorization is granted and activities are started; certain parts of amendment 27, notably the deletion of the section on the prevention of conflicts of interest, the limitation of delegation of tasks to elements of management decisions and the deletion of the general decision-making process of member states in the field of delegation; the commission has not yet adopted the amendment 31 because it is of the opinion that the application of article 44 of the directive, in its unamended form, on the trading of units in ucits has proved to be appropriate. the application of the provisions of the directive on the provision of investment services in securities, more commonly known as isds, is therefore not necessary and could create difficulties or confusion. amendment no 33 is not clear on the 'language' of the host country, especially when there are several official languages, and on the advantage of translations into two other languages. amendment no 34 is unacceptable because the mere removal of any reference to pension funds could create ambiguity as to whether a management company can carry out these activities or not. i also think that pension funds could benefit from this possibility if management companies were not clearly treated as pension funds but were only allowed, by delegation, to carry out part of the management. amendment no 35 cannot be accepted because it cannot have any legal effect. management companies that are refused authorisation in one member state should establish themselves in another legal form in order to be authorised in another member state. amendments nos 49, 50 and 51, which are based on the same basis, are not acceptable because they make substantial changes to the commission's consistent approach to regulating delegation to third parties and do not provide sufficient assurance to the competent authorities and investors. i would like to conclude by referring to the remarks made this morning by some members and, if you allow me, mr president, i will do so in english.
the rapporteur. - (it) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, by letters of 3 august and 3 december 1999, the council invited the european parliament, in accordance with article 39 of the treaty, to express its position on a draft convention between the member states aimed at ensuring better mutual judicial assistance in criminal matters. as you can see, this is a very important project which will enable the member states of the union to have a more complete and homogeneous instrument for mutual legal assistance. in fact, there are still some differences within the council today as to the type of convention and certain clauses it contains. some have already been flattened, others persist. the project aims to provide judicial authorities - mainly magistrates, but also the citizens concerned - with a valid operational instrument to combat crime while respecting the fundamental guarantees of the defence and the general principles of human rights. that is why, despite the many shortcomings of the text, the provisions contained in it can be accepted - i said 'may', mr president - but only if they are amended in due course so that they are functional for the judicial authorities and acceptable to the citizens. the commission has therefore proposed various amendments, all of which are intended to systematically rework the council's proposal by suggesting a series of technical adjustments to make the text harmonious and consistent with the proposed amendments. these amendments consist of highlighting the fundamental rights of the defence, making various technical changes necessary to clarify a whole series of obscure and contradictory passages, and deleting the part concerning remote telephone interceptions for which not only technical knowledge but also the consent of the governments of the various member states of the union are still lacking. the proposal, as formulated by the council and subsequently amended by the commission, provides for a convention consisting of three parts: the first part provides guidance on the standardization of procedures and formalities relating to letters rogatory; the second lists a series of specific requests for mutual legal assistance and sets out the formalities and procedures to be followed in relation to those specific mutual legal assistance activities; finally, part three provides and codifies the procedures for the execution of telephone interceptions concerning citizens in a state other than that which is conducting the interception. mr president, international cooperation is undeniably necessary both to deal with crossborder crime and to combat crimes committed in the territory of a member state, the evidence of which can only be obtained abroad. it is nevertheless essential to reach a new convention as soon as possible which takes account of other, even more delicate issues, such as double criminality, the special nature and credibility of a state of the union in the eyes of the judicial authorities of the other states of the union. these are therefore very important issues which we hope the council will address as soon as possible in order to formulate a new opinion. for various other points on the subject, mr president, i refer you to the contents of my written report.

the rapporteur. - (it) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, despite the delay and indecision of the european union in implementing a genuine community policy on tourism, interest in tourism as a sector capable of creating new jobs has increased. one of the reasons for the interest of the european union in this sector is the structural flexibility of this segment of the labour market. this explains the attraction of the programme to women and young people, who are often offered their first job opportunities. the importance of the tourist industry, its impact on employment - although it is perceived by everyone today - is nevertheless based more on impressions induced by an empirical verification of the phenomenon than on statistically demonstrable data. this vague identity, due to a lack of knowledge of the phenomenon, due to a lack of sufficiently reliable and scientifically correct statistical information, has considerably impeded the possibility of implementing a homogeneous policy in favour of this sector and the possibility of creating employment to a greater extent. in this case, it is therefore useful to base certain considerations on the impact of tourism on the lives of the citizens of the union, the need and the economic and social interest in supporting european tourism. firstly, i would like to point out that the tourism industry is one of the essential infrastructures of an advanced society; the world of institutions, business and work could not function without it. tourism must therefore be seen as a set of goods and services needed by citizens who are temporarily away from their usual residence, a factor which makes possible the mobility characteristic of the way of life of contemporary society. tourism can no longer be synonymous with sun, sea and holidays, which reduces the degree of institutional interest. secondly, i would like to demystify a common ground arising from an obvious paradox, which is clearly evident from eurostat statistics: the world tourist powers are not the countries traditionally considered as tourist, but the most advanced nations where the quality of life of the resident populations becomes a determining factor of promotion and attraction. it goes without saying that the importance of tourism for the life of regions traditionally considered as tourist, such as the southern regions for example, is quite different and must be assessed with a very different attention. it is nevertheless true that, either because it is visible or because it is comparable with other economic and social indicators, tourism has enabled many mediterranean regions to radically and positively change their economic and social character and the lifestyle of their populations and to reduce considerably the scourge of emigration. it is only where the activities necessary to meet the demands of tourists have been born and developed, through the creation of a production system, that social growth has been witnessed. in these cases, it was measured that employment increased more than tourism growth due to a spiral of local economic expansion. this shows that tourism is not the oil of the poor at all because it requires considerable investment in structures, infrastructure, entrepreneurship, professionalism, social services and training; whereas the tourism industry is fundamental to the balance of many regions as a direct source of employment and as a market for all local productive activities: agriculture, small businesses and craft industries, transport, services, trade, training; whereas the development of community tourism is closely linked to its sustainability in relation to community objectives; the european union is committed to the protection of the environment and the protection of the environment. in my view, the european union can, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, complement the action of the member states and contribute to the strengthening of tourism potential by means of certain measures, such as the adoption of a specific legal basis for tourism policy in the treaties; the adoption of programme and project mechanisms within the framework of regional and other union policies, capable of promoting tourism in all its forms: rural, environmental, cultural, research and training, congress, spa, for the elderly and sports; the amendment of directive 95/57 on the collection of statistical information in the field of tourism; co-financing of projects for the implementation of new transport services and infrastructure; the co-financing of pilot actions for the exchange of experience and benchmarking. these and other concrete measures in my report can, in my view, add value to the actions that the competent national and regional authorities should take to promote tourism and create jobs, starting with the adoption of positive fiscal measures for small and mediumsized enterprises, particularly those designed to reduce the burden on the labour factor.
- (it) mr president, commissioners, i should like to begin by saying a few optimistic words that were offered to us in the communication of the high level group in october 1998. the first page of the latitude, climate, many factors, many elements of interpretation; it can be synonymous with a holiday or it can actually be a place of production, income, wealth and employment. we're running out of data. we have no information on the economic impact, which remains a mystery. we have criteria for collecting and interpreting statistics which are absolutely at odds with each other, despite what a directive of the commission and parliament said in 1995. i believe that it is essential, in order to be able to develop a strategy, to have a uniform and the most rigorous reading of this data, so that we can ensure that tourism is really able to generate jobs. there is no automaticity in this: in the past, the development of the tourist industry has often led to large accumulations of wealth without leading to an increase in employment. we lack a legal basis and we believe that this gap is the great limitation of any intervention in the tourism sector today. a legal basis means the ability to coordinate, plan and plan strategy, which are essential if tourism in the european union is to be competitive with other markets. a legal basis would avoid having to draw, as in the past, from the structural funds a sort of pocket money, which is also distributed to a lesser extent. it should be recalled that the commission's communication indicated a sum of eur 4 700 000 000 over the last five years, which corresponds to the cost of 400 km of motorway. the possibility of sending a strong signal to the states is lacking: recognition of the legal basis for tourism would allow the enterprises involved in the tourism sector in europe - conditions which are truly competitive on this market; give special attention to vocational qualifications within the european union and flexibility to be understood in a purely negative way and to be mistaken for seasonality as irregular work. it should be remembered that 50 percent of the work, especially in the southern european countries, is undeclared work. we believe that the european union and the commission must make a strong commitment to sustainable tourism, which means having a strategy of environmental compatibility after the excesses of recent years when private wealth often did not correspond to so many jobs. first and foremost, we must be competitive in terms of quality. finally, we believe that tourism can be not only a factor of growth but also a factor of democracy, and we ask the commission to make a strong and conscious commitment to this.

commission - (sv) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the common position on cocoa and chocolate products is the result of long and complex discussions. it represents a delicate compromise, which has been achieved with great difficulty, but which is balanced. the common position allows the free movement of these products, but with strict conditions as to the method of manufacture and consumer information. it authorizes the use of vegetable fats other than cocoa butter in addition to the minimum cocoa content laid down in the directive. however, the addition of other vegetable fats may not exceed 5%. the only substances authorised shall be those listed in the annex. all are of tropical origin, produced by acp countries. the presence of these fats must be indicated separately on the packaging, in the same area as the product name and the list of ingredients. consumers will thus be able to choose and differentiate between these products and those made exclusively from cocoa. these conditions and limits, which have nothing to do with health issues, are the point of gravity on which the whole balance of the text rests. the common position also addresses the questions and concerns of consumers, such as those of cocoa exporting countries and chocolate producing countries, whether or not they use other vegetable fats. any change would seriously undermine the balance of this agreement, on which the council has reached agreement, and risk condemning it to failure. the second reading recommendation of parliament contains two proposed amendments. the first is the commission's policy and can therefore be accepted. the second does not have a place in a specific directive, since the introduction of genetically modified organisms on the european market must be in writing. - (it) the decision not to vote on the duff/voggenhuber report is not a criticism of the content of the fundamental rights recognised by the member states, demanded by the treaty on european union, applied by the luxembourg court of justice in many of its decisions, long since introduced into the convention on human rights, and from which the new charter seems to want to draw inspiration. these rights are the constitutional backbone of all the countries that join the union: in this way, they protect the european citizen against possible attacks and abuses in each of the member states and are translated, through the interpretation of case law, into specific national realities. it is possible to agree on the drawing up of a charter which is nothing more than a political declaration with a high moral content, in which the union will again emphasise - as far as is still necessary - the importance, stability and durability of fundamental rights. the new charter could thus inspire a philosophy which the member states, or some of them, could transpose into their systems. on the contrary, it is believed that the extension of a charter of rights of the union, binding on the institutions but indirectly also on the member states in their relations with their citizens, could change the game in terms of relations between the union and the member states, relegate the principle of subsidiarity to the background and lead to a system where the various levels - national, european - on which these fundamental rights have an impact, with their relative protection, would inevitably overlap, leading to dangerous confusions due to differences in interpretations of the same principle. in the final analysis, such a situation would be paradoxically at odds with the principle which inspired a charter of rights of the union, namely the improvement of the protection and security of european citizens.

commission - (es) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, one thing is very clear: the 'hushkits' regulation will come into force on 4 may in the european union. that's the only thing that's absolutely clear. it will be necessary to see how we proceed with the negotiations with the united states from that point on. the aim of this regulation is very clear: we must ensure that what has already been agreed in the icao is respected, that is to say, that aircraft landing at our airports actually comply with the icao noise standards. this regulation has no other claim, but i think we must be more ambitious. the current standards, as mr bockland pointed out, date from 1978. since then, the world's aviation technology has made tremendous progress. today, older aircraft emit noise levels that are 20 times, 40 times, or even 50 times greater than those of modern aircraft. that is why we are trying to get new noise levels, like international standards within the icao. and in this area we must work with the united states, which is also our ally and friend. the rapid entry into force of this regulation does not mean that negotiations with the united states should not be continued to improve the situation of noise standards within icao. what can we negotiate ? two things. the first is that we will seek better international standards within the icao framework, that we will work together within the icao and that we will pursue a common objective, which is to further reduce noise pollution at airports and therefore to achieve better noise levels, through the application of the most modern technologies, with a phase-out period for the noisiest aircraft and the creation of a chapter 4. the second is that we can negotiate that the americans suspend their action in the icao under article 84 and that we suspend - we can negotiate this - the part of the regulation concerning third country airlines, in no case the part concerning european airlines, since this regulation will come into force on 4 may. in other words, as far as european airlines are concerned, there is nothing to add, we can only negotiate the part concerning third country airlines - commission - mr president, i would first of all like to thank the members of this house very much for the questions they have asked and the comments they have made. perhaps you will allow me to make a few remarks on what various members of this house have said. in reply to mr rothley, i would say that the commission has in fact reserved the right to formally oppose this patent. as i said earlier, i wrote a letter on behalf of the commission to the european patent office. i have no objection to making this letter public. the penultimate paragraph reads: 'in this context, i must inform you that the college of commissioners has already decided to take more formal action, including lodging an objection on behalf of the commission or the community, in the event that a practical solution cannot be found.' in other words, we would prefer a negotiated arrangement, because it would be quicker than the nine months provided for by the rules of the patent office, but we reserve the right to oppose the patent if no progress is made by this quicker route. so, from this point of view, mr rothley can be assured that the commission reserves the right to do so. on the other hand, i agree with mr liese who stressed that the directive is not at issue in this case. i agree with him. i think that's a good directive. mr rothley himself said that this directive was the first of its kind in the world and that it had been universally applauded. indeed, when i read paragraph five of the directive, which states that certain processes cannot be considered patentable, it seems to me that the directive is perfectly clear. mr blokland said that the directive was ambiguous and incoherent and the commission would very much like to have a demonstration, evidence to support this statement. mrs gebhardt also said that the cloning of human beings should be banned. but, mr president, it is forbidden. i would draw mrs gebhardt's attention to the fact that the directive specifically prohibits this. i think that is all we have to do, provided, of course, that the directive is properly applied. the last issue i would like to deal with is the community patent. several speakers this morning spoke of european patents. what the european patent office issues is a european patent. the correct term to use is community patent. in other words, it is a single application to the european patent office in munich, which would then grant a community patent valid simultaneously throughout the european union. we're working on it. i would point out to mrs gebhardt and mr de clercq, who have mentioned this subject, that we are doing our utmost to achieve a community patent. this is not easy, mainly because the european patent office is not a community institution. we therefore want the european patent office to act on behalf of the european commission, but not as a community institution. which raises some legal issues that we're trying to resolve. it is quite true that the language problems are considerable. the average cost of a patent is about eur 30 000, which is much higher than in the us, because 40% of this amount is due to language problems - translation costs - and we are trying to control this problem. finally, the commission intends to publish a document before the summer justifying the introduction of a european patent and i look forward to entering into a dialogue with parliament on the content of this document.

in writing. - the delegation of the democrats of the left in the european parliament, which i have the honour of chairing, voted against the stauner report on discharge 1998, because it does not agree with the wording of the substance. the report does not focus on the commission's 1998 acts which are the subject of the discharge exercise - as defined in articles 205a and 206 of the treaty and article 89 (5) of the financial regulation - but it focuses on alleged cases of fraud, most of which date back to the early 1990s, in the context of acts of previous administrations. the prodi commission is involved in a wide-ranging reform effort, which is necessary to modernise european public administration and to adapt its structures to the many challenges it will face in the coming years. we too are convinced of the need to reform the budgetary control procedures and the programme management procedures, systems which have proved inadequate. it is not only necessary to prevent the recurrence of past fraud cases but also, and above all, to ensure that the rate of management errors, as noted by the court of auditors in its annual report, is considerably reduced. however, it is not by seeking to reopen disciplinary proceedings which have now been closed in the absence of new evidence that a serious and effective reform of the commission can be implemented. it should be remembered that 80 per cent of community funds are managed at national level: it is therefore pointless to consider improving the financial management of the european union budget without the involvement and collaboration of the member states. we are also concerned that behind this unjustified relentlessness there is an attempt to use these events to undermine and weaken the actions taken not only by the commission but by the european institutions in general. we cannot therefore associate ourselves with those who promote such actions, and therefore we rejected the report.

the commission shares the concerns expressed in the debate. it regrets iraq's decision not to accept un security council resolution 1284. as mr collins and mr morillon have pointed out, this decision delays the entry into force of the new control instrument and, consequently, the relaxation of the sanctions regime. we believe that the oil-for-food programme remains the best short-term solution to alleviate the suffering of the iraqi people and we believe that the iraqi government must reverse its policy of non-cooperation and comply, as has been said, with all the un security council resolutions. since the gulf war, the community has been the main source of humanitarian aid to iraq. eur 240 million or more was granted to alleviate the considerable suffering of the iraqi people. we could have done more if the iraqi government had not imposed restrictions on the activities of non-governmental organisations which jeopardise the implementation of humanitarian aid programmes in iraq. but let us not be mistaken: humanitarian aid can only mitigate in the short term some of the effects of this terrible economic and human situation. the economic situation in iraq can only be improved by the development of economic activities after the lifting of sanctions, which implies engaging the iraqi government, perhaps more than at present, in a dialogue on the implementation of the security council resolutions. on this point we agree with the draft resolution.

- (it) mr president, i live ten kilometres from milan malpensa airport and have been a member of the flight crew for my entire professional career. so i am very interested in this problem. i must say first of all that many of the problems stem from a lack of planning. airports have been built in a haphazard way and cities - or some of their neighbourhoods - have developed around airport structures without any concrete environmental impact assessment. land planning is a recent development, but airports have been around for decades. let us not forget that the first flights, and malpensa in particular, date back to 1910. of course, there are other structures that disturb the population. i am thinking here of the landfills where people often simply choose an old career, without any other form of planning, but the consequences of airports are seen, or rather heard, every day. furthermore, the information is wrong. i notice, for example, that many point the finger at cargo planes. well, cargo planes are no more noisy than passenger planes. it depends only on the type of aircraft, not its payload. a boeing 747 cargo plane is much quieter than a boeing 727 passenger plane. therefore, a great deal of knowledge is required to make a decision. the legal framework is quite complex. perhaps we are dealing here with the application of the principle of subsidiarity in all its forms, even beyond the european union, because the rules are set by the international civil aviation organisation, a supranational body. i appreciated the commission's intervention when we talked about a european legal framework. for example, we should define - as one of our colleagues has already said - what is meant by 'night'. does the night begin at 10 p.m. or midnight? does it end at 5: 00 or 7: 00 ? that 's something to consider ! the activity of local authorities is another matter, because each airport has its own characteristics. within the same airport, the impact varies according to the runway used. take runway 25 at rome fiumicino airport, which faces the sea and hardly disturbs anyone. if the plane took off from runway 16 straight from the same airport, it would cause disruption to about half a million people living in the conurbation of ostia and fiumicino. the intervention of local authorities - i repeat - in a general european legal framework is therefore essential here. as far as night flights are concerned, i think it is relatively possible to eliminate them, to prohibit them, depending on - i repeat - the local characteristics and the type of aircraft. whether the aircraft is fitted with a silencer or not should not make much difference: the engine decibels are measured and then it is assessed whether the aircraft is silent or not, regardless of the year of manufacture or the type of silencer used. in any case, the problem must be considered as a whole and not on a case-by-case basis.

the rapporteur. - (it) mr president, this draft recommendation is the culmination of a political and institutional process begun almost ten years ago by the then president of the commission, mr delors, which envisaged the swiss confederation's entry into the common european area as early as the beginning of the 1990s. as you all know, this project was blocked by the swiss referendum held in december 1992, in which the swiss people decided to reject, by a very small majority, admittedly, the swiss confederation's entry into the european community. this was the beginning of a period of uncertainty, of agreements largely sectoral, to which this package of seven agreements, strictly related to the economic framework but nevertheless of wide scope and global interest, now puts an end. these are seven agreements on the free movement of persons, air transport, road and rail freight and passenger transport, scientific and technological cooperation, public procurement, agricultural products and mutual recognition of conformity assessment. these agreements are characterized by a precise clause of simultaneity, providing - and this was a just requirement of the european community - that these agreements will not enter into force or not, unless they are all approved or all rejected. that is why, even if draft legislative resolutions are considered separately for technical reasons, they are tabled and approved simultaneously because, as i said, they enter into force simultaneously. the agreements were signed in june 1999, ratified by the swiss parliament on 8 october 1999 and will be submitted to the european parliament for ratification tomorrow. i would nevertheless like to point out to members that once again the swiss people will have to decide on this package of agreements and, therefore, on their relations with the european union in a referendum on 21 may. this is a formally and substantially different approach from that of 1992, and it should be made clear. at that time, the swiss people were called upon to decide on switzerland's accession to the european union; on 21 may the swiss will be called upon to decide whether to approve or reject a package of agreements of a purely economic nature, which does not, of course, have the political implications inherent in the 1992 agreements. i think it is extremely important, however, that parliament should be able to vote, to approve - if that is the indication of this house, as was the substantially unanimous indication of the committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy and of all the parliamentary committees which expressed their opinion - to give its assent before the referendum which will take place in switzerland on 21 may. and this, of course, is not because the sovereignty of the swiss people in voting is weakened in any way, but rather as an additional gesture of confidence and conviction that the development of a common european economic area and the development of an ever greater integration between the markets and economies of this europe - of which switzerland is undoubtedly the heart, one of the certainly central countries - represent a shared interest and are considered to be predominant, also in relation to procedural skirmishes. the fact that parliament has been able to vote before 21 may, thus allowing the swiss citizens to express themselves in a certain and determined legislative framework, is, in my view, an important and positive political fact - and in this respect i must thank the chairman of the committee on industry and services for the efforts they have made possible. the opinion of the committee on industry is entirely favourable and, as such, it is recommended that the house vote in favour at tomorrow's sitting.

proper functioning of the internal market. there is an amendment to that, amendment no 6, and i should like to go into that. as regards amendment no 6, i would say that the commission is not in favour of reintroducing checks at the community's internal frontiers. the single market is now a success and there is no reason to hinder its smooth operation. the commission does agree that the fight against counterfeiting and piracy must be strengthened and improved. but it believes that this objective can be achieved in other ways than by reintroducing internal border controls. the fourtou report contains a number of interesting measures, in particular to strengthen mutual assistance between member states, to impose more severe penalties and to improve civil law measures and procedures. commission. mr president, as you know, counterfeiting and piracy have become a widespread phenomenon with a global impact over the last decade, and this has been acknowledged by several speakers this morning. such activities harm recognised trade and distort competition, in particular when they exploit differences in protection systems in the member states. moreover, criminal organisations are increasingly involved in the trade in counterfeit and pirated goods, which is causing a loss of confidence in the internal market and a drop in investment. the success of the internal market requires excellent report. the reforms in the flax and hemp sectors for fibre production have been under discussion for almost five years now, taking 1996 and the proposals made by the commission at the time
