carefully studied parliament's amendments. many of them are inherently acceptable to us; the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive. unfortunately, we cannot accept some others. the first proposal is the introduction of flax and hemp in the arable crops regulation. on the substance, i am prepared to accept amendment no 2, which concerns the wording of the objectives, and amendment no 1. the idea of doubling the aid to the surface, provided that proof of the transformation of straw into fibres has been provided, seems to me at first sight very attractive, mr graefe zu baringdorf. but in my opinion, it is doomed to failure. we would first of all be creating de facto new incentives for bounty hunting and would have to resort once again to controls which have so far proved ineffective. that is why i do not agree with amendments nos 3, 9, 10 and 12 and, for similar reasons, amendment no 38. in amendment no 4 there are, however, concerns about the provisions on the eligibility of arable land, concerns raised in particular by mr adam and mr wyn. i agree with you that we need a proper solution; i can therefore support amendment no 4 in principle. the same applies to amendment no 37, which goes in the same direction. amendments nos 7, 8 and 15, which concern the exceptions to the arable crops regulation as regards arable land and freezing of land, are acceptable in so far as they are in line with the agenda 2000 agreement, but only in this context. in my view, they are no longer necessary at all, since there are areas within arable land where flax and hemp can be grown without limiting other crops. however, there may be some problems in certain areas. we are trying to find a solution to reduce the constraints that may arise. i can accept amendment no 6 on hemp. however, we cannot simply abolish controls on so-called illegal crops, as amendments nos 5 and 16 suggest, at least implicitly: i cannot support these amendments. however, a certain degree of flexibility could be provided for in cases where a high level of control is required. i would therefore be prepared to accept these amendments, at least on this point, as well as amendment no 14. because of the image risks of hemp, the commission is proposing a ban on the use of hemp and fenugreek in food products, although the species to be used in our country do not contain any psychotropic substances. it is a highly political issue, which can certainly still be debated. at the present stage, however, i am not prepared to accept amendments nos 11, 13 and 32. but the objective itself is clear. i come now to the second proposal, on the regulation on the common organization of the market in flax and hemp for fibre production. the processing aid must be reasonably proportionate to the production costs and must take into account the market value of the products. processing aid for long fibre flax generates higher costs. it must therefore be differentiated from the aid for short flax fibre and hemp fibre. the maximum legal level of impurities must also be fixed; the aid must encourage the production of high-quality fibres and not the presence of waste in the fibres. the policy of the sector must be clear. we can only accept investments in products which are profitable on market terms. the same principle applies here. that is why i cannot accept amendments nos 18 and 34, even though they would be very thought-provoking. i agree, however, with the considerations underlying amendments nos 23, 25 and 26, namely a reconciliation between the amounts of aid and the granting of aid according to the results of the checks. however, the limits set by the budget may not be exceeded. the second important issue concerns the national guaranteed quantities. in view of the well-known difficulties in controlling the results of the harvest, they are absolutely essential. the commission proposal reduces the risk of abuse at the processing stage, without the need to set quotas for the various processing undertakings and therefore without the inconvenience that such quotas would entail for an expanding market. a guaranteed maximum threshold for the whole of the community cannot be a solution. experience shows that this only leads to conflicts between member states and makes it difficult to find a genuine solution. the annual allocation of the maximum guaranteed quantities between member states, based on their uncontrolled processing capacities, is really not a realistic alternative. that is why i cannot accept amendments nos 20, 21, 27 to 30 and 35. nevertheless, i find the idea of introducing some sort of quotas for newcomers and of distributing them annually among member states which currently produce little or no flax and hemp to be extremely interesting. i can accept amendments nos 24 and 33 in cases where the operators and the first processors are the same. as regards the import of hemp and fenugreek, i agree that we should find a workable solution. however, i cannot agree to amendments nos 22 and 31 in their present form, because they imply the abolition of all controls. finally, as regards the timetable, i am also prepared to accept amendments nos 17 and 36, according to which the new rules must not enter into force until 1 july 2001. however, the area aid should be fixed this year for the next marketing year, in accordance with the regulations in force. in that case i would be bound by the figures in the 2001 budget. reform of this sector is absolutely necessary! i think you agree with me. we must orientate the 'flax and hemp for fibre' sector towards the market, so that it can make an effective, indisputable and useful contribution to the national economy and no longer be publicly criticised. in these circumstances, i think it would be important for you to vote on the resolution this week, so that the council can also take a decision as soon as possible. in this way we will be able to avoid the market disturbances that would occur in the 2000-2001 financial year if the aid amount were not fixed by 1 august. i can still accept 13 amendments, as i have already said. i have also expressly stated that i cannot accept many of the amendments in their present form, but that they are a matter for reflection, including in the debates i intend to initiate in the council. however, since the market disturbances will be really serious if we do not have adequate regulation in time, we should take interim protective measures, for which the budgetary forecasts for 2001 are to be taken into account, or we will have a harvest without the producers knowing what aid they may receive. we really cannot allow such a situation to occur. it would simply be impossible to explain to the producers and to the processors that they have to do this because we have not been able to take a decision on a proposal which has been under consideration in this house for eight months already.

- (it) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european union is facing a whole series of challenges arising from globalisation and the birth of a new economy based on knowledge and new technologies. the union's strategic objective for the coming decade must be to promote economic growth and free enterprise without breaking the social question through policies based on competitiveness, sustainable development and the creation of new jobs. on the latter point - as the katiforis report points out - there has been a slight decline in unemployment in europe, but it still remains at unacceptable levels, especially among women and young people. the situation is even more dramatic in some regions of southern europe and particularly in southern italy, where jobseekers represent no less than 21.9% of the working population and 56.6% of the 14-25 year olds. the main guidelines for economic growth and employment should therefore, in my view, include certain measures to improve the competitiveness of the european market and to introduce greater flexibility in work. sustainable growth will require the completion of the internal market and the removal of existing barriers by liberalizing sectors which are not yet fully open to free competition, such as transport, gas, electricity and postal services. the reforms which the member states will have to implement to reduce the burden on business, to reduce the cost of labour, to support actions to help lifelong training in a knowledge-based economy, to promote research so that europe can bridge the gap between the united states and japan, will have to be pursued. support will be needed for structural reforms of public administration in countries where excessive bureaucratization is an obstacle to private investment, and for adapting social protection and taxation systems to the requirements of the new economic rules and the constraints of the stability and growth pact.

the commission is aware of the fact that the commission has not yet adopted a proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos. in particular, i thank parliament for its support for the commission's initiative and i am pleased that it is supporting the efforts to increase transparency in the use of public money in order to ensure fair competition. you welcomed the fact that the commission wanted to consult parliament, even though it was not obliged to do so from an institutional point of view, as mr jonckheer and other speakers have pointed out. in addition, the way in which this debate has developed confirms my view that this consultation has been useful to the commission and to the successful completion of this initiative. the transparency directive, as it stands, gives the commission the power to investigate financial relations between member states and their public undertakings. in summary, the proposed amendment to the directive is intended to ensure the introduction of separate accounting for specific types of undertakings. the undertakings concerned by such a measure are those which, on the one hand, provide services of general economic interest, in return for which they receive compensation of all kinds, which may consist of special duties or payments, and, on the other hand, carry on normal business activities and thus compete with other companies. it is clear that the revenues generated by the pursuit of reserved activities or by payments granted for reasons of general interest or public service are not intended to finance competitive activities and cannot therefore give rise to internal subsidies. in recent years, however, the commission has had to deal with an increasing number of complaints concerning such internal compensation. in the course of its investigations, ms peijs recalled, the commission had to study these cases of internal compensation and often failed to obtain adequate information on the costs and revenues of the various activities. the commission is therefore now proposing that separate accounts be introduced for this type of undertaking, so that it can properly fulfil its duties as a guarantor of competition. i would also like to emphasize that the obligation to keep separate accounts is a useful instrument for the member states as well, because it provides them with the information necessary to comply with the obligation not to grant state aid incompatible with the treaty and to notify planned aid to the commission. the directive requires separate accounts for undertakings which provide services of general interest and which, at the same time, are active beyond this public service mission. this provision applies equally to private and public undertakings. it does not cover companies which only provide services of general interest without carrying out any other activities and does not impose a separation between the various activities which all fall within the definition of a service of general interest. in other words, ladies and gentlemen, the directive seeks to clarify the area where the boundary between services of general interest and other activities is drawn by means of transparency. it wants to do this by causing as little trouble as possible in order to allow for this transparency. i would like to stress that the directive does not, of course, alter the provisions of the treaty on the award of services of general interest, nor does it alter the award of management of these services to certain undertakings. the directive lays down the principles for greater transparency, while leaving the member states free, under the principle of subsidiarity, to adopt appropriate national measures. i now come to the remarks that have been made. mr jonckheer wonders what can be said about internet access, whether it should be included in the universal service or not. i can only remind you that the last telecommunications council discussed this. as regards the doubts expressed by the rapporteur, mrs randzio-plath, i should like to briefly review them. as regards the definition of services of general interest, i would like to reiterate that the directive does not in any way alter or reduce the current competence of the member states - mrs berès, mr langen - to define the public interest. this is also true in the public broadcasting sector, for which the amsterdam protocol reaffirmed the competence of the member states for this definition. mrs maes and mr berès, mr jonckheer, mr crowley and mr skinner objected that perhaps this area could be excluded. i have to say that this sector could be one of the areas where the transparency directive will be most applicable and most useful because, while taking account of the amsterdam protocol, it leaves the commission the task of verifying that the performance of the public service function is not overcompensated in relation to its cost. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the directive is implemented. there is no question of the size of the companies. i am referring to mr langen and other members: the threshold of eur 40 million excludes small and mediumsized enterprises. increasing this threshold would exclude undertakings where, certainly because of their size, it cannot be assumed that the aid has no impact on trade between member states. however, to give an idea of the magnitude, only 0.2% of all non-agricultural enterprises in the community exceed this threshold. finally, i would like to point out - and i think the members have understood this perfectly well - that this directive is not an attack on public undertakings. on the contrary, i regard it - to be honest - as a great ally of public service. why would you do that ? because it allows the light to shine and therefore does not expose the public service to attacks that would otherwise be unleashed. this transparency - as mr olle schmidt has emphasized - is not only essential for the proper application of competition policy, but - let me say this - it is even vital for maintaining proper relations between public authorities and taxpayers, the citizens. i therefore believe that this directive, which appears to be very boring, as mrs peijs has called it, actually allows us to touch on a very important point, not only of competition but also of civil coexistence and economic democracy.

commission. - (sv) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am pleased with the outcome reached by the european parliament and the council on this important issue. i commend the two institutions for the intensive efforts they have made to reach agreement on the many technical aspects of this complex regulation. we have worked hard to find this compromise and to ensure that we have effective environmental legislation in this area. i would like to take this opportunity to thank in particular the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, the european parliament's delegation to the conciliation committee and, in particular, the rapporteur, mrs hulthén, for their thorough and constructive work. the new text provides for a series of measures to minimise emissions of substances responsible for the destruction of the ozone layer. the most important complementary measures are those aimed at reducing the production and use of hcfcs, stopping the production and consumption of methyl bromide by 2004, banning the use of materials such as cfcs and halogens, the production of which is already prohibited, stricter rules for the handling of substances that deplete the ozone layer, stricter requirements for the training of the personnel concerned, an obligation to recycle or destroy these substances, and improved control and licensing criteria. the adoption of this provision will lead to the elimination of the substances concerned in the european union, which will take place more rapidly than the montreal protocol allowed. this not only means improvements in the health of the union's citizens, but also means that the eu is taking the lead in global policy on this important issue. i would also like to answer the question that was asked earlier. i'll answer in english.

the various operators, which opens up legal fronts which all still need to be verified.
commission. - mr president, i should first like to thank mrs thors for her excellent work. the commission welcomes its report. it raises the question of the need for a balanced approach to regulation. we must balance two things: first, trade freedom and investment incentives, and second, the protection of the public interest defined in a targeted and proportionate way. the new regulatory framework will provide the legislator with much more flexibility to achieve this balance. the guidelines which the commission will propose this month take account of the three key points raised in mrs thors' report. first, the previous regulations on digital television must be updated. the new framework will allow the legislator to address new gateways such as application programming interfaces. secondly, the report supports a limitation of the rebroadcasting obligations imposed on public service broadcasters, as defined in protocol 32 annexed to the treaty. the report also stresses that there should be negotiations to balance the revenues of operators against the value of public service channels to operators. the commission will address these issues in its future legislative proposals. thirdly, we need to increase interoperability between different television platforms. the report specifically identifies two key elements. first, the need for interoperability where possible and access rules under which exclusive standards contribute significant market power; and secondly, the need to define a new, open decoder architecture, the home multimedia platform. the commission prefers an industry initiative rather than imposing standards. we have reserve powers to intervene if the market players do not agree. however, the market is developing open standards. in dynamic markets, the standardisation process lags behind the state of the art. the use of open standards reduces regulation and the number of competition cases. the report sends this very clear message to the markets. i fully support that. the report also raises a number of issues of substance which therefore go beyond the scope of the new framework for electronic communications. we must separate the rules on the network and the rules on content as much as possible. the reception of cross-border digital coded television services raises several sensitive issues. firstly, copyright is already badly abused: pay-tv services buy the rights for one member state only. even the front desk is coded. this creates tensions with the principles of the single market in pay-tv services. the deferral of the content approach to regulation may also play a role. but i have to discuss this with my colleagues, mrs reding and mr bolkestein, who have specific expertise in this area.

relationship with the european parliament, both in plenary and in committees. it is in this spirit that she is presenting her vision of the feira european council to the plenary. let me make a first reference to the programme as it stands at the moment. on 19th morning, there will be the usual meeting with the president of the european parliament, followed by a meeting with the president of the convention, roman herzog, who is responsible for drafting the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. as is fitting, this is not a meeting for deliberations, the charter is being drawn up according to the methodology that has been chosen, but it is an exchange of information which we consider necessary at this stage, on the one hand, so that president roman herzog can inform the heads of state and government of the progress of the convention's work on the drafting of the charter, and, on the other hand, so that the sensitivity of the various heads of state and government can be imbued with this problem. but it will not be a deliberative meeting, as it obviously cannot be. it is mainly an exchange of information. the european council will then hold a working session with the participation of the finance ministers, which will cover the follow-up to the extraordinary european council in lisbon and economic and financial issues. the lunch will be devoted to the intergovernmental conference and, more specifically, to enhanced cooperation. the council will have to indicate whether these are on the agenda of the conference or not. the afternoon session will be devoted to the issues of enlargement of the union, the common european security and defence policy and external relations. i would point out that the presidency has sent an invitation to the president of south africa, mr thabo mbeki, to join us at that time and that we can also discuss the subject of relations between the european union and africa and political issues of regional significance. we be devoted, as is the tradition, to the revision of the draft conclusions of the presidency. the council thus has an opportunity to take stock of the progress made during the six-month period in areas to which we attach particular importance. in this way we will try to ensure the continuity of european integration and deepening, facilitating as far as possible the resolution of the many issues that await us in the near future in the framework of the european agenda. since i do not have time to describe in detail the issues to be dealt with at feira, i should like to mention a few of them which are of priority for us and which deserve our full attention. the intergovernmental conference will be brought to the attention of the council by the presentation of a report by the presidency. the report is already ready, it was formally handed to the president yesterday and will be available today in all languages on the internet. as you know, this parliament has participated with great interest and collaboration in the work of the intergovernmental conference, and the contribution of this institution is remarkable and represents a qualitative step forward compared to all previous intergovernmental conferences devoted to the reform of the institutions and the treaties. the presidency's report is essentially in two separate parts: the first deals with the evaluation of the progress made by the conference so far and describes the trends that will emerge from the discussions, and the second deals with a set of proposals, lists and tables illustrating the options that the intergovernmental conference will present in the next six months. i would like to emphasise that, in the exercise of the mandate given to us during the presidency in helsinki, and after the analysis of the member states, we recommend that the issue of enhanced cooperation be included in the agenda of the conference. i am convinced that, on the basis of the work done, we will be able to conclude, with the french presidency, the intergovernmental conference at the end of this year, as planned. as regards the development of the common european security and defence policy, i believe that, also on the basis of the report we will submit to the european council, significant progress has been made. i would mention the creation and launch of new civilian and political-military crisis management bodies for the first time in the history of the european union, and the approval of the regulations on relations between the european union and nato, and the european union and certain third states. the rapporteur. - (it) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism has examined the tenth annual report of the european commission on the structural funds, on the implementation of assistance in 1998. you know that sound and efficient implementation of the structural funds is of fundamental importance for the credibility and efficiency of the community institutions and, in particular, of the european parliament, given its supervisory functions. in our report, which was unanimously approved, we noted that the resources made available for 1998 had been fully used up, but we had to note that there were still considerable differences in implementation between the various member states and regions, and that this full use was only possible thanks to compensation mechanisms which in fact made it transparent. we therefore hope that the new programming rules, which are now in force, will make it possible to guarantee more transparent budgetary management and to avoid the usual annual cash bottlenecks. as regards coordination, we call on the commission and the member states to coordinate more closely the policy of the structural funds with the cohesion fund, the other regional development instruments and the various financial instruments of the european union, such as the transeuropean networks and the european space development scheme. we are convinced that the structural differences between the regions and the zones of europe can only be reduced by coordinated action. as regards additionality, one of the fundamental principles of the structural funds, we call on the commission to find as soon as possible the instruments which can better control it and more transparent procedures for assessing it. we urge the member states to apply this principle rigorously. we also believe that, in accordance with the principle of partnership, decentralisation of management must be accompanied by an explanation of the responsibilities and role of the various partners and a clear distinction between the various functions and responsibilities. we also found that the results of mid-term evaluations were often not comparable and quantifiable due to the use of inadequate and insufficient indicators, which is why we need to have more objective criteria and better evaluation methods to measure the results of the programmes. secondly, we found that the control missions carried out under the regulation in 1998, although inexplicably and dangerously reduced in number compared to the previous year, had revealed a whole series of shortcomings, ranging from the absence of control systems in certain programmes to the co-financing of ineligible expenditure. this led us to believe that the commission's control activities in 1998 were unfortunately still unsatisfactory and that they needed to be adequately reinforced in order to ensure the proper application of the structural funds regulations. in our report we therefore call on the european commission and the member states to adopt as soon as possible a series of measures aimed at both intensifying controls and better informing parliament of the measures adopted to increase transparency and the proper implementation of the structural funds. since this tenth annual report was devoted in particular to measures to promote local development, we have noted their strategic importance and emphasize their considerable contribution to regional development. finally, commissioner, i would like to emphasize that our report is in line with the view you expressed in brussels on 5 june last, that for the sake of transparency, the last of the european taxpayers should know where and how community resources relating to the structural funds are spent. i leave it to you to assess whether a commission report, such as the one for 1998, can enable not just the last but any european taxpayer to satisfy your wishes. mr president, let me conclude by giving my opinion on seven amendments which we shall be voting on friday. i myself tabled a technical amendment, the third, to correct a transcription error which could have caused confusion and made paragraph 28 inconsistent with the rest of the report. i also accept amendments nos 1 and 2 because they are in line with the report. i cannot accept amendments nos 4, 5, 6 and 7 because they are, in my view, excessive compared with the rest of our report. i would like to thank the authors of these last amendments, mr nogueira and mr ortuondo larrea, and i publicly welcome the consistency of their position, even if i do not share it.

the rapporteur. - (it) mr president, article 13 of the regulation establishing the european monitoring centre for drugs and drug addiction provides for the possibility for third countries which share the interests of the community and its member states to participate in the work of the centre. following norway's request to participate, the commission submitted to the european parliament a draft agreement between the observatory and norway, which allows norway to participate in the reitox network and to be represented on the observatory's management board and scientific committee. in this connection, the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs unanimously approved eight amendments which give a favourable opinion, but with conditions: our opinion, which was mainly conditioned by the evaluation report of the observatory, requested by the same committee to an independent and external consultancy firm. the external evaluation found that the observatory suffered from a lack of coordination and communication between its various departments and from excessive centralisation of decisions. it also shows that the reitox network is not a true network, that the national relays are not used enough when they could contribute more to the work of the observatory, that the role of the scientific committee is still unclear and its contribution is not central to the programme, that the board of directors is not effective in achieving its objectives - its agenda planning is poor, its meetings do not allow for real strategic discussions - that there is no strategy for disseminating the material produced and that, therefore, only a small part of the information produced by the observatory is published and disseminated. it also points out that, as regards work planning, the management coordination of the director and heads of department is inadequate, that administrative procedures are costly and not appropriate for such a small organisation, with the obvious problems this causes in terms of administration, management, planning, evaluation, development, recruitment and training capacity; whereas the current balance sheet should be revised so that the real costs of activities can be traced; the commission has also been concerned that too much of the staff and funds are being spent on the purely administrative operation of the observatory. these are the assessments of the independent external consultancy company to which the european commission has entrusted the work. it is on the basis of these assessments that we should decide today whether or not norway can join the work, which is completely inconsistent with the mandate and the real capacity for action. however, our committee unanimously considered that the draft agreement between norway and the observatory, as well as the proposal for a council regulation to adapt the observatory's rules to the possible participation of the applicant countries in the work of the observatory, represented an opportunity to underline the need for a thorough revision of the observatory's rules in order to ensure their effectiveness and reliability. i expect a concrete response from the commission on the amendments adopted by the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs.

the rapporteur, mr president, after directive 98/71/ec on the legal protection of designs, we must now assess and take a decision on the proposal for a regulation, which is of course defined in the framework of the directive. this proposal therefore contains both the dark and the bright areas of this directive on such a conflicting, competitive subject, and where many interests are at stake. the directive, in the final analysis, has eliminated part of this subject, the part of complex products, in order to allow for repair. i am referring to the famous repair clause, spare parts: the very complex and articulated world of the automobile industry. the committee has worked very carefully - i thank its chairman in particular - although in the end a rather conservative and cautious view and interpretation has prevailed. we did not want to go any further until the directive was completed by three years of observation on the above-mentioned subject. on the other hand, the regulation has the power to define the community design of products, registered and unregistered designs and manufactured products: the proposal to use the single trade mark office at community level also for designs and models, and therefore an exclusive right of protected use at community level, with a few exceptions. this clearly goes against the basic requirement of the single market and against a unified discipline on the subject of nullity, refusal and the possibility of use, and above all on two very significant terms: that of novelty, which is linked to disclosure, and that of individuality, linked to creativity. these are two aspects of a very fascinating world which naturally requires protection but also flexibility. that is why i insist in particular on a minimum number of amendments which, in the whole of the protection between the community design and copyright - i entrust the european parliament with the task of making a modern but above all realistic assessment of the complex world of designs - do not block the monopoly situation. i would therefore say that if we were to set, as amendment no 23 provides - and i will go into more detail if necessary - a ceiling of 25 years for the protection of registered designs, that ceiling would be sufficient. on the other hand, the directive does not allow us to have contraindications. according to the directive, member states must be able to allow the combination of the community design and copyright. it should be remembered that copyright in many countries lasts up to 70 years. so if we add 25 and 70, we end up with a blocked average product which often - and let's say, by its very nature, its novelty and its creativity - cannot last that long, not beyond the life span of a man, which is why it seems to me that 25 years is enough. i therefore take the liberty of insisting that this moderation of requirements should at least be put in place and that community europe, the single market, should be given such an important role, especially for small and mediumsized enterprises, where the productivity of designs, models and imagination - which for european countries naturally represents a plus in terms of employment - fits perfectly into this network of rights and freedoms. i believe that this proposal for a regulation, which opens the way to a unified system with uniform protection throughout the community, nevertheless contains the limits and restrictions which i wanted to stress, by way of correction also in relation to my colleagues; the european union is a great example of this and it is indeed an important objective for the way we build europe.

the rapporteur. - (it) mr president, the right to the confidentiality of personal data is a fundamental right in the european union, but the market interests in the free movement of data are also legitimate. to ensure a balance between these requirements, directive 46 of 1995 provides for a series of standards which the member states must transpose - and have done so - into their national legislation, and the establishment of an independent authority to ensure that these standards are met in accordance with the principle of self-determination in the field of information, that is to say, that everyone must have the possibility of authorising or prohibiting the processing of his personal data, and to whom and for what purpose. in addition to recourse to the guaranteeing authority, provision has therefore been made for the right to legal recourse in the event of infringement of rights enshrined in law. for the transfer of data to third countries, it is necessary to ensure that these countries ensure an adequate level of protection. if such protection is not ensured, it is possible to transfer such data under appropriate contractual clauses. the council of europe is currently studying general contractual clauses to facilitate agreements with countries which do not guarantee this legal protection. the adequacy of protection in the third country is monitored by the european commission, which commits the member states to harmonise their legislation. today, these problems do not arise when the third country has data protection laws, as is currently the case in switzerland and hungary, and the european parliament has no reason to intervene. the case of the united states of america is different in that there is no general legislation on the protection of personal data. the commission has therefore sought a solution in the negotiations with the us department of commerce to allow the transfer of data to private companies which voluntarily submit to a self-regulatory system known as the 'safe harbour'. on 6 june the european commission sent us the documents relating to the conclusions which it considers to constitute adequate protection. the committee of representatives of the member states gave a favourable opinion, but the committee of the supervisory authorities of the member states expressed some reservations. some of the concerns raised by the committee of supervisors can be considered to have been resolved by the clarifications provided by the commission, for example on the scope of the system. however, several issues remain open, in particular a fundamental one, namely the imposition of measures, i.e. ensuring that the undertakings of the safe harbour companies are respected. because there is no law or contract, individuals cannot assert their rights before a judge. there are forms of safe harbour control and sanctioning, but only in the case of unfair or fraudulent practices subject to the discretion of the federal trade commission. there is also the possibility of applying for dispute resolution to private bodies chosen by the data controller, but there is no right of appeal for the person who considers that he has been wronged. it may be thought that the safe harbour system only guarantees a proper level of protection under article 25 of the directive if effective protection is ensured for european citizens whose rights are violated, i.e. the possibility of obtaining the erasure of illegally processed data, the compensation for damages suffered through recourse to a court, arbitrator or other independent third party with this task. the resolution also calls for data to be transferred only when the system is fully operational and for its application to be monitored. we do not want the united states to change its system, even though there are many voices calling for legislation on this matter, but only that european citizens be properly protected, as european consumer associations demand and as american consumers would like. this is the meaning of the resolution before you, which i ask you to approve, so that in this delicate area an international model is not introduced which offers fewer guarantees and which other countries might be tempted to apply, but above all so that the european parliament can prove that it defends the rights of citizens, rights which are guaranteed to them by community legislation.
- (it) mr president, we fully endorse mrs paciotti's report and share its conclusions. with the 'safe harbour' agreement, we would have a transfer of data to us companies, corporations and firms without any possibility of recourse to an independent authority in the event of improper or illegal use, which would cancel out the minimum guarantees we enjoy within the union. during the hearing in the committee on civil liberties, we heard the complaints of the representatives of american consumers about the inadequacy of the protection system in their country and we took note of the need, expressed by president clinton himself, for the united states to adopt organic legislation on the protection of personal data. in approving this report, we are not only reflecting the political will to reach an agreement containing safeguard clauses which respect european law, but we are also encouraging a large part of the american public and congress to develop a range of legislation on this subject. without such a system and without the changes called for in the paciotti report, it would be more appropriate to call the agreement with the united states an 'insecurity zone'.

in writing. - (i) we welcome the process of liberalization under way in the sector, because we are convinced that the creation of a large european market offers great opportunities for growth and improvement. we share the council's common position because it represents a balance which marks a new stage in the opening up of the railway market, pending provisions guaranteeing balanced intra- and inter-modal competition. the railway activity is the result of a permanent and technically strong assembly of activities carried out by different actors - infrastructure managers, railway undertakings, station managers, etc. - who have varied functions. if economic efficiency requires, these actors can alternate between the role of infrastructure manager and railway undertaking. there is no indication that complete separation will improve the system in terms of openness, efficiency or safety. total separation is not a necessary condition for the opening of the railway market in the european single market. the existence of undertakings performing both infrastructure management and railway undertaking functions does not preclude such opening, as transparent and non-discriminatory procedures are implemented and controlled by an independent regulator. in addition, the integrated undertaking is generally better placed to develop new technologies for both the infrastructure manager and the railway undertaking. a railway undertaking which directs its decisions towards the technical and economic optimum is in a position to implement the necessary innovations quickly and to assume responsibility for the investment risk. the railway system is a technically diverse system which requires a high degree of coordination in all cases, whatever the chosen organisational solution. safety is certainly better guaranteed when the management of the railway system is entrusted to an integrated undertaking, because: - the undertaking controls all the elements of the system and their interactions; - it benefits from more complete and faster feedback on events concerning the system; - it offers the authorities the security of a single person responsible for the safety of the system. respect for the principles of fairness and transparency in capacity allocation or pricing is essential, but it is not certain that the separation system is adapted to best ensure respect for these principles. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the railway system is not disrupted by the introduction of new technologies. the railway authority provided for in the council's common position would thus be able to supervise competition in rail transport more effectively and more extensively, in addition to the existing state supervision bodies. finally, as regards the derogation, i fully agree with the view put forward by my colleague, mr collins.

commission. - mr president, i should like first of all to thank the members for the keen interest they have shown in this matter and, in particular, mr arvidsson, the rapporteur, for the continuous and constructive efforts he has made to find a solution acceptable to all. the commission has also made considerable efforts to find a solution to the phthalates problem. after discussing the risks of pvc toys containing phthalates and hearing the opinion of the scientific committee on toxicity, ecotoxicity and the environment, the commission took two decisions last autumn. the first provided for a temporary emergency ban, renewable every three months. the second concerned a proposal for a directive to restrict the marketing and use of phthalates in soft pvc toys. all the speeches in this parliament have been on the first decision, not necessarily the proposal for a directive. the commission's proposed directive has two parts. the first concerns the prohibition of the use of six phthalates in toys intended for use by young children. the ban is based on the opinion of the scientific committee that toys containing certain phthalates pose a risk to the health of children when they are placed in the mouth for long periods of time. since it cannot be ruled out that children may put other toys in their mouths, which are not necessarily intended for this purpose, the proposal calls for a warning label to be applied to other toys which may be placed in the mouth. this proposal is not only about protecting children's health but also about the internal market. the internal market is currently fragmented, with more than half of the member states applying national bans which go beyond the emergency ban decided by the commission under the general product safety directive. mrs jackson asked whether the member states had provided scientific evidence to the commission. the answer is: not to my knowledge. the proposal for a directive would harmonise the regulations in force in the member states. i have noted in today's debate that members are divided on this commission proposal. some consider it too strict, others feel that it does not provide sufficient protection. the proposal is based on the various opinions of the scientific committee, applies the precautionary principle and is therefore a proportionate measure. it introduces a ban on products which could present the greatest risks, namely toys intended to be placed in the mouth, and a less stringent measure - labelling - for products not intended for this purpose, but where the possibility of a risk cannot be excluded. the commission cannot accept parliament's amendments which would extend the scope of the ban to cover plasticisers other than the six phthalates mentioned or toys other than those intended to be placed in the mouth. the commission cannot accept amendments which would extend the scope of the ban to include toys for older children. we believe that these various proposals cannot be justified on the basis of the risks, whether they are defined in the opinions of the scientific committee or in application of the precautionary principle. the commission cannot accept amendments which introduce migration limit values, but it can accept amendments which provide for a revision of these values as soon as test methods have been approved. the commission can accept, in principle, amendments which would prohibit the use of flavouring substances in toys intended for children under three years of age and containing the six phthalates mentioned. it may also accept amendments which would advance the review of the directive and broaden the scope of that review. to sum up our view, the commission can accept, at least in principle, amendments nos 2, 4, 5, 9, 10, 11, 18 and 24 and it rejects amendments nos 1, 3, 6, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23 and 25. we want to continue the dialogue with parliament and i am confident that we can reach a constructive solution.

commission - (de) mr president, on behalf of the commission, i should like to give answers on the five subjects raised. i would therefore like to say briefly that, as far as human rights issues are concerned, the commission's foreign policy continues to be aimed at avoiding conflict and human rights violations and at promoting democracy and human rights. where there are violent conflicts and human rights abuses, we are determined to use all the opportunities at our disposal to positively influence conflict resolution and support for democracy and human rights, whether through dialogue, diplomatic action, economic cooperation or assistance to those countries. this is particularly true of the conflicts we are discussing today - in uganda, sudan and indonesia. as far as the death penalty in the usa is concerned, i would just like to say that nothing has changed, unfortunately. the position of the european union is and remains unchanged. according to our european catalogue of values, the death penalty is a barbaric act that is not justified by anything. that is why we are continuing our efforts to achieve a worldwide abolition of the death penalty. the debate which has just been opened in the united states is to be welcomed. it shows very clearly that a key argument for our opposition to the death penalty is beginning to take effect in the us, namely that the death penalty is not worthy of a state of law, because a mistake in judgment can no longer be corrected. we have learned that many trials have resulted in the execution of innocent people. as regards iraq, i would say that the commission is of the opinion that saddam hussein and his regime are solely responsible for the appalling conditions in that country. the situation could change overnight if the regime were prepared to fully meet the demands of the international community, which it had promised to meet partially. unfortunately, the iraqi regime must always be considered as a regime capable of destroying not only the peace and stability of an entire region but also world peace. that is why the lifting of sanctions can only be achieved by full implementation of the security council resolutions, and the iraqi regime is well aware of that. the european union is endeavouring to take account of the humanitarian consequences of this policy and to provide assistance where possible. that said, all members of this house are also aware that the oil for food programme suffers from certain shortcomings for which the iraqi regime is once again responsible. that is why we are also active in iraq through our echo programme. i would like to say a little more about the subject which is being discussed for the first time in this parliament, namely the question of hooliganism and football. the commission welcomes the importance which parliament attaches to the fight against hooliganism at football matches, as reflected in the various motions for resolutions in question. for several years, member states and the commission have been working towards closer cooperation in this area, which has resulted in several joint measures. for example, there are common standards for stadium security, common standards for screening fans, sending police officers abroad to work with the police in the host country. there is also an exchange of information. another important instrument is the handbook adopted by the council in june 1999 on police cooperation and preventive measures against violence at international football matches. this manual contains the rules of police conduct which were first used in the netherlands and belgium at euro 2000. euro 2000 will provide many useful lessons on how to improve the fight against hooliganism. a belgian-dutch project co-financed by the european union under the police and customs cooperation programme is completing the scientific evaluation. the evaluation of police intervention at euro 2000 could be used for similar events in the future. this is particularly important for germany, which was awarded the hosting of the 2006 fifa world cup. the commission wants to wait for the results of this project before making concrete proposals to improve the current measures. however, it is already clear that at eu level we must agree on a travel ban for convicted hooligans for high-risk football matches and that we must find a way to effectively combat fighting at sporting events to ensure that football really remains a game - as one member of the assembly has said. in this connection, i would like to remind you that, in the context of their cooperation in the fields of justice and home affairs, the netherlands and belgium are planning to submit proposals for additional measures to combat hooliganism at football matches. however, this work is still at an early stage. the lessons of euro 2000 will give rise to practical contacts between the commission and these two countries.

commission - (de) mr president, the commission has received almost 40 different comments on the discussion paper 'the commission and non-governmental organisations: strengthening the partnership'. these comments are published on its website and on the europa server. various working groups in the directorates-general with the most frequent contacts with ngos are currently working on further developing the reflections in the document on the basis of these comments. these working groups are now focusing on the issue of operating grants and on measures to improve consultation of ngos. this last point should be addressed by developing guidelines for effective consultation practices, as already provided for in the white paper on commission reform, measure 4. the court's judgment in case c 106/96 and the interinstitutional agreement of 13 october 1998 on legal bases have modified the conditions for financing non-governmental organisations with a social character. in addition, the new financing rules must be strictly respected for all programmes and budget lines. as a result, organisations that have been funded so far will now only receive further financial support if they meet the conditions set out in the decisions on certain action programmes, which will form the legal basis for the various budget lines. subject to approval by the council or the council and parliament, the two programmes could therefore be co-financed as from 2001. as the commission's proposals indicate, the rules of the vade-mecum and the procedures for granting operating subsidies should be respected. a limited number of networks of ngos and platforms at european level, experienced in the fight against discrimination and social exclusion, would then benefit from support, as the two programmes i have mentioned deal with discrimination or exclusion. the criteria for deciding which organisations will be supported should be established in agreement with the programme committee concerned. the commission will then approve the annual grants, using detailed work and funding plans. the 1999 vade-mecum for the management of financial aid has already been hailed by ngos as a step forward. the conditions laid down therein should be incorporated in due course in the financial regulation and its implementing provisions. the commission is fully aware of the importance of promoting civil dialogue and attaches great value to collaboration with non-governmental organisations, especially in the social field. in recent years, the creation of various european networks and the european platform of social ngos has made it possible to finance many projects of ngos active in the social field. the two programmes proposed by the commission - combating discrimination and social exclusion - should cover the bulk of the management costs of ngos operating at european level in the social sector. the commission also believes that civil society within the european union is very important. there are indeed a number of actions in different fields - social, environment, training, development, agriculture, etc. - which have led to the establishment of a close partnership relationship, as was emphasised in the working document on the commission and ngos, adopted on 18 january 2000. increased citizen involvement and new forms of partnership with civil society are among the commission's main priorities. this was clearly set out in the commission document 'commission's strategic objectives 2000-2005'. in line with these priorities, the president and several members of the commission have on many occasions expressed the importance they attach to civil dialogue. the above guidelines for effective consultation practices would be a first step in this direction. the president of the commission intends to address civil dialogue in the context of the white paper on 'strengthening democracy in europe'. the white paper will be published before the end of next year. as regards the the rapporteur. - (it) mr president, the framework decision presented by the council merely copies the 1998 council of europe convention on the fight against environmental crime, which has not yet been ratified by any council of europe member country. this proposal for a framework decision is only intended to speed up the pace, at least for the 15 member states. almost all our countries have environmental protection legislation based mainly on very modest fines, which encourages environmental destroyers to maximize profits by trying not to use all modern environmental protection techniques. in recent years, for example, we have seen serious disasters such as the sinking of the erika, which was nothing more than a sea-going barge used to transport crude, or the pollution of the danube by cyanide from the romanian mine, all because the big companies who are responsible know that they are protected by a kind of impunity which ensures them enormous profits. this framework decision allows european countries to increase fines in order to make this offence - the environmental offence - uneconomic. as long as the cost is borne by the community and not by the culprits alone, we have no hope of protecting the environment effectively. this framework decision is also important in that it encourages european countries to adopt penalties or at least a system of criminal liability for legal persons. few european states have this responsibility of legal persons in their penal code, but some are moving in this direction. in its new penal code, italy intends to insert the responsibility of legal entities, especially since today, major environmental offences are not committed by isolated individuals but by large multinational companies which, because they do not invest in prevention, cause incalculable damage. i believe that european countries should soon adopt a relatively common discipline and, in any case, review the penalties upwards and ensure that the cost of these offences is not borne by the community. another important aspect is the cooperation between the countries established by this framework decision, namely the creation of an information network ensuring a rapid exchange of data, a treaty requiring environmental offences to be considered as offences authorizing the extradition or confiscation of property and profits or making them in any case uneconomic. i would just like to point out that this report was adopted unanimously in committee, with one abstention, and that all the political groups, from the epp to the pse to the greens, have contributed to its improvement. it is therefore a report which expresses the opinion of the committee on civil liberties and human rights in its entirety and, hopefully, of the european parliament, which must ensure that european countries finally have effective legislation to protect the environment.
