commission. – mr president, i very much welcome the interest that parliament has shown in the external service, in particular, mr galeote quecedo's report. i want to assure parliament that we will consider its recommendations very carefully. i want to pay particular tribute to mr galeote quecedo. he deserves considerable respect for the very professional and open-minded way in which he has carried out his work. i can say without any reservation that the commission has benefited from the report and it is bound to make a permanent impression on the way we run our external service in the future. it is already a subject in which we have been taking a keen interest. i left a special meeting of virtually all our heads of delegation in brussels early today specifically to be here for this debate. when apologising for my early departure i was able to inform them of the close interest that parliament takes in these matters. the fact that we called all our heads of delegation to brussels at this time is a sign of our determination to give a firm lead to the external service and to provide it with the career structure and the leadership that it deserves and needs. members will have seen the communication on the development of the external service that was adopted by the commission on 18 july. it recommends continuing to rebalance delegation staff between officials and local agents and continuing the regionalisation of our representation in a way that will free up 32 official posts immediately to be redeployed to delegations that need reinforcement. the communication updates the list of priorities for the opening of new delegations and offices. however, even though some of these are urgent priorities, our first concern must be to use available resources to reinforce some of our existing delegations. the communication also describes the measures we are taking to devolve authority from brussels to delegations in the field, known in jargon as "deconcentration". this is closely linked to our efforts to reform our external assistance programmes. the communication makes it clear that what it proposes is only a first step. we intend to continue and to ensure the best use of the resources we have at our disposal on the basis of an evaluation of the workload of each delegation. i want to make this point very clear because it is the backdrop to mr galeote quecedo's report. if we get through our reform proposals and if they are supported by the budgetary authority, in the scr and the bureau d'assistance technique combined we will have fewer people managing our external programmes, though we will have more than at present in the scr. but we will have fewer people in brussels and more people in the field. that is the balance we should be striking: to have more of the work done on the ground in our delegations. we will be preparing a follow-up communication on the external services in the first half of next year. let me comment specifically on mr galeote quecedo's report. it makes recommendations in three main areas: the training of officials assigned to external relations, the legal status of delegations and coordination with member states. a number of the points raised by the resolution, for example on regionalisation and on the evaluation of our network of external representations, are already covered in our own communication. the report stresses the role of the commission and its delegations in the community's external activities and it is, of course, essential that the commission's external service be able to continue to contribute properly. the first step must be to develop the training of officials in the commission who deal with external relations. i am delighted that the report puts so much informed stress on that point. we have already made good progress but we need to build on it very fast indeed, particularly given the deconcentration that i have talked about. we should try, as the report suggests, to benefit from the skills and experience of existing training institutions in the member states. we are already in contact with many of them and we will seek to deepen that relationship. whether it is now time to set up a college of european diplomacy is something that we will have to look at very carefully with parliament, the council and others. we will certainly consider that proposal very carefully and it underlines the importance of training – language training, management training, all the other sorts of training that are essential in order to make our delivery of programmes and our representation overseas more effective. on the legal status of delegations i should say that although delegations are formally delegations of the commission they are under clear instructions to give all possible assistance to all the institutions of the european union and indeed to member states. i am not convinced of the need to formalise this state of affairs since it exists already. i do not want to complicate procedures further, but again i am open-minded on the issue. we have made it absolutely clear to our delegations that they should regard themselves as working for the high representative and for the other institutions of the european union, both when it comes to reporting and when it comes to logistical issues. on relations with the member states, i wholeheartedly endorse the proposal for greater cooperation. this is already our policy and the discussions this weekend at evian very much concentrated on how best we can achieve that in practice. in our 1998 communication on the external service, we made it clear that any member state that wished to keep a presence in a third country without maintaining an embassy was welcome to use the commission's delegations. this has already happened on two occasions: in sierra leone by germany and in burundi by austria. there is already a considerable degree of cooperation between member states' embassies and commission delegations. there are regular meetings at all levels. joint reports are produced, either at the request of headquarters, or on the initiative of heads of missions. the commission also supports and, when appropriate, seeks to participate in co-location projects where more than one member state and/or the commission agree to occupy premises jointly. we have a programme of secondment of member states officials and diplomats to our delegations. there are ten in our delegations at the moment, with a few more due in the near future. the restriction on the development of this programme is not lack of will on our part – i want to make that clear – but to some extent a lack of resources and also a certain reluctance on the part of the member states to respond to our invitation to second diplomats to the delegations. i want to underline the importance of coordination. we have to cooperate better without finding ourselves in a situation in which everything we do is second-guessed, not just in brussels, but in other countries as well. all this discussion about coordination and about the future of the external service takes place against the backdrop of a treaty which talks about a common foreign and security policy, not a single foreign and security policy in a union of fifteen member states, each with its own foreign minister. i strongly suspect that we will have fifteen foreign ministers in the european union for the foreseeable future. but what we have to do is make coordination and cooperation more effective, more meaningful and more professional. a final plea. in welcoming this report and in promising active cooperation in following its recommendations i must stress that if the external service is to carry out the role which parliament wants for it, it must have the resources to do so; that is, not just resources to place officials in third countries but also to ensure that they are properly trained, that they are equipped with the necessary information technology and that they have secure means of communication. last and by no means least, it is very important that they are provided with adequate physical protection in what is an, often, very dangerous world.
the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i am very pleased to present, on behalf of the committee on development, this report on the winding-up of one of the projects which has perhaps worked better or has been judged more positively in the field of north-south cooperation: the ecip (european community investment partners) project, which, according to all, has worked well, even though it has experienced, like many other projects, the delays that have accumulated in the field of external relations, delays that we all know and of which commissioner patten has recently drawn up a very precise analysis. in this case we have almost 600 projects, which were approved in good time and which have to be honoured on ecip funds. the commission has therefore proposed - with a delay which we criticise in our report, a delay which is of course due to everything that happened in 1999 - that we adopt an extension, not so much of the instrument as such, but of the technical assistance offices, the means indispensable for managing the important remainder of ecip - 590 projects - and it proposes that we do so in two years. i must say, commissioner, that the committee on development has been confronted with the opinions of the other committees of this parliament on this subject: the committee on budgets and the committee on budgetary control. as you will have seen, those two committees put up sticks, to put it in italian, to tighten the barriers to the commission: the commission has been asked to complete its work six months in advance and to report back to us on the progress of the matter at a later date. we in the committee on development understood the message that was coming from the commission, the request to help the ecip project - which, i repeat, along with other projects, has contributed to the birth and growth of thousands of small and mediumsized industries in the third world countries and has actually allowed the union to become visible and to penetrate a new and therefore important sector for the commission - and we therefore decided not to follow the more restrictive opinion of the other committees and not to make amendments to the main request of the commission, namely to give the commission two years to be able to manage the conclusions of this important instrument of economic cooperation and to honour those contracts, which were signed by 31 december 1999. but at the same time, commissioner, we have made a request. we have asked that parliament be informed in good time so that we can also reflect together on what you intend to do with the future of this instrument. we have seen that this instrument is effective, that it has responded to real needs and that it has mobilised resources which go far beyond the funding provided by the community budget. we therefore ask you to accept our amendment so that the codecision procedure can be carried out quickly and the procedure can be closed, if possible in one reading, so that you can have the means to act immediately. we ask you - i would say it is not much - to tell us by the end of the year what your intentions are. we know the differences of opinion, the possible conflicts of competence between external relations and development and therefore between the competence of the various directorates-general and perhaps even of individual commissioners, but we also know how, in restructuring, the responsibility for external relations is being reviewed by you in particular, mr commissioner, and by the whole college with great attention. so, we didn't put a direction, we didn't say, ecip must remain an autonomous instrument, ecip must and can be integrated into a wider instrument. we simply asked for this to come in response to the confidence placed in the commission in allowing this two-year grant: we are asking for this, and i ask you, commissioner, to answer whether you accept the amendments we have tabled.
commission. – let me thank mr dell'alba and the development and cooperation committee very sincerely for their excellent work on the commission proposal on the future of the european community investment partners. let me commence with a bit of background. the ecip instrument operated successfully for 12 years, from 1988 to 1999. more than 2 500 actions were approved in that period for a total amount of over eur 290 million involving 1 400 joint ventures and eur 4.3 billion in investment. from 1991, the commission sent annual reports on the implementation and on the results of ecip to parliament and to the council, of which the last covered operations in 1999. parliament also received the independent evaluation report that was completed in december 1999, but, as honourable members will know, from 1997 ecip began to run into trouble. the lack of sufficient staff to ensure the smooth management of an ever-increasing number of actions resulted in delays in the implementation of the programme, which in turn caused growing discontent among its beneficiaries. these difficulties were compounded by the introduction of more stringent financial procedures needed to guarantee the proper use of the resources managed by the commission. they are typical of the problems we face, namely insufficient resources to do the job wedded to overly restrictive practices and procedures. the commission decided not to extend the instrument beyond 31 december 1999. this was a painful decision, but, i am sure, the right one – and to reappraise the instrument in order to prepare a redesigned programme. this will allow better coordination with other similar european union instruments and ensure improved management and financial procedures in the light of the new commission guidelines on development policy and the management of external aid. mr dell'alba's report contains extremely helpful suggestions in this respect. the approval of the proposed regulation will make possible the continued sound management of existing ecip projects and their orderly closure and winding-down as they reach completion. as far as the suggested amendments are concerned, the commission agrees with amendment nos 1 and 2, which correspond with our views on the need to reassess, improve and redesign the existing financial instruments for the support of private investment. as regards amendment no 3, the commission agrees with the principle behind it but is not in a position to provide the legislative proposals requested by parliament by the end of this year. we are presently engaged in a comprehensive review of all our existing financial instruments. we need to be candid. we need more time to present a properly thought through and fundamentally revised programme. the commission therefore proposes to evaluate all the options by june of next year and then make proposals. the honourable gentleman has been generous, courteous and understanding. he therefore deserves the assurance from me that the timetable i have set out is one we intend to observe, and i hope he will accept our determination to present our proposals within that sort of time-scale in good faith. i wish we could act more rapidly, but to do the job properly we need a bit more time. let me finish by thanking the european parliament for the support which the house has given to the proposed regulation on ecip. it will allow the commission to bring this programme to an end in a responsible manner and to launch renewed and improved initiatives for promotion of the private sector in developing countries. i am sure that we will have other future opportunities that will enable me to explain to some honourable members why i do not equate that with nineteenth century imperialism.
the rapporteur. mr president, first of all i would like to thank all my colleagues in the various groups who have given me a substantial contribution to the preparation of this report, to express parliament's position on the commission's communication on echo's activities, first aid and humanitarian aid. if the committee on development and cooperation voted unanimously on this report, it is because there has been a very fruitful collaboration, which i hope will be reflected in the final vote in the house tomorrow. to speak of echo, to speak of humanitarian aid, is to record the greatest tragedies and the greatest contradictions of our time. it means talking about war, about catastrophes, about the damage being done to the world's ecological system. it means talking about the continuation of dramatic ethnic conflicts, civil and military wars; it means talking about the underlying inequalities in the north/south relationship and the suffering, in particular, of the most vulnerable populations, children, women, the elderly. if we are serious, we must say that the forecasts for the next few years are not forecasts for improvement over this situation. i am referring to a few newspaper reports from the last few months: the north pole that gave signs of melting where absolutely no one imagined it; the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat the pollution of the water in bangladesh, which is endangering the safety, hygiene and health of 25 million people. or the drought situation in many parts of africa. we must therefore be serious and realistic, we must plan for the future, even more than in the past, in terms of preventing disasters and responding to the consequences of tragedies which are often, almost always, caused by man. this programming requires better coordination at international level between the european union and all the other actors involved in humanitarian aid, and it requires better coordination within the european union between the commission and the instruments at the disposal of the member states, in order to avoid duplication, repetition and, therefore, waste of energy and resources, as has often happened, as the commission document says, and as the evaluations have confirmed. in this context, i think it is unacceptable - and my report and parliament's position is clear on this - that echo should be reduced to a donor for basic needs, period. i think we need to look at the bigger picture: the commission's proposal is to be accompanied by a report on the situation in the former yugoslavia, which will be presented to the council in the near future. we are talking about perhaps limited figures, if we are talking about more general budgets, but we are talking about eur 2 500 million over the last four years, which has been earmarked by the european commission, 56% for non-governmental organisations, 25% for united nations agencies, 11% for the red cross and then for other direct interventions by echo or specialised agencies of the member states. i believe that the analysis presented by the commission obliges us to take action to further strengthen echo and to prevent certain positions within the council, which is divided on these points, from prevailing. some in the council are saying that we should reduce echo's intervention, but i think the opposite is true. one last point, mr president: echo cannot be seen as an atm service by some international agency or even by non-governmental organizations, for which money is taken and then the beneficiaries are not even told where the funding comes from. the european public and the beneficiaries need to be informed about this extraordinary echo intervention. that is why we have proposed - and i hope that commissioner patten, who is not listening to me at the moment, will take this proposal seriously - that there should be an information campaign for the public in our countries, so that they know how our money, our resources are being spent, and that this information campaign should not be financed with echo funds, of course, but with ad hoc funds.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i think that the document on the community's audiovisual policy in the digital age, which the commission has presented, is important because this technological innovation to some extent directly affects the cultural future and even sensitive issues such as pluralism and the quality of democracy on our continent. with digital and media convergence, everything will change. the way we know, communicate, work, produce and know. there are risks - as always happens when innovation breaks through - but the digital shift brings with it immense opportunities for pluralism and opens up huge productive possibilities for the system. it is no coincidence that a few days ago british prime minister tony blair proposed, in a revolutionary move towards the traditional management of the electromagnetic spectrum, that frequencies should also be auctioned for digital television in order to accelerate the technological transition. and it is no coincidence that blair himself proposed free distribution of the set top box, foreseeing a double advantage: the commission has already taken a number of measures to promote the development of the information society. the technologies change and the perspectives change, and so do the legal approaches. the european parliament has a duty to ensure that the digital age is an opportunity for culture, for pluralism, for cultural and linguistic diversity, for the european economy and for technological innovation and research on our continent. we believe that these objectives can be achieved by means of the instruments already identified in the commission's text. however, the debate which has taken place in parliament, which has taken account of various points of view and has endeavoured, as we have done in the committee on culture, to find a common point of convergence, so that the report was voted unanimously, proposes some additions, limited but important. first of all: the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive on the protection of the environment. secondly: in order to avoid the risk of our cultural industry becoming dependent on the expansion and multiplication of channels, the possibility of productive investment in the audiovisual sector is envisaged. the financing of the media is essential, but i think that it is also necessary to provide, as has happened in some countries, for appropriations from the broadcasters themselves, in order to reserve a share of their revenues for the production of european works, a model which i believe is useful and important because it encourages and supports industry. thirdly, by controlling media concentrations, possibly on the basis of specific european rules to protect pluralism, taking up the idea of a media directive and a body at european level to monitor the application of the rules in this sensitive area; the commission has also proposed a policy which, in the age of convergence, will protect a universal service for access to content, understood as non-discrimination and affordability of access to services. recognising the role of public service broadcasting as a significant part of the digitised system, it will of course have to be rethought and revised in the light of technological changes, but it must also play a role in ensuring quality services for a wide audience, which will continue to use home television sets and over-the-air reception for their daily information for a long time to come; the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the future of the european telecommunications industry. the report also proposes integration to ensure that particular attention is paid to the safeguarding of cultural diversity, international negotiations and the need to strengthen the european audiovisual industry so that it can be competitive on the global market. this is the spirit of the report and its attempt to move within the framework proposed by the commission report. the tdi group has tabled amendments based on a different vision, on a different legitimate cultural and political inspiration. i believe that their approval would have the effect of removing the reasons on which we have reached agreement in committee. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the legal basis for the proposal is established. mr president, i am speaking in place of mr tajani, as a member of the same delegation and of the same committee, the legal affairs committee. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, while welcoming the overall content of the commission's initiative, it is clear that the regulation of audiovisual policy is important in the high-tech era in which we live today and increasingly in the near future. the complexity of the subject and the shortness of time allow me to make only a few brief summary remarks, which i consider essential and which i hope will be taken into due consideration by the commission. the free flow of information and freedom of expression are and will always be the safeguard of rights and freedoms. citizens' trust in the audiovisual service must be guaranteed by respect for the principles of the protection of human dignity and the protection of minors. in this rapidly changing field, precise but not rigid rules are needed to prevent them from quickly becoming obsolete. technology and content cannot have the same regulations: the technology must be neutral and the content must be regulated. the financing must comply with the principles of proportionality and transparency and must not affect the market and competition. in the commercial activity accompanying the public service, differentiating costs and revenues will make clear the compensation for the service provided, thus avoiding fraudulent state aid and ensuring that private companies can also provide the public service. there must be no national restrictions on transposition, and this will result in real european harmonization, both in the present and in future enlargement. by including self-regulatory codes in the regulatory framework, transparency, accountability and equal dignity between public and commercial enterprises will be achieved. it is clear that, in the context of new technologies, it is necessary to prevent state subsidies to public service broadcasters from being used for commercial purposes, altering the principle of competitiveness with private operators, rather than ensuring compliance with precise programming obligations. finally, it is necessary to ensure the diversity and plurality of supply and to give all operators the opportunity to play an innovative and driving role, thereby liberalizing access to public financing.

commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, this is the first time since the entry into force of the treaty of amsterdam that the european parliament has been consulted on a proposal for a directive from the commission to the council on legal immigration of persons from third countries. it is therefore a sign of the profound institutional changes introduced by the treaty and considered a priority on the european political agenda by the heads of state and government at the tampere european council. the commission has understood that it is through a proposal for family reunification that we should begin this journey, this considerable effort to build a common european immigration policy. and i would like to begin by saying why we have chosen this topic - to respond to a critical remark by mrs klamt, whom i would like to congratulate, despite our differences of opinion, on her work as first rapporteur on this subject. i believe that family reunification is a concept which is profoundly consistent with the obligations which all member states have assumed under international law for several decades. from the reference in the universal declaration of human rights to the international agreements within the united nations in 1966 to the european convention on human rights itself, all these instruments of international law enshrine the protection of the family as an essential element of the guarantee of social peace. i think that no one can deny that family reunification is also an important instrument for integrating immigrants from third countries into the host societies. this has been recognised by the european union bodies. since 1993, the council has devoted constant attention to the issue of family reunification. and it must be acknowledged that, in quantitative terms, this question of family reunification is relevant, because it represents today one of the main causes of immigration to european countries. it is not the directive that creates this migratory flow, but the directive seeks to regulate a reality on the ground. and so anyone who does not want to understand that this directive is intended to create legal rules to respond to a situation which is already on the ground and who wants to hold the commission responsible for inventing a new migration dynamic is being unfair in the analysis of the reality we are facing. the commission therefore considered that family reunification deserved priority treatment over other forms of legal immigration. it is not about deciding on entry and residence for economic purposes, or immigration of workers, or immigration of students. we believe that this is a matter of regulating a different form of admission which is in keeping with values - in particular the protection of the family - and a strategic political objective, namely the promotion of the integration of third-country nationals already legally living in the union into the host societies. we start from a principle which is debatable, but until proven otherwise i believe it is demonstrable. family reunification is a factor that promotes the personal stability of the emigrant, since family life is always an important instrument to support integration in the host countries. the heads of state or government in tampere also unanimously stressed the need to ensure fair treatment of third-country nationals legally resident in the member states of the union. they also stressed the need to develop a more dynamic integration policy in parallel and that this policy should aim to offer third-country nationals rights and obligations comparable to those of union citizens. these are, ladies and gentlemen, the values and political commitments on which the commission has built its proposal. and i would like to stress that the commission has proposed an initiative where family reunification is conceived as a right. but it is not an absolute right for third country nationals who are legally resident in the union. it is, on the contrary, a right subject to conditions, whether procedural or material, as regards the definition of the status of family members in the country where they have been admitted and the rights they enjoy. and i'm available to discuss this proposal in all its implications. in fact, the french presidency has considered this subject to be central to the six months for which it is responsible. and we are ready to put forward an amended proposal as soon as possible so that we can achieve a positive result during the french presidency. i would like to thank all the members who took part in the debate. it was a lively debate, as it was in the commission, and sometimes even a passionate one, because it dealt with a sensitive subject in which there is naturally a great deal of force in the projection of national realities. it is difficult to find common ground at european level. but above all, this debate has one fundamental feature. it is no longer a debate about declarations of intent, it is a debate about rules, binding legal rules, which will have to be applied. so it is natural that there is a lively, even passionate debate, and a debate where there are differences. the commission will attach the utmost importance to your opinion. and i would like to congratulate mr watson on the work he has done in presenting a report in the difficult circumstances in which this debate has unfolded. i would like to explain to the honourable members what the commission's position is on the most difficult political issues in this directive. firstly, as regards the scope of the proposal: the commission believes that refugees should be included in its scope, because it would not be politically understandable to grant economic migrants a right to family reunification which we do not grant to refugees recognised under the geneva convention. but i accept that it is necessary to exclude beneficiaries of temporary or subsidiary protection. this is not a change of principle. i am convinced that certain types of beneficiaries of temporary or subsidiary protection should also have the right to family reunification. but i recognize that the lack of harmonisation of the concept at european level and, above all, the intention of the commission to present to parliament and the council a directive on temporary and subsidiary protection next year will allow the right to family reunification to be dealt with very closely in that directive. we therefore agree to amend the proposal to exclude beneficiaries of temporary or subsidiary protection. as regards the concept of the family, i should like to make it very clear that the commission does not intervene in this proposal in the matter of defining the concept of the family. this proposal fully respects the competence of each member state to define what constitutes a family. and the question of de facto unions, for example. this proposal does not say that all member states will be obliged to recognise de facto union and to admit de facto couples in all circumstances. all we 're saying is this: the court of justice has already held that the principle of equal treatment for men and women in matters of family law is not applicable to the application of the principle of equal treatment for men and women in matters of family law. and so i would like to say clearly that there is no indication in this proposal that it favours family reunification of polygamous families. sorry, the text is clear! you can't promote the coming of a second wife! and there is only one exception, an exception for children of a second marriage if the interests of the child so warrant. but how do you explain the treatment of children of a second polygamous marriage differently from that of children of a first marriage or of children of a common-law marriage? i'm not a moral subverter, but i think we have to put the best interests of the children first. finally, mr president, the commission is prepared to accept a number of other amendments and other modifications concerning the rights of family members, the conditions and clarification of the conditions for family reunification, the situation in which the person who is reunified may acquire an autonomous status, and the rules of procedure. this will be done before the vote. i would like to conclude by saying that this is of course an exercise which gives rise to debate. the debate with the council will not be easy, nor will the debate with the european parliament. i respect the opinion of all members. i would like the opinion of the european parliament to have as wide a support as possible. and i hope that - irrespective of our differences of opinion, which are natural, i would say useful, which are essential for democracy - it is possible that once this directive is adopted we can all join our efforts to solve the essential question we have on the table - how to create a clear and transparent legal regime that ensures the integration of legal immigrants in the host countries - because this integration is the key to the success of a common immigration policy at european level.

- the next item is the report (a5-0187/2000) by mrs lucas, on behalf of the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism, on the communication from the commission to the council, the european parliament, the economic and social committee and the committee of the regions on air transport and the environment (com (99) 640 - c5-0086/2000 - 2000/2054 (cos)).
commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i should like to congratulate mrs lucas on the report which forms the basis of our debate today. as we all know, the environmental consequences of air transport have recently been a subject of great interest. at local level, discussions on airport development are increasingly driven by environmental considerations relating to noise reduction and improving air quality in the vicinity of airports. many citizens living in these areas feel that much more could be done to improve their situation and that is what they are demanding. in addition, the long-term impact of air transport gases on climate change is undoubtedly a cause for concern in the world today, as is the impact of other types of emissions. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the environment is not affected by the new technologies. we must try to reconcile interests which are not always easy to reconcile because, undoubtedly, there are economic interests in air transport which are characterized by high investment costs which require a long service life for their repayment. for example, an aircraft requires a much longer life span than other types of investment to have an adequate payback. this requires a stable operating environment, without any game-changing fluctuations or changes that could have disastrous economic consequences for the operation of the aeronautical companies. a high growth sector, based on very expensive technologies, has an immediate impact on the employment of related sectors such as research and industry, and also tourism. in my view, trying to safeguard the environment simply by curbing the growth of the aviation sector and the airline industry is not a valid option we can consider. but there is no doubt that citizens, not only those who are in the vicinity and who suffer more directly from certain types of pollution, such as noise or even emissions, but also citizens in general, who want a quality of life and sustainable development over time, have the right to demand from us actions and movements that guarantee that way of growth which must be the european model. in its communication on air transport and the environment, the commission argues that the aviation industry must redouble its efforts to improve the environmental quality of new aircraft being built. if the current rate of growth is maintained, the necessary improvements to offset the environmental impact of the expected growth in air traffic will not be made. i know that this statement is not well received by many in the sector, but there is undoubtedly no alternative to be found in the medium and long term if we do not want air transport to become a victim of its own success. but the commission is also aware that the air transport industry is quite right in saying that before environmental measures are put into practice, a serious and thorough study of the economic and social impact of such measures is necessary. i have the impression that those who are most concerned about the environment are now gradually but increasingly accepting the fact that when developing a particular environmental policy, it is necessary to take account of the balance between the cost and the effectiveness of the proposed measures. the report before us addresses these essential aspects and takes account both of the need to strengthen environmental protection beyond routine efforts and of the cost-benefit analysis factor. and i want to thank mrs lucas for the effort of flexibility she has made, because it is clear from her amendments that this is not exactly what she would like as a report, but she is looking for a compromise that will allow parliament's approval. for example, what you say about kerosene seems to me to be a reasonable way of putting this problem, which cannot be solved at european level, but rather globally in the field of world aviation and the icao. because it is in the field of aviation, the industry in which globalization is most evident, that these questions must be resolved. i would like to thank the rapporteur for her support of the commission in the report and say that we are at a difficult stage in the debate on new noise standards and on regulations to phase out the noisiest aircraft at icao level. we have repeatedly stated our preference for an international solution to these problems and the commission has been pleased to note the positive development of the us position on the standardization process taking place in the icao. i have to say that the regulations on the so-called 'hushkits' for the noisiest aircraft, adopted at the time by parliament, the council and the commission, were based precisely on the fact that the united states had unilaterally adopted measures outside the icao. there is no doubt that this work should be carried out at icao. we will coordinate the actions of the various member states in the context of the caep, since it is the member states who are the holders of licences in the icao framework, and i hope that parliament will support initiatives such as the single sky, to which mr ojeda has referred, which will of course also have consequences for the saving of kerosene, if it can be put into operation, and the improvement of the allocation systems and the general management of slots. mr president, i again thank you for the effort you have all made to try to obtain a text that is realistic, flexible and acceptable to the various parties. we await parliament's vote, which the commission will of course take into account.

- the next item is the recommendation for second reading (a5-0218/00) on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection, on the common position of the council with a view to adopting a european parliament and council directive amending council directive 92/23/eec relating to tyres for motor vehicles and their trailers and their fitting (c5-0220/2000 - 1997/0348 (cod)) (rapporteur: mr de roo).
commission. - mr president, this proposal for a directive aims to limit the rolling noise of tyres on the road, without sacrificing adhesion and therefore road holding and braking safety. in preparing the proposal, the commission involved several bodies independent of manufacturers, which had worked for a long time with experts in the member states to find the appropriate level of severity expressed in decibels for the different classes of tyres for cars, vans and trucks. as a result of this extensive prior consultation of experts, the member states unanimously agreed, in a common position, on the level of severity chosen in the proposal. the european parliament itself was satisfied with the level of severity of the proposal and did not introduce any amendments. it should be noted at the outset that the quality of the road surface is to a very large extent responsible for the noise generated by contact with tyres, up to 6 decibels. it should also be noted that the commission is continuing its action, launched two years ago, on the fight against the various sources of noise, covering all the union's sectors of activity. now, on second reading, four amendments are tabled. amendments nos 2, 3 and 4 propose to reduce the threshold values by 2 decibels. if such a reduction of 2 decibels were applied today, more than 70% of the tyres currently on sale would fail the test. manufacturers would then be forced to make urgent changes to the structure of the tire and the hardness of the rubber, reducing its grip. as long as membership requirements are not applied, these three amendments are therefore not acceptable. this correlation between noise and rolling, tyre grip and fuel consumption is precisely at the heart of the concern expressed in amendment no 1. this concern is currently being sought for consensus in a working party of the united nations economic commission for europe, which is being monitored by the european commission. this topic is also being discussed in the transatlantic business dialogue to promote the emergence of a global standard, the global type standard gts 2000. the european commission is following up this work with the intention of transposing the results into directive 92/23/eec in order to determine the right balance between safety, noise and rolling resistance. however, the proposed timetable is unfortunately too strict. the complexity of the problem and the wide range of products covered must be taken into account. for these reasons, article 3 as drafted in the common position states that the adhesion and rolling resistance requirements will be integrated with the noise requirements within the extended timeframe of 24 and 36 months respectively after the entry into force of this directive. amendment no 1, which proposes to legislate again and twice within one year of the entry into force of this directive, is not acceptable. due to the complexity of the methods for measuring adhesion on dry and wet surfaces and rolling resistance and the wide range of products, the results of the experts' work will not be available until 2002. the commission will then be able to amend this directive to include wet and dry grip and rolling resistance for all tyre classes.
- thank you very much, commissioner. the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at 12 noon.
- the next item is the report (a5-0168/2000) by mr bakopoulos, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive amending for the 19th time council directive 76/769/eec on the restriction of the placing on the market and use of certain dangerous substances and preparations ( azo dyes) (com (99) 620 - c5-0312/1999 - 1999/0269 (cod)).
commission. – mr president, i would like to thank members for their interest in this subject and especially mr bakopoulos, the rapporteur, for his constructive work. certain azocolourants used in textile and leather pose the risk of cancer for consumers and workers, as has been said. following an opinion of the scientific committee on toxicity, ecotoxicity and the environment confirming such risks, the commission proposed in december of last year a directive restricting marketing and use of certain azocolourants which could pose a risk of cancer if they come into close contact with the skin. the commission proposal for a directive would introduce a ban on the use of certain azocolourants in textile and leather articles that come into close contact with the skin. the colourants concerned are xylidines which may release any of the 21 cancer-causing amines listed in the proposed directive. furthermore, textile or leather articles dyed with these same xylidines may not be placed on the market. the test methods to be used to show compliance with the provisions are specified in the proposed directive. the proposal provides not only for the protection of consumers' and workers' health. it also addresses an internal market issue. at the present time, the internal market is fragmented, as some member states are already applying national bans. the proposed directive would harmonise the rules of member states. i would stress that the proposal is based on the results of independent studies on the risks of azocolourants and of the costs, benefits and trade effects of the proposed restrictions. it also takes account of the opinion of the competent scientific committee on risks. i believe it is a proportionate measure. the commission is unable to accept those parliament amendments which would extend this ban by replacing the proposed list of examples of product categories covered by an exhaustive list by covering articles other than those made of textiles and leather and by including other amides. amendments nos. 3, 4 and 7 of the committee on the environment are the ones i refer to. the commission feels this could not be justified on the basis of the current knowledge about the risks. nor is the commission able to accept amendments that would introduce a second testing method to show compliance with the provisions. this applies to amendment no 5 of the committee on the environment. these would make it more difficult for suppliers, especially in the third world, to show compliance as the method proposed by the commission is the method most widely accepted and used. however, the commission can accept that when available a more reliable standardised testing method could be introduced. the commission can accept in principle an exemption for handmade oriental carpets from the example list of product categories covered by the proposed directive as the risk from such carpets is likely to be low. however, the commission cannot accept that the exemption is only temporary. to summarise our point of view, we can accept amendment no 1 of the committee on the environment. we must reject six amendments, namely nos. 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 of the committee on the environment. however, the commission can in principle support parts of amendment no 3. we wish to carry on the dialogue with parliament. i am convinced that we can reach a constructive solution.
- thank you very much, commissioner. the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at 12 noon.

community's social policy is not distorted by the fact that the social partners are not involved in the decisionmaking process. finally, underage work also affects children under the age of 15! we commission. – i should like to thank mrs glase for her excellent report. the commission has opened the debate with its communication on undeclared work in the spring of 1998. we are pleased to say that it has stimulated debate both with the european institutions and within member states. the time has come to bring together the fruits of this debate. therefore i especially welcome parliament's initiative in taking up this issue now. the commission's communication focused on the policy strategy to tackle this important problem. it has highlighted the need for an integrated approach to combating undeclared work, involving both preventive measures and sanctions. these deal with the two dimensions of undeclared work: it can be viewed as an issue of individuals taking advantage of the system and undermining solidarity in the process or as the outcome of greater flexibility in the labour market and slow adaptation of existing legislation. i am pleased to see that parliament has agreed with the commission's analysis. parliament also seems to share the view that the main action has to be taken at the level of member states. indeed it is the mix of the situation in the labour market, the tax and social security mix, as well as the social acceptance, that determine the level of undeclared work. for that reason, the action that can be taken at community level can only be minimal and has to be clearly targeted in those fields where the community can have an impact. the commission is also convinced that undeclared work should be dealt with within the framework of the luxembourg process. we believe that undeclared work should be actively taken into account in the national action plans for employment. we are working with the member states to ensure that this is so. we welcome parliament's support in this. however, the commission can have an impact in developing a standard methodology to describe and record the extent of undeclared work and to assess its impact on the economy and on social solidarity. this we have done with the communication in 1998 and we will continue to do so. indeed the commission is now carrying out a study on different measures used to combat undeclared work in selected member states in order to identify good policy mixes. results of this study will be presented in a conference at the end of the year. however, to have annual monitoring and reporting on this problem would be heavy procedurally while not adding much new. we must not forget that undeclared work is a deeply rooted phenomenon. changes take time. to keep this item on the agenda and to ensure that progress is reported we would suggest a triennial reporting exercise. the commission agrees with the analysis of parliament that women, while not the majority of undeclared workers, often operate in situations of greater insecurity and exploitation. within its possibilities the commission will continue to monitor the situation and report on it within the framework of existing reports on the principle of equal treatment. that is very important to the need to maintain momentum in introducing and reinforcing equal opportunities for women and men.

the rapporteur. - mr president, as far as sport is concerned, the european union must ensure that it has the right role and the right attention and that it is governed by clear and certain rules. the sports system to which europe must aspire must ensure that the right to sport is exercised by all citizens, while aiming to preserve its social function and traditional values, while taking account of the economic and legal evolution of sport. for this reason, the declaration on sport annexed to the treaty of amsterdam is no longer sufficient to guarantee the achievement of the objectives set. sport needs a new definition: the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work is based on the principle of equal treatment. sport must, in essence, be an essential element in promoting education and the integration of all social classes. it must also be able to adapt to the new commercial environment in which it must evolve without losing its autonomy. in order for the european union to be useful to the changing and evolving world of sport, some innovations are needed. the central committee has repeatedly stated that it can no longer guarantee the pyramidal structure in which sports organisations and the social function of sport are currently organised. a legal basis is therefore essential, since without it the objectives achieved so far risk being frustrated. europe must be more decisive in the fight against doping, a phenomenon which is unfortunately on the increase and which no longer concerns only the sports world: the spread of this scourge has led to the growth of highly profitable illegal activities, to which many criminal organizations have turned, and it must be admitted that the fight against doping, which is the sole responsibility of sports organizations, has been a complete failure. europe should therefore consider the possibility of enacting a community criminal law applicable to all member states and should consider the establishment of an independent and transparent european anti-doping agency. in addition, all economic activities linked to sport must be subject to the rules of the treaty. the monopoly activity of sports organisations has caused a number of problems and must therefore be closely monitored and possibly reduced. association in sport should be encouraged, provided that it has a purpose of solidarity in favour of poorer sports activities and of socially disadvantaged individuals, particularly the disabled. the role of sport and the teaching of physical education in school curricula should be improved. in addition, the employment and status of sportsmen must be adequately protected and taken into account by the member states. i believe that the european union has a duty to help those athletes who have not thought about their future after their sporting career to find employment. europe must also demand that the professional qualifications of sportsmen and women be recognised at european level and that their professional training be encouraged. we must fight against the trafficking of young sportsmen and women with determination and force, and we must demand that the entry and registration of young people into the professional world be delayed as much as possible. the statutes of national and international sports federations must also be clear and precise in their mission and rules. it is necessary to combat violence at sporting events and to ensure the protection of its citizens. the indefinite sports league, which is in force in many sports federations, must also be abolished, since it violates the most basic principles of the constitutions of the member states. in conclusion, without a legal basis for the word 'sport', europe will be unable to do much in this field and will therefore have to consider the possibility of assuming a certain autonomy in this area, not to take it away from other bodies but to make an indispensable contribution to the safeguarding of the values and functions of sport. and in its future actions. mr president, i should now like to focus on the helsinki report on the social dimension of sport. for the first time, the commission has adopted a 'doctrine' in the field of sport. in this sense, this report is fundamental, and i thank parliament for playing a key role in this development. in 1997, parliament called on the commission to prepare a community action in the field of sport and in the same year a declaration on sport was annexed to the treaty, inviting the institutions to consult sports associations when important sports-related issues have to be dealt with. the commission then launched a wide consultation process with sports organisations, which inspired the helsinki report. i myself have been fortunate to have the substantial support of three presidencies, namely the finnish, portuguese and now french presidencies. i hope that this combination of favourable circumstances will allow progress to be made in such a way as to give sport its rightful place in community activity. ladies and gentlemen, i think sport is doing well, if not very well. if we take into account the amounts of television rights or the sale of sporting goods, the economic situation of sport is stronger than ever. it is clear that this economic performance must not be undermined by the threats we have all identified: the phenomenon of doping, the lack of protection for young athletes, excessive marketing, violence in and outside stadiums. in the face of these problems, a common approach must be put in place and the commission has made it clear in its report in helsinki that it cannot solve all these problems on its own. there will be three levels of action: the sports world, national officials and the community dimension. first, the sports world. the commission has regularly stated since 1989 that it is concerned with respecting the autonomy of sports organisations. but autonomy also means responsibility, the willingness and ability to integrate the new economic framework and to adapt structures to the new realities of the sports world. the federations must make a further effort to democratize their internal structures and adapt them to the requirements of amateur and professional sport. they must ensure more transparency in the way they manage sponsorship and television rights. and if the principles of solidarity and social responsibility, as emphasized by the european parliament, are clearly respected, we can provide for a temporary derogation from the competition rules, for example in the case of the collective sale of television rights. it must be clear that a general derogation from these rules can never be justified. we are counting on transparency and dialogue. i therefore received all the european sports federations in brussels on 17 april and, with mrs buffet, on 26 and 27 october.

mr president, we must acknowledge the great work done by mr wallis and the attempt to maintain a certain balance in a very complex report, as we are trying to outline future scenarios which are extremely relevant to all of us. the debate this evening seems to be technical, but it actually hides very important political elements. we must, among other things, lay down the basic rules for the functioning of the market and for the relationship between two of its fundamental players: the service provider and the consumer. it 's too easy to say: protect the consumer by saying that the law applicable and the competent court are always those of the place where the consumer resides. in reality, the market, especially the new economy, is a complex environment where rigidity is swept away by the commercial relationships between actors and the variety of ways in which a transaction can be concluded. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. the idea that our regulation should lay down a rigid rule for determining the jurisdiction, the applicable law and the place of residence of the consumer does not seem to me to be something that can be achieved in practice. if the buyer is a resident of italy, he might be interested because, given the biblical times of our civil justice, we might be interested. we believe, however, that the market requires rapid solutions to possible disputes by referring them to alternative justice systems, to mediation by experts. today, new players are emerging in the construction of the rules of the world markets: i think, for example, of the impact that big law firms, global players, have on international transactions. they are the ones who are setting up new rules and new ways of settling disputes. the morality of law, which interprets the flexibility of markets, of justice in the concrete case, is increasingly taking the place of written law. the globalisation of markets leads to a plurality of rights created by the social groups themselves who use them. they express the market's continuing need for movement and expansion. there is an interaction between regulation and self-regulation. the principles of sovereignty and territoriality, which are the foundation of the nation states, are objectively being weakened. in the face of strict and punitive rules, how do you think businesses, especially small and mediumsized ones, will react? either they do not trade outside their own country, to avoid incurring excessive legal costs, or they face the risks of litigation by raising prices. in the end, it is the consumer who pays the cost in terms of less availability of goods and services, of high prices, vainly defended by our regulation. we would also have undermined the economic development and employment growth that the new economy seems to be enabling. that is what a section of this parliament wants, which today is demonstrating, with its amendments, only demagogic attitudes. we are not in favour of this, also because in the directive on electronic commerce which was adopted a few months ago we have laid down rules for concluding online contracts and we have reaffirmed the validity of the principles of the internal market, the rule of origin and on country control. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the legal solutions to markets now require global responses, all the more so if we regulate the new economies - i thank president prodi for his strong speech, which reflects a great vision that many of us share. i also share what has been said about the innovative value of the charter of rights, which enshrines the indivisibility of fundamental rights by overcoming traditional divisions between civil rights, economic and social rights, rights of the new generation, a charter which enshrines equality between men and women in all fields of human activity. but today the charter is essentially a symbol, the symbol of the transition from a market europe to a political europe, from a europe of states to a europe of citizens. the european union, made up of different peoples and nations who want to remain different in their traditions, languages and religions, bases its identity not on belonging to the same ethnic group, the same land, the same blood but on sharing the same principles, the same fundamental rights of persons. this is the model of european civilization which has guaranteed us, after centuries of bloody conflicts, lasting peace between our peoples, and it is this peace and social model which we offer to the candidate countries, from whom we do not ask to share traditions or beliefs but to accept the same rules which safeguard the freedom and dignity of each individual. the original method used to draw up the charter - it has been rightly said - quickly bore fruit, thanks to the participation of the representatives of the peoples and governments, the consultation with all the members of civil society who wanted to make their voices heard, the transparency and collegiality of its work, the willingness to listen to different positions, the acceptance of worthy compromises. the exhausting semi-secret or confidential negotiations of the intergovernmental method do not produce the same results. this symbolic document is a milestone in the process of constitutionalising the european union - because, in my view, the constitution of the union will not be the result of a single act at a single moment but of the progressive consolidation of the common institutions and the definition of common basic rules - and must become law that can be applied in practice. the treaties have made the union an area of freedom, security and justice. this cannot be done without the obligation to respect the fundamental rights clearly stated. it is the duty of the states, the masters of the treaties, to establish this link by giving the charter the most appropriate legal value. the charter, which is the soul of the union, cannot remain in limbo for long, but must be incorporated into the body of existing rules. governments take the rights of individuals seriously, give them effectiveness and force, give tangible content to european citizenship. only then will citizens take europe seriously as their common home. - mr president, mr president of the commission, mr president of the council, ladies and gentlemen, we are living through a very important moment in the history of europe, of the planet, and not just of the union. the drafting and adoption of the charter of rights, together with an intergovernmental conference which could bring about a major breakthrough and enlargement, are historic events which could mark the beginning of this century. this important historical juncture will not be able to fulfil its potential if the charter does not have legal force, if the intergovernmental conference does not make the necessary reforms, and if enlargement is likely to become a brake on political integration. the dilemma which is now close to the hearts of many citizens who want a political europe and not just a great commercial reality is this: if the intergovernmental conference does not bring about the reforms we want, will it still be advisable to proceed with enlargement? if we do indeed go ahead with enlargement - which is desirable - the only hope will be that of enhanced cooperation. the latter perspective must therefore not be confined to pre-established narrow limits but, while remaining within an accepted legal and institutional framework, must enable those member states which are ready to embark on the road to greater political integration, while leaving the others free to follow it when they see fit. it is a question of allowing everyone to pursue his own political project in the union, in a harmony of diversity which, in the end, has already been tried as a winning solution in the history of the european union.

the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, poland, the country for which i am rapporteur, is the largest and most important but, as we know, also the most problematic of the countries preparing to join the european union, so problematic that there are voices of its possible exclusion from the first group, that of the countries which will enter first. these are unfounded rumours and i am pleased to say to you, and especially to our polish friends, that yesterday we had a meeting with the italian foreign minister, lamberto dini, who categorically denied that he had ever heard of such a hypothesis at international meetings. poland will enter when it is ready, when the european union is ready to receive it, but it will certainly be in the first group. that said, the difficulties are not to be hidden, and the report i am presenting to you is a summary of the progress made and the difficulties encountered on the road to accession. the government and parliament in warsaw have been working hard in recent months to speed up the transposition of the legislation. the polish authorities have recently launched important reforms and, while the commission's annual report on poland's progress towards accession was quite negative last year, i believe and hope - and the words of commissioner verheugen a short while ago comfort me in this regard - that the one to be published in a few weeks' time will be more encouraging. however, as i said, there is still a lot to be done in poland: i am thinking of administrative reform, industrial restructuring and, of course, the agricultural sector, which needs profound structural changes. so, to overcome these difficulties, to solve these problems, the poles - like the citizens of the other candidate countries - need stimulus. if, for example, we question the possibility for citizens, for workers in the candidate countries, to move freely throughout the european union from the outset, if we want to delay the recognition of this right for citizens of the east, which is one of the union's key principles, we will further undermine support for the difficult reforms required to be able to join. and here's the other pain point: public support, inside and outside the european union. this support is weak and diminishes with time, as pat cox and many speakers after him have noted: i would therefore welcome the information campaign mentioned by the commissioner, even though the funding for this campaign seems rather meagre. the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter, but it is not yet clear whether the council will take a decision on the matter. we must convince the citizens of the europe of today and of the europe of tomorrow, of the europe of the future, of the enlarged europe, that the costs - serious, heavy - are less than the benefits that will be forthcoming in the immediate future. many of us feel that in order to stimulate and maintain this support, it would have been useful to set dates for accession. in the past, the use of dates has served to speed up the process of integration, but it was difficult to reach agreement on this point and we agreed to refrain from discussing it in our individual reports and to mention it, rather vaguely, in mr elmar brok's report. in poland, at least on an official level, people are still talking about 2003; i am not saying that the european union should not be involved in the negotiations, but that it should be involved in the negotiations, and that it should be involved in the negotiations, and that it should not be involved in the negotiations. we have made too many unfulfilled promises to poland, the countries of the east, the former communist countries. get rid of communism, we said, and we'll help you. they got rid of it and we didn't help them. now, therefore, it should not surprise us that in these countries, in the face of the growing gap between rich and poor, the spread of crime, prostitution and drugs, the number of those who would even prefer to return to life under the old regime, under the communist dictatorship, is increasing. if this trend were to intensify, it would be the most obvious confirmation of the failure of our policy towards the east. we must try to avoid this, ladies and gentlemen, with all our might.

in writing. - the enlargement of the european union is a political priority, and that priority cannot be conditioned or reduced by any other motivation than the rigorous assessment of the applicant countries' possession of the parameters of the acquis communautaire. i would also like to stress the following three concepts: first, enlargement must go hand in hand with a consistent policy of openness and attention by the european union to the east and the south. the momentum for cooperation and friendship with the nations of the former ussr and the mediterranean must develop in parallel with the enlargement process. secondly, enlargement inevitably implies a revision of the financial perspective of the european union, which was envisaged and decided before enlargement was in sight. a larger europe, with more tasks and responsibilities, requires more financial resources. the financial perspective must therefore be revised as a matter of urgency and the budget for pre-accession programmes must be increased immediately. thirdly, the consequences of enlargement on the union's regional policy cannot be overlooked. cohesion policy is and will continue to be necessary for many regions which are now classified as objective 1 areas and which are destined to leave objective 1 after enlargement. it is necessary to consider new instruments and new forms of intervention for the benefit of all areas where there are deficiencies in infrastructure and service networks, such as southern italy.
in writing. - the enlargement theme was a constant feature of our speeches and discussions today; i am sure that each of us, even those who will not be speaking, will have had an opportunity during the proceedings to ask ourselves what europe means to us, to our party and to the state we represent. for me, talking about enlargement does not mean sanctioning the membership or non-membership of certain countries in europe. europe and the european union are two different things: the latter is a political entity whose genesis goes back fifty years, the former is a geographical, historical, religious, cultural, social entity whose origins are lost in the mists of time. to become a member of the union requires an application, whereas to be part of europe is like an act of birth, a blood bond that unites all the peoples of this wonderful continent. let us not forget this when we talk about enlargement; we are here to assess, rightly, economic, political and social criteria, but let us be careful not to make meaningless an act which is in itself essentially inevitable and predestined. poland, hungary, the czech republic, to name just a few of the 'candidates': can anyone deny that they are part of our history, our culture, our origins? of course, this does not mean that we are abandoning our responsibilities: it is essential to verify the introduction of the acquis communautaire, and it is also necessary that the union fulfils the commitments it has made to these states in the context of the pre-accession strategy. for the proper management of this extremely delicate transition, we must not underestimate the need for a healthy pragmatism, in order to avoid unnecessary conflicts of principle. on the whole we are all in favour of an enlarged union, but this result will only be fully achieved when the candidate countries have carried out the necessary structural reforms, when the european union has equipped itself with the institutions and decision-making procedures appropriate to the management of such a situation and, above all, when we finally realise that europe is not a matter of political status but above all of common origins and history, blood and tears, dreams and hopes that bind us together beyond political and economic problems.

it is not a question of a single currency, but of a single currency. it is a matter of the technical group of independent members. after all, as the great anglo-saxon democracies teach us, racism and discrimination are fought with liberal democracy, not with the limitation and progressive erosion of freedom of opinion and expression, of association and economic freedom.

commission - mr president, in reply to the honourable member's question, i should like to say that the preliminary draft budget adopted by the commission on 10 may contains an appropriation of eur 1 million under budget line a-3015 for the european lesser spoken languages office and the mercator centres. the commission has not entered specific appropriations for the financing of projects directly in favour of regional and minority languages, for the reasons i shall explain. the interinstitutional agreement of 6 may 1999 between the european parliament, the council and the commission on budgetary discipline and improvement of the budgetary procedure states that appropriations for actions without a legal basis - as is the case - for projects relating to the promotion and safeguarding of regional and minority languages and cultures, may be entered for a maximum of three financial years only, provided, however, that a legal basis is envisaged at a later stage. in view of this limitation and in view of the possibilities for financing projects involving minority languages, in the context of the european year of languages 2001, it was decided not to enter specific appropriations in 2001, but i am considering the possibility of more sustainable support in the future for these languages, and within the framework defined by the 1999 agreement. in other words, i really hope that the european year of languages will get something going and that by the end of that year we can all come up with a sustainable solution that does not force us to come back every year and fight for funding. it is noted, however, that regional and minority languages and cultures may be supported under a number of other actions in the programme. for example, preparatory activities to stimulate the use of digital content on global networks and to promote linguistic diversity in the information society: culture 2000, media, and to the extent that the proposed projects contribute to the achievement of the objectives of these actions. however, there is no specific amount for minority languages within these activities, which does not prevent the use of these programmes for these purposes.
