the commission is not prepared to accept this. i am not going to go into the details of the commission's proposals. the commission's major reform project, summarized in the white paper, is primarily aimed at increasing efficiency, that is, a real improvement in financial management, and this is comprehensive for all parts of the budget. the money will be spent more effectively and more efficiently in the future, and of course there will be better guarantees that the money will be spent for the purposes for which it was earmarked by the budgetary authority. this is the ultimate objective and my colleague, mr kinnock, has made it clear again and again how many steps we are going to take to achieve this objective, because the reform process is made up of many actions. i would point out that we have already implemented a lot of these individual steps, whether it be the question of job descriptions, or the setting up of a central financial service in the directorate-general for budgets, to name just two important steps. we are now dealing with the amendment to the financial regulation, which was actually introduced only in 1998, when it was realised that it was very important not only to carry out ex ante control but also to carry out internal ex post control, that is to say to have an internal audit service. it is only since 1998, with the seventh amendment to the old financial regulation, that the independent financial controller has been responsible for both tasks. and then, shortly after that, the independent expert council decided that this construction cannot be the ultimate wisdom because it involves conflict. whether or not such conflicts have actually occurred, there is a potential for conflict. this alone can lead to the question whether the person who has given his approval for an issue before is really able to control it accurately afterwards - with all critical distance. the very fact that there might even be the appearance that perhaps there is no independence should lead us to consider this function separately again. that is the proposal. it was also pointed out that this proposal should of course be part of the overall revision of the financial regulation, but since the overall revision of the financial regulation will take more time - simply because of the complexity of the matter - the commission has asked that this single point be decided in a fast-track procedure. i would like to say very briefly on the question of the budgetary regulation as a whole that i am very sorry that the revised version is still not available in all the languages. i will do everything i can to speed up the process so that parliament finally has this work available in all the languages. i would like to thank both committees - the committee on budgetary control and the committee on budgets - for this intensive debate and especially the rapporteurs, mr van hulten and mr dell'alba, who cannot be here today. i really appreciate that mr van hulten has made it his personal business to come up with a very good solution for this change in the budgetary system and thus to get this key element of the reform under way. the commission has not yet adopted the proposal. the commission agrees with the introduction of this additional recital. this recital - and the amendments to article 2a which you have proposed - relates to your concern expressed here that the financial controller could be weakened in his ex ante control function during the transitional period. it will not be so, but we have decided - and i am assuming only the number of posts - that this area of ex ante control will have 80 posts available for this transitional period. i would like to point out once again - because there is sometimes a misunderstanding - that ex ante control is based on a sampling method. it has so far controlled 10% of operations, but these accounted for 89% of the budget. that's why you always have to talk about it. at present, this has been reduced to about 80%, but it is based on a risk assessment. this means that in some areas where there is a high risk, there is even 100% control. i can understand the concern that if we do not carry out such prior checks before we start spending, we could run a deficit. the commission naturally shares parliament's concern. i can therefore only emphasize once again that we have developed a very precise procedure to check whether the individual directorates-general which will be responsible for this ex ante control in the future are capable of doing so. only if they are able to do so will the sampling, the selection, which is often controlled, be reduced. of course, that's a security that must be present. i would like to say briefly that the commission accepts amendment no 2, which indeed - and this is very important - provides for an annual report to be sent to the financial controller in order to ensure greater transparency. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the financial interests of the european communities against fraud is a very good one, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for the work he has done in this area. it's a matter of experience, of course. perhaps you will eventually come to the conclusion that it should be made compulsory, but first you should give them a free pass. i believe that this will also facilitate the implementation of this reform. i find this proposal so sensible that i am almost sorry i did not come up with it myself. but it also shows how important it is that the commission and parliament complement each other constructively. i would therefore like to thank you for your suggestions and advice. the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner reding, ladies and gentlemen, i believe that this report on the possibilities of parental control of television programmes for minors deals with a subject of extreme importance and topical interest, all the more topical and important in view of the proliferation of television programmes and the increasingly wide and uncontrolled spread of the internet. i would like to add two points: the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the proposal for a directive on the protection of children against the dangers of ionizing radiation. just to give an example, last week in italy, a traffic of images of pedophilia pornography via the internet was discovered. the news was then broadcast on public television, unfortunately using some of the images taken from the sites under investigation, thus causing great concern among the public about the unwarranted use of these images, which are or have been definitely inappropriate and harmful to minors. as you know, the european commission is preparing a report on the implementation of the 'television without frontiers' directive in the coming months, and it is in this report that the guidelines and assessments on the protection of minors will also have to be included. i would also like to point out that article 22 (2) of the directive explicitly requires all member states to take appropriate measures to ensure that the broadcasts of television broadcasters do not include any programme which is likely to seriously harm the physical, mental or moral development of minors, in particular programmes containing scenes of pornography or gratuitous violence. so beyond simple words, we are all aware that the task is not easy. however, in the light of these considerations, our task is to identify the objectives which we can reasonably hope to achieve in order to achieve genuine and serious protection of children. first, we must identify all those technological systems for consciously managing the increasing stream of broadcasts, both television and network, which can be considered harmful to the psychological development of children: i refer in particular to filtering systems and programme guidance systems. this is particularly so in view of the introduction of the digital system which would facilitate their use and dissemination. second point: it is important to point out that all the technological control systems i have mentioned cannot, however, be without two other elements, which are, so to speak, propaedeutic. firstly, it is necessary to encourage the development of information and awareness-raising policies at national level for families and for the education sector in general. secondly, there is a need to encourage serious responsibility on the part of producers for the quality of television programmes and on the part of broadcasters for the way in which they are broadcast. of course, there is no need for harmonization of legislation on the protection of minors, not only because, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, each member state is sovereign in this matter, but also because cultural and moral conceptions, and therefore assessments of these issues, differ greatly from country to country: the definition of violence is different, for example, in the case of the definition of the age of the child, and so on. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the media are not used to the detriment of children. i would like to sum up the proposals in this report which i consider to be the most important and the most practical. first, the creation of an expert group of senior figures, appointed by the member states, to help define minimum standards for the protection of children in the media; secondly, the creation of a code of self-regulation among all operators in the sector; thirdly, the possibility of encouraging and making filtering systems accessible to both tv and the internet. i conclude by saying that, in line with the votes in committee, i cannot agree with amendments nos 1 and 4 by the liberal group and amendments nos 5 and 6 by the socialist group, while i can accept amendments nos 2 and 3, also by the liberal group.

president of the italian republic. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i feel the importance and responsibility of addressing this parliament, which is the only directly and democratically elected european institution. i pay tribute to the europeanist spirit of your president and his determination to advance the european political project. working for europe today means not delaying the central question of the governance of the union, and proceeding with institutional reform and enlargement; it is important to recognise that the introduction of the euro has been a turning point in the integration process. we are once again deciding the fate of our continent, as the great statesmen of the 1950s did. half a century of peace and active coexistence between peoples repeatedly torn apart by war testify to the meaning and usefulness of european unification. but we know that the process is incomplete and that incompleteness threatens its viability . italy is a founding country of the union; it intends to remain an active member. this will is supported by genuine popular feeling, which has already been expressed on several occasions in the italian parliament, with broad consensus on the fundamental issues of european policy and security. our own successes present us with new tasks. enlargement, which now requires radical institutional reforms, is the result of the triumph of a democratic and united europe in the long confrontation with the eastern bloc. the stakes are high, starting with the forthcoming european councils in biarritz and nice, from which the following must emerge: a charter of fundamental rights, recognising those who are proud to be citizens of europe; a union moving towards integration; the launch of enhanced cooperation to give strength and flexibility to the union. each member state must assume its own responsibilities for the future of the union. the experience of these 50 years confirms that there is always a need for a driving force: a vanguard open to all, without legal members, and made up of countries convinced of the project's validity and determined to implement it. institutional reform, enlargement, economic governance, the defence dimension and a common legal area are the new pillars of a cohesive union ready to meet challenges. the commission must promote the common interests of the union, advance the governance of the economy. i would like to thank the president of the commission for his authoritative remark yesterday in this house on the role, collegiality and management capacity of the commission. (applause) we have identified the path to follow and the goals to achieve. the commission's proposal is to set up a european network of national experts to help the commission to develop its own strategy. the complexity of the european functions makes institutional reform an absolute necessity. the problem is not new. it was put in place with the first enlargement to nine in 1973, then to twelve in 1986, and finally with the last enlargement in 1995, and was at the centre of the amsterdam european council in 1997 because of the obvious need to adapt to a union of 15 members the instruments and rules designed for six and for a community with more limited functions and a more restricted political scope. the matter was then adjourned; it's inevitable that we'll have to face it. the individual national states, like europe, will continue to be convincing actors in the international community. the isolation of the european states in the world of globalisation would lead to self-sufficiency and marginalisation. the union must speak with one voice in foreign policy, project a common defence and security capability. enlargement is an ethical as well as a political imperative: we must offer the candidate countries the same opportunity to contribute to the great european construction that our countries have enjoyed in the past, favoured by their democratic development and the security enjoyed by western europe. enlargement means strengthening; the european council in brussels on 14 and 15 december adopted a resolution on the situation in the middle east. in addition to the countries concerned by enlargement, there is an arc of countries to the east and south that yearn for a strong link with europe. in our own interests, the union must project stability and prosperity across its present and future borders, and look innovatively at the relationship to be built with non-candidates. there is a wider european area to anchor to the union by rediscovering the historical soul of a larger geographical area. in 453 days, euro banknotes will be in circulation. in a few years' time, the new generations will have only the memory of national currencies. the euro, with its centralization of monetary governance in the european system of central banks, has pushed the integration process beyond the point of no return. the euro is only one stage in the creation of an economic, social, political and cultural europe. it makes it inexorably necessary. when monetary union was decided, it was understood that an asymmetry was being formed, but it was hoped that this would be eliminated by progress towards a common governance of the economy. the concerns generated by the current level of euro quotations are justified, but it should not be forgotten that the major currencies have been alternately in the dust and on the high side in the daily quotations of the markets. the european economic recovery is now a fact. we are using the current weakness of the euro, which is fuelling greater price competitiveness, to accelerate the productivity leap that innovation can generate in both production tools and modes of production and in the organisation of markets. the debate on the european constitution, ladies and gentlemen, is a sign of vitality and of confidence in european ideals, and of the awareness of a genuine community of values. the affirmation of an idea is nourished by realism and idealism. the drafting of the charter of fundamental rights was prompted by the need to place europe in the consciousness of civil society. it is a testament to the fact that european integration is not an artificial construct but has a soul: the european identity. the european charter is meant to tell the world, and even more so ourselves, who we are and what we believe in. if we do not say so now, at this delicate and tumultuous juncture in european and world history, when will we say so? the contours of our community of values are better carved and more advanced than we ourselves sometimes believe. the debate, to which each country contributes its own sensibility, tradition and culture, is the vehicle for bringing these issues to the fore, defining and affirming them. with the charter of fundamental rights, europe is taking an important step in transforming an area which has hitherto been predominantly economic into a common area of rights, by establishing values and rules which define the notion of european citizenship. it is important that the charter, once adopted by the european council, be disseminated to citizens so that they can recognise their european identity in its content. the charter must also be linked to the reformed treaties. the connection can be made in various ways: by incorporating the charter into the new legal body, or by linking it as a preamble. i personally think of a charter as the first part of a constitution, to be supplemented by a second part which defines the different institutions, their powers and their mutual relations. the question of whether europe should have a federal or a confederal configuration is likely to lead us astray. the time has come to identify and bring out the elements of convergence and to proceed pragmatically, free from schematics. the reformist will of europeans will find solutions which allow federal institutions, such as the european central bank, to operate jointly with other institutions on an intergovernmental basis. the image and role of europe and the individual european states in the world of the 21st century depend on the results we will achieve at the forthcoming european council meetings. regional integration processes in the americas, the pacific and asia look to the european union as a model and as a partner. in these respects too, let us not be deceived into thinking that time is our ally. we are not the only ones who are dictating the timetable for the european unification process. the dimension that only the union can achieve becomes a necessity in order to keep pace with the other major players on the international scene. two regions of vital interest directly challenge europe: the balkans and the mediterranean. in the balkans, the political signal has been and must remain crystal clear: violence, ethnic sectarianism do not pay; the fact is not acceptable. the consolidation of democratic values and human rights cannot be a signpost. (applause) the recent elections in yugoslavia have shown how strong the yugoslav people's desire for freedom and democratic will for change is. we must ensure that in the european aid for economic reconstruction in the balkans, the results strictly follow the promises. finally, we must give the countries and peoples of south-east europe hope of joining the union's institutional framework. in the mediterranean, there is still a lack of a real sense of the european presence and the role of the union. europe is in the mediterranean! (applause) the euro-mediterranean partnership, as it has been implemented so far, is not enough. it must be made a force for cooperation in the field of interdependence, an interdependence which the oil boom evokes immediately. we need a decision-making forum to deal with issues of central importance to both sides, such as migration flows, the transfer of production factors, energy supplies. above all, we must believe in the mediterranean vocation of europe. the explosion of violence in recent days in the west bank, jerusalem and gaza has caused anxiety. it shows the confusion resulting from theexhausting slowness of the negotiating process. what has happened confirms that there is no alternative to peace but war with intolerable human costs. the whole of the civilised world is calling for an end to all acts of violence, for normalcy to return and for negotiations to resume. europe must be an active part of this. (applause) i would like to thank europe has a unique cultural, social, legal and scientific heritage, which is nourished by the variety and vitality of its national components. european originality is not afraid of confrontation with any other cultural matrix; it fades when its historical and cultural identity is discoloured; it is a fact that the european community is not only a political group, but also a political group. the united nations millennium summit concluded by identifying the major global issues on which the world community is called upon to act in the interests of all humanity: the european union is a global community of nations, and its members are all citizens of the union. how can we not imagine europe playing a leading role in each of these? in a very short time, compared with the many centuries of history of our continent, the 'idea of europe' has gone from 'utopia' to agreements, institutions, a community, today a 'union'. those who have lived in our time and look back, see peace instead of war; the spread of unprecedented prosperity; the growth of open and democratic societies that are mutually reinforcing. if i speak of europe today, i identify it with the national interest, because i am witness to the incalculable benefits that italy, like the other member states, has received from the success of european integration. as an italian citizen and president of the italian republic, i have never made a secret of my europeanist convictions. they do not diminish the love i have for my country, which i have served for sixty years; i am not saying that the commission has not taken the necessary steps to ensure that the budget is properly implemented. the europe i believe in is an exaltation, not a negation, of our national societies and the values they express. (applause) i would like to thank i would like to express this feeling with the following quote, taken from the notebooks of a great european and a great frenchman, charles secondat de montesquieu: if i knew something that would be useful to my family but not to my country, i would try to forget it. if i knew something useful to my country but harmful to europe, or useful to europe but harmful to mankind, i would regard it as a crime". ladies and gentlemen, our common future begins in this house. being a member of the european parliament means looking to the future and to the legacy we want to leave to the new generations of our countries, of our entire continent. being a member of the european parliament means contributing to the creation and consolidation of institutions which are the best guarantee of stability, coexistence and prosperity. in half a century, the union has changed the face of europe and transformed the relations between our peoples. the elimination of armed conflict from european life is itself a landmark achievement. it is an achievement so well-earned that it is becoming less and less known. two whole generations have known nothing but this europe of interdependence and open borders. as the guardian and interpreter of the achievements of the past, the european parliament is the guarantor and active participant in the completion of the major changes under way. the deadlines ahead call for strong cooperation between all the institutions. the challenging work of the european parliament, the council and the commission must interact with the initiatives of the member states in the interests of the union. the greatness of the work must not discourage us. it takes determination, firmness and political will to follow a path that has already been set. biarritz and nice are the obligatory passage of an institutional reform that can no longer be postponed and of the charter of fundamental rights. 2002 will be the first year that the euro will be used, no longer just as a currency but as a tangible banknote in the pockets of all european citizens. subsequently, with the entry into force of the treaty on the reform of the institutions, the union will be ready to handle the new major and most pervasive responsibilities for which it is already preparing: welcoming the first new members; consolidating the common foreign policy; preparing a common military force; to give final effect to the area of freedom , security and justice; the european council also adopted the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. but we all know that if we believe in them and want them firmly, we will have already come halfway. the very content of the project, the global context in which we operate, requires us to make a close, high-profile advance: the european union is not a mere institution, but a political body, a political body, a political body, a political body. the european parliament is alive and well! long live the european union! (loud and prolonged applause)

- madam president, the case of mr pacheco pereira has been examined very carefully by the committee on legal affairs and citizens' rights: the opinion, which was adopted and is before the house today, is that immunity should not be withdrawn. it is justified and substantiated in the excellent report by mr mccormick, whose main reasons are as follows: there can and must be no influence of political affiliation or nationality; the legal basis must be sound and definitive; immunity is not a personal privilege but a guarantee of parliament's independence through its members from any other power; the date of the contested act is irrelevant, nor is the personal willingness of the person concerned to waive immunity. the reference in the protocol to national legislation does not mean that the european parliament is being superseded but is a procedural matter, whereas each parliament - in this case the european parliament - retains ownership of its autonomous decisions. finally, mr pacheco pereira has been politically active and therefore cannot be held responsible for any crime. the ppe's position is clear, but it should be pointed out that if mr pacheco pereira had been italian, he would have been tried without the european parliament knowing anything about it! the italian judiciary does not ask for any authorization when the person concerned is a member of the european parliament and acts in violation of every principle of due respect for this institution. already in this parliament some members have been tried without a request for waiver of immunity. i could not personally speak to denounce the fact, as it concerned party colleagues who have always been targeted for political reasons, and so my speech would have seemed instrumental. but today the same thing is happening again and it concerns a colleague, yes, from the epp but not from my political area in italy. mr cocilovo has been sent to trial without parliament's knowledge, in contempt of parliament itself. this is a very serious fact which you, madam president, cannot ignore. the autonomy of the european parliament is at stake!
- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i believe that the lisbon summit has given us a preview of a europe which can no longer be and must no longer be merely an economic europe but must become a political entity. the european parliament has been a political actor for a long time. i therefore believe that the commission's proposal on the social agenda is absolutely positive. i would like to thank the rapporteur for the report, but i also feel that i share a large part of the report drawn up by mr van lancker, because i do not think that when mr van lancker makes a precise reference to certain and clear objectives, to concrete instruments and above all to precise deadlines, he is referring back to an old socialist logic, as someone here has said. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. if we are talking about a charter of rights and if we are looking favourably at a european constitution, we cannot be blind, but we must say that all the necessary steps must be taken, even if this requires more precise legislation. i do not think that mr van lancker intended to create laws to regulate absolutely everything. i think it is rather necessary, when coordination measures do not produce the desired results, when citizens have encountered and found disparities between one state and another and when there is no social harmonization, to ensure that this harmonization is achieved. the problem of open coordination must therefore be accompanied by a whole series of measures to focus on the social legal bases, without which we shall have difficulty in persuading the states to harmonize a social policy in the sense of equality and equal opportunities.

- mr president, i too would like to congratulate the rapporteur, the commissioner and the minister, mrs péry, on the presentation of the social agenda. i believe that the social policy agenda is a very important political document which identifies the instruments, the areas of intervention, the timetable for implementation and which is intended to ensure a positive and dynamic interaction between economic, social and employment policies. these instruments are intended to make the european social model more responsive to the changing reality. i fully share the view of mr van lancker in his report and i would like to stress one point in particular, which has already been mentioned by both the rapporteur and mr péry in their speeches, namely the need for all the instruments to be activated at european level and, therefore, for the methodology of open coordination to be accompanied by a strengthening of the legal dimension. that's what happens in many countries. in conclusion, i would say that, for example, in my country last week parliament passed a new law on assistance proposed by a female minister, as well as three representatives of the three institutions, which represents a revolution after more than a hundred years in which an old law on assistance was in force.

the commission. - mr president, i would like to thank the rapporteur, mrs van lancker, and the french presidency in particular for the excellent cooperation we have had so far. i shall try very economic policy and the employment strategy. this means that it is the only way to meet europe's objective of competitiveness, since our concern for business and the economy is constant, but also for social cohesion, since our concern for citizens and their well-being is also constant. the second element of the new approach is quality. quality as a new political concept that addresses the issue of working conditions, industrial relations, social services. these two policy approaches run through the whole of the content. what are the key elements of the content? there's three. a set of actions and proposals concerning employment. i would say that our effort through the employment strategy, to strengthen and enrich it along the way - because the whole social agenda has a dynamic of change - is to support competitiveness and entrepreneurship in the european union, flexibility in the labour market, along with security, mobility, by supporting new models of work, and supporting and analysing new models of relations between enterprises and workers, as well as the effects of competition and major restructuring on employment and the welfare state. the second element of the social agenda is a set of actions relating to social policy. i would like to mention here the proposal to combat poverty and exclusion, the new work we have undertaken on pensions and social protection, policies for the disabled, but i would particularly like to stress politically the need for a new approach to social policy. it is not only important to calculate the cost of social policy, which is often seen by some political viewpoints as an obstacle to economic development, but we must calculate the cost of not having social policy. i think this analysis will lead us to some interesting new results and approaches. the third content issue is enlargement. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work is a very old-fashioned to talk about deregulation, legislation, whether or not we need legislation. it is clear that in europe we have a fairly complete legislative system, but changes in the labour market, changes in the economy, changes in the environment due to globalisation and the information society are creating new needs. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. if they can be dealt with in other ways and other methods, we will use them. the proposal for a scoreboard, for a specific way of monitoring the social agenda, is a great challenge. the difficulty is that the social agenda, because of its legal basis in the treaty, is not a set of legislation, a set of directives with concrete steps for the member states. it is also difficult to define european objectives which will have the same effect for all member states, given that the reality is different. we therefore believe that, firstly, the common european indicators, a task which is currently in the process of being completed, but also the national objectives, the need for each country to draw up a scoreboard for itself and to have a monitoring system, are a first step which can give us concrete results. finally, as regards procedures, i should like to congratulate parliament on its initiatives in the dialogue with civil society and the important contribution that this dialogue has made to the agenda, but i should also like to stress that there has been a debate with parliament, with the member states, with the social partners, at european and national level, and i believe that there has been the possibility of combining national specificities so that the agenda is not just ambitious, but above all feasible and effective. the commission's proposal for a directive on the approximation of the laws of the member states relating to the labelling of foodstuffs intended for human consumption is a very good one.

- the next item is the report (a5-0277/2000) by mrs sartori, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, on the report from the commission to the council and the european parliament on the review of the single mediumterm financial support mechanism for the balance of payments of the member states (com (99) 628 - c5-0307/2000 - 2000/0807 (cns)).
the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs i am presenting to the house today a motion for a resolution on the commission report on the single mediumterm financial support mechanism for the balance of payments of the member states. at present, financial support is governed by council regulation no 1969 of 1988. this mechanism can be activated either at the request of a member state or under article 119 of the treaty establishing the european community, a provision which remains in force during the third stage of economic and monetary union for the states with a derogation, currently denmark, the united kingdom and sweden. this regulation and this proposal for a regulation have combined two mechanisms, namely the medium-term financial assistance and the community loan mechanism to support the medium-term balance of payments of the member states, into a single medium-term financial support mechanism. this proposal is aimed at the ceiling of the mechanism. the fact that only three countries are currently eligible for the programme suggests that the sum available to date, amounting to eur 16 billion, may be adjusted; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. therefore, even if the increase in convergence of states reduces the likelihood of the mechanism being activated, it must have adequate resources if it is to be activated by several states at the same time. that is why it is proposed to reduce the amount available from eur 16 million to eur 12 million only. the resolution i am presenting also considers the possibility of studying the creation of a special balance of payments support mechanism for the applicant countries. it is obvious that this is a hypothesis that looks to the future and therefore does not weigh on the situation we are experiencing today, but it is a hypothesis that i thought could, at the very least, be studied in depth to prepare ourselves if these problems should arise.
the commission mr president, i thank mr sartori for his report, which we very much appreciated. the aim of this commission report is to provide a basis for examining the single mediumterm financial support mechanism and for a possible review of it. the financing mechanism implements article 119 of the ec treaty, which remains in force during the third stage of economic and monetary union only for member states not participating in the single currency. the last review was carried out in october 1997 on the basis of a report drawn up by the commission. on that occasion the council approved the commission's position that the mechanism should be maintained and decided that a new review, under the same procedure, would be necessary in the light of the changes linked to the start of the third stage. the commission is therefore required to submit a report to the council so that the council can re-examine the mechanism. the report makes three main recommendations. first recommendation is: the single mechanism should be maintained as an instrument for the implementation of article 119 of the treaty, which will continue to apply to member states that are not part of the euro area; as long as they do not participate in the single currency, these member states, as well as all the new members of the community, may encounter problems with their balance of payments and may therefore wish to use the mechanism in question. given the current level of economic, financial and monetary integration, the likelihood of some member states encountering balance of payments difficulties is extremely low from an institutional point of view; however, the mechanism must remain in place. second recommendation: the possibility of using credits granted by other member states to finance loans granted under the mechanism should be abolished as, for various reasons, it has never been used. in future, recourse to the capital market should remain the only possible option. third and final recommendation: the reduction in the number of member states that could now require this form of financial support, as well as the need to cover the potential needs of new member states, justify the reduction of the intervention ceiling for the mechanism from eur 16 billion to eur 12 billion. the economic and financial committee drew up an opinion which it forwarded to the presidency on 14 july 2000. the committee of the regions considers that the conclusions of the commission's analysis of the single mechanism are in line with its own views.
- thank you, commissioner. the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at 12.30 p.m.
- the next item is the report (a5-0195/2000) by mrs klaß, on behalf of the committee on development and cooperation, on the proposal for a council directive amending directive 68/193/eec on the marketing of plant propagating material for vines (com (2000) 59 - c5-0090/2000 - 200/0036 (cns)).
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the need for a new directive to review the conditions for marketing vine propagating material in the community is now very strong. the basic legislation in force dates back to 1968, but in the meantime great strides have been made in this field: new materials have been experimented with, often naturally, sometimes through genetic modification. hence the urgency of a new discipline which recognises these new possibilities for european vine growers and, at the same time, is concerned with the safeguarding of traditional vine varieties. i think that the klaß report should be approved, especially with the additional guarantees provided by amendments such as that of the committee on agriculture clarifying the reference to 220/90, as will be amended for the gmo aspect. another amendment, by myself and mr garot, calls for a further application of the precautionary principle and calls for the protection of those traditional vine varieties which might otherwise lose ground to new experimentation. i also believe that referring to the possibility of genetic modification, with this precautionary principle, means, for example, reducing the intensive use of plant protection products. the amendments tabled by mr auroi and mr graefe zu baringdorf, chairman of our committee on agriculture, are also a precautionary measure, as a further guarantee of experimentation. i therefore believe that mr klaß's report is a step in the right direction in this area, which urgently requires new legislation, and which is a key and strategic area for european agriculture and the wine industry.
the commission the answer is yes, mr president: the amendment is accepted.

mr president, i am referring to a resolution which was discussed and adopted unanimously last week by the committee on constitutional affairs, and i thank the president, mr napolitano, for having tabled it and for having signed it. this resolution draws the attention of the community institutions and the forthcoming intergovernmental conference in nice to the question of islands, of insularity, or rather to the principle that insularity as such should be recognized as one of the criteria for community intervention, in view of the objective conditions which any form of insularity implies for these regions. anyone who has studied the problem knows that there is a "yellow" in translations: the italian version accepts the principle that insularity is one of the criteria sufficient for community action, the french version expresses a different concept, followed by other languages, and the english translation is exactly in the middle, lending itself to both interpretations. i shall not dwell on the linguistic issue; i would simply point out - because it is an important historical fact - that the official version drawn up by the intergovernmental conference in amsterdam, written in french, is exactly the same as the present italian text. it expresses the idea that insularity is in itself a sufficient criterion. in fact, the official text of that intergovernmental conference - which i will send to commissioner barnier and the minister if your legal offices have not sent it to them - clearly shows that this opinion actually came from that place, and was then erroneously translated into other languages. but i won't go any further because there are stronger arguments than the literal one. there are the passages in the treaties which establish the principle of cohesion and there is declaration no 30 which, in stating and applying the principle of cohesion to this case, says exactly and verbatim: 'the conference recognises that island regions suffer from structural disadvantages due to their insularity, the persistence of which hinders their economic and social development.' it is not on the basis of a number of languages or a number of translations, but on the basis of a fundamental principle of the charters, of the treaties, namely the principle of cohesion, that we ask that the islands be recognized as such, as a possible object of special intervention and special attention. we are not asking for charity, commissioner, mr president. we are only asking the community to allow us to be citizens on an equal footing with others, not citizens who are more favoured than others. if you look, for example, at the development map, you will see that in italy, in these decades, it has followed exactly the limit of communicability: the commission has also taken the initiative of drawing up a report on the situation in the community, which is to be submitted to the council in the near future. mr president, i come from a land, an island, which has always had this problem, eternal - as have other italian islands and, i believe, tens and hundreds of islands in other countries - an island which has always made a strong contribution, has always been convinced of national development and which, today, to the idea of national development couples and adds the european one: but on this island, the effects of development, progress, news, communications have always, as on all other islands, come years behind. if europe does not want to be merely the battleground of globalisation but wants to be a community as a whole, which in all its articulations and in all its expressions is marching unitedly and compactly towards a new progress and a new civilization, we ask you not to have more than others but to be able to be citizens like others. we are not asking for anything concrete or special, we are not asking for aid: we are asking for this principle of insularity to be accepted by all, so that all citizens of the union are equal at the starting lines, so that all have the same chances of arriving. the rapporteur. - mr president, in the countries with high technological development, the protection of private life is increasingly at risk and therefore adequate protection is needed. the countries of the european union are at the forefront of privacy protection in comparison with systems adopted in other parts of the world, at least those countries which have implemented the two directives - 46 of 1995 and 66 of 1997 - which ensure the protection of individuals with regard to the processing of personal data. the european model considers the protection of personal data as a fundamental right, guaranteed by rules with legal force, inspired by the principle of informational self-determination, i.e. the principle that everyone must be able to decide whether and how data concerning him or her can be collected and used. in this model, compliance with the rules and procedures is ensured by an independent authority and, ultimately, by the courts. since a large number of personal data are also collected and processed by the union institutions and bodies, the system of safeguards of the european model must also apply to them. the commission has therefore taken steps to include in article 8 of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union a provision defining the right of everyone to the protection of personal data, which must be processed fairly, for specified purposes, with the consent of the person concerned and under the control of an independent authority. furthermore, article 286 of the treaty establishing the european community, introduced by the treaty of amsterdam, provides that community acts relating to the processing of personal data - namely the two directives mentioned above - apply to the community institutions and bodies and that an independent supervisory body is to be set up to monitor their application. the proposal for a regulation, which parliament is now considering, implements these provisions, transposes community legislation and establishes the european data protection supervisor, thus ensuring concrete and adequate guarantees for this fundamental right. it is hoped that, in the course of months of work and with the constant help of the commission, a detailed regulation has been sought and identified which would respond to the concerns expressed both in the council and in the parliamentary committees responsible for examining the merits and expressing opinions. the willingness of all the institutions concerned to discuss this matter has made possible exemplary cooperation which will, i hope, enable us to reach an agreement at first reading. the many compromise amendments largely reflect the solutions identified in the council, which already take account of proposals which have emerged from the parliamentary debate. acceptable solutions were thus reached, for example on the appointment of the european controller and the deputy controller, which was left to the agreement of parliament and the council on proposals for names selected by the commission following a call for tenders. your rapporteur, with the unanimous support of the committee on civil liberties and human rights, nevertheless insists on certain amendments which, for example, offer an original solution to the debate on the scope of the regulation. this remains confined to the community but a form of protection is identified also against the activities of the institutions outside the first pillar; this solution is achieved by reference to the rules on the protection of privacy which govern the right of access to documents, as regulated by article 255 of the treaty establishing the community. article 255, unlike article 286, is also referred to in the treaty on european union. the commission also intends to cooperate with the national supervisory authorities and the authorities established under the third pillar with a view to coordinating and progressively harmonizing the whole of the rules in this sensitive area. in addition, an autonomous budget line is provided for, in accordance with the system in force for the european ombudsman, in order to better guarantee the independence of the controller of personal data. i am confident that the patient work carried out will find the full support of the european parliament and the council. for the first time, there will be a codecision procedure at first reading on a text which is extremely complex and fraught with technical difficulties, and which concerns a particularly sensitive area for the protection of individual freedoms. the technical complexity of the text itself suggested that the vote be postponed until the next part-session to allow for a thorough checking of all the language versions, which has not yet been done. if this result is achieved, as i hope, it will be due to the mediating capacity of the council presidency, the positive contribution of the commission and the sensitivity to the common interest and to the rights of citizens of the members of parliament from all the political groups who contributed to the adoption of the report in the committee on civil liberties, which i wish to thank publicly.

forget that article 299 (2) also says that community cohesion and the unity of the internal market must be respected. and that means, ladies and gentlemen, that we must - i say: we, you and i - find a balance between respecting the general rules and adapting policies to the specific needs of the outermost regions. to seek, as mr marques said earlier, equality of opportunity for all citizens, but to balance, ladies and gentlemen, must first be sought on a case-by-case basis. let me give you an example. your report, mrs sudre, rightly emphasizes the need for action over the long term. mr ripoll, earlier, also stressed the importance of the sustainability or permanence of the measures taken, precisely because of the permanence of disabilities. what is the situation in this respect? some measures, such as the posei agricultural regulations, have an indefinite duration. on the other hand, in many areas, such as taxation or customs, the coherence of community law and the unity of the internal market require that there be deadlines, even if they are quite long, preferably a mid-term review. ladies and gentlemen, i believe that our report of 14 march 2000 outlines a strategy which should enable the european union to contribute more effectively to the sustainable development of these outermost regions and thus to implement article 299 (2) in practice. we believe that this comprehensive and coherent strategy must make it possible to achieve the real qualitative leap that your report calls for. this strategy is based on three main components: support for traditional production, agriculture and fisheries. that's the first point. support for the revival, modernization and diversification of economic activities through a better coordinated and more targeted use of the community instruments at our disposal. that's the second part. and finally, the strengthening of cooperation with countries which are located around these outermost regions, in their geographical and political environment. that's the third point. and it is the combination, the articulation between each of these components, the coherence of this overall strategy, which must make it possible to really move forward. mrs margie sudre has just mentioned, as if in a moment of concern, what she has indicated as a kind of reluctance or reservation on the part of the commission. i would like to say mr president, the vote by parliament closes this first phase of consultation on food safety issues. i only hope that this vote will not exhaust the will to act quickly and effectively in a field which touches so closely the daily lives of citizens and is one of the main test-beds of our ability to rebuild their confidence in the institutions and in politics. the momentum will be all the more necessary because the high expectations raised by the white paper are not, in my view, fully reflected in the report presented by mr bowis, despite the considerable work he has done. the creation of the european food safety authority and the definition of its powers, while a key element of the strategy proposed by the commission, do not exhaust it. a european food strategy cannot be reduced to the creation of a surveillance authority and the application of certain, albeit necessary, hygiene and health standards. there is an inseparable link between healthy eating and good eating, a link which is about raising consumer awareness even further, promoting quality and supporting typical local products which represent a great wealth of the european peoples. the vote in the committee on the environment has restored some balance by including nutrition issues and some important references to the role of small and mediumsized enterprises in safeguarding different eating habits. that is why i shall be voting in favour. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i must congratulate the rapporteur, mr bowis, on his excellent work. i should also like to say that we have recovered a very important aspect, namely the concept of a network as a european food safety authority, which should be set up in a way that complements and does not replace the safety bodies in the individual member states. however, it is also necessary to call for a balanced approach to the problem because in articles 152 and 153 of the treaty the european union provides, as a general rule, for a high level of protection of human health and consumers. these principles are the basis of the overriding and absolute interest in the human person. it is therefore necessary to ensure that the european union has the highest possible standards of food safety, but this approach - which is unanimously supported - must also analyse the economic consequences for the sectors concerned by a production requirement. article 2 of the treaty recalls that the union is committed to promoting a harmonious, balanced and sustainable development of economic activities. therefore, any legislative measure affecting a sector such as food, which represents one of the engines of european industry - 15 per cent of the total output of the manufacturing sector and 2.5 million workers - must be assessed on the basis of this twofold consideration, both principles being aimed at ensuring the overall well-being of the community. any measure to protect consumers is only profitable and in their interests if it avoids unduly harming their overall economic well-being by placing disproportionate obstacles in the way of the sector's production processes and thus of economic growth and employment. i therefore urge the commissioner, when he moves on to the legislative series, to avoid as far as possible excessive regulations and burdensome bureaucracy, particularly as regards small and mediumsized enterprises. commission. – let me first of all thank the rapporteur, mr moreira da silva, who has produced two excellent reports on our current climate change strategy. let me also express my appreciation for the continued importance the european parliament attaches to the global problem of climate change. i welcome the comprehensive debate on this issue today. this debate is particularly opportune as key decisions are to be taken only four weeks from now at the sixth conference of the parties to the convention on climate change – the so-called cop6 – in the hague. as you know, the european union strongly supports the entry into force of the kyoto protocol by 2002 at the latest, which will mean rio plus ten years. the european union intends to ratify the protocol as soon as cop6 is successfully concluded with decisions that safeguard the environmental integrity and credibility of the protocol. to achieve this, it is essential for the european union to play a strong and proactive leadership role. in this regard i would summarise the main objectives of the eu for cop6 as follows. first of all, we need to ensure that action is taken at home by industrialised countries. industrialised countries emit most greenhouse gases and have a responsibility to show leadership in tackling climate change. the outcome at cop6 should ensure this by balancing the use of kyoto mechanisms such as emissions trading with domestic action – supplementarity – and by addressing the need to demonstrate progress on policies for reducing emissions by 2005. secondly, we need to make sure that the kyoto targets are respected. industrialised countries agreed on reduction targets under the kyoto protocol. to ensure these targets are met we need to agree at cop6 on a solid framework of rules for the kyoto mechanisms and a strong and effective compliance system. these are necessary to make the mechanisms work effectively because markets can only work efficiently in a solid institutional framework. thirdly, with regard to keeping the targets meaningful, the european union has serious concerns about the inclusion of sinks because of the scientific and other uncertainties and risks associated with them. it also has concerns about the potential scale of sinks because this affects the need for action by industrialised countries to reduce their emissions. unless these concerns are met, we cannot agree to include additional forestry and land use activities other than afforestation, deforestation and reforestation. sinks should not be included in the cdm – the clean development mechanism – because this is a mechanism that should be used to bring social and economic development to countries. fourthly, we need to address the needs of developing countries and the economies in transition by promoting capacity building, transfer of technology and assistance for adaptation. in this regard, the needs of the least developed countries merit particular attention. at cop6 we should develop these issues and agree that the clean development mechanism should be based on safe, environmentally sound technologies which will help these countries develop in a less polluting way. i welcome the participation of members of the european parliament in the community delegation to cop6. a final decision concerning the number of meps to attend cop6 is expected by 31 october; the commission has proposed that the european parliament be represented by eight members. taking into account the institutional rules for such participation, these members can attend plenary meetings, and i can assure you that my staff and i will do our utmost to inform all members present at cop6 on the negotiations which are not open to observers, on a regular basis. i can also give a commitment to organise an appropriate briefing before cop6 starts, maybe between 7 and 11 november, if possible – we will try to arrange that in the best possible way. let me also comment on the question about ratification without the united states. the european union is very committed to the ratification and entry into force of the protocol by 2002 at the latest. on every occasion we urge the other parties, particularly the us and russia, also to start preparing for ratification. while theoretically the protocol can enter into force without the us ratifying, it would clearly be the second best option not to have the world's biggest emitter of greenhouse gases included in the regime. also, this would most likely have significant effects for eu competitiveness. i am pleased to note that the commission is supported by parliament and the council in its efforts to build up an effective european climate change programme. the opinion of the european parliament's committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy on this programme stresses that policies and measures should be the priority of eu climate change strategy. it is important that this strategy is endorsed by all stakeholders and that is why the commission has embarked on this multi-stakeholder process in the framework of the climate change programme. the environment council recently adopted conclusions on policies and measures to limit emissions of greenhouse gases, confirming the choices made in the framework of the european climate change programme. at the same time they indicate some specific priorities in the transport, energy efficiency and industry sectors that should be developed, taking into account the environmental impact and cost-effectiveness of these measures. these suggestions will be carefully considered in the ongoing work in the european climate change programme. as you know, the programme is up and running and the six existing working groups – flexible mechanisms, energy supply, energy consumption, transport, industry and research have been operational since last june. right from the start the european climate change programme has been a challenging integration exercise bringing together commission services, industry, ngos and national experts. the first impression is certainly positive after the first four months. a constructive attitude has developed in the different groups. a progress report on this programme will be the basis for my oral presentation at the special climate council on 7 november. despite the very short time available, the programme is already suggesting a first list of likely measures in all the relevant sectors. the promotion of combined heat and power and of renewables, the encouragement of the switch to fuels with a low carbon content, support for energy efficiency in buildings, awareness-raising in transport, improvements in light-duty vehicles, measures to control leakage and the recovery of fluorinated gases are among the preliminary proposals emerging from the european climate change programme. at the end of its consultative process, by next summer, the climate change programme will have given impetus and will have accelerated existing proposals. but, at the same time, it will have promoted new ideas. therefore, this climate change programme is a unique opportunity to bring together all the elements of an ambitious eu climate change strategy and the commission will follow-up by finalising the most promising proposals. on the green paper on emissions trading, i would like to thank members for having considered it so substantively. the commission is eager to hear the views of stakeholders and of course those of the european parliament. differences of opinion on the details should be expected when approaching a new instrument in environment policy and i warmly welcome the supportive and constructive attitude that parliament has taken. emissions trading is a new concept and there is understandable mistrust in some quarters. i hope that the green paper has gone some way towards overcoming this mistrust. emissions trading within the european union would be another policy measure that would coexist with other policy measures that are now in place or are being developed by the commission in the context of the climate change programme. the commission is not putting all its eggs in one basket. significantly reducing emissions will require a whole range of policies and measures. for the purposes of furthering the discussions within the european union, the commission outlined a vision of how emissions trading would work. it was most certainly not a definitive outline. while it might be felt that the green paper was weighted towards given options, the commission's motives are primarily to have an open mind towards this new instrument and to advocate a prudent, cautious, stepwise development of emissions trading within the eu. it was this caution that prevented the commission from envisaging from the outset that all greenhouse gases and other sectors, including the transport and household sectors, should be subject to emissions trading. ultimately a scheme that is shown to work can be extended, but first the system has to prove itself. i do not think that emissions trading favours nuclear power more than any of the other climate change measures that are being considered within the european climate change programme. it is not envisaged that nuclear power will be included in an emissions trading scheme. the case for getting started by 2005 remains as strong as ever so that the community can benefit from learning and by doing. indeed member states are already moving and the community's common interest should be kept at the forefront of our minds. moreover, it is my intention – and i have already had talks on this last october – to involve the central and eastern european countries in any future emissions trading regime. finally, the responses to the green paper that have been received so far – about 50 in number – reflect the high level of interest in this instrument. opinions on what to do next vary and the commission will decide how to move forward within the next few months, after the submissions have been analysed in more detail and when we know the results of cop6. it has always been and remains the commission's wish that whatever the community does on emissions trading should be fully compatible with the kyoto protocol's emissions trading system when it comes into effect. as you know, the eu system would come into force in 2005 while the kyoto international trading would not come into force until later. in conclusion, i can express general support for your resolutions and i should once again like to express my thanks and appreciation for the constructive efforts made by parliament to raise awareness of climate change and the support it gives to the commission on implementation. commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the case of non-italian foreign language assistants in italian universities is well known to the commission and to most of the european institutions. this case has been ongoing for over a decade, and following the intervention of the european institutions, in particular the commission, the situation of the assistants has improved. as you know, the case is very complex and involves some 700 people working in more than 25 italian universities. the commission has worked actively during this decade to resolve the problem of foreign readers in italy concerning the right to free movement of workers guaranteed by the treaty. as you have pointed out, the court of justice has already delivered three judgments concerning readers, and with the case pending in luxembourg, the commission has continued to take action to further improve the situation. in particular, following the decisions of the court of justice in 1989 and 1993 (allué case law) which ruled that the restrictions on the duration of contracts imposed by italian law were discriminatory, the commission took steps. it had initiated an infringement procedure which was closed in 1995 following the italian law which brought the legislation into line with the court's judgment. as regards subsequent claims by readers concerning acquired rights, the commission initiated a new infringement procedure on the grounds that, in a number of italian universities, the acquired rights of assistants were not properly safeguarded. the commission has devoted a great deal of resources to the investigation of this case. the commission's services have collected hundreds of pages of documentation on specific cases from various universities. we exchanged considerable correspondence with the relevant actors and made a great effort to select from piles of irrelevant documents the evidence conclusively proving that former lettori had indeed been discriminated against by some italian universities in respect of acquired financial rights such as salaries and pension contributions. in july 1999, the commission brought this infringement procedure before the court of justice. it awaits the court's ruling on this new infringement and on the procedure initiated by the commission. the participants not only cited the lack of protection of their acquired rights, but also deplored the new legal regime introduced by the italian legislation of 1995. they considered that the italian state should have included them in the category of university teaching staff, or, failing that, created a specific category for them among the teaching staff. in the opinion of the assistants, this right is a direct consequence of the right of workers to free movement. on this point, however, the commission disagreed with the participants. in our view, free movement means that european citizens are not discriminated against in the national legal order. it does not entitle them to any special legal status. each member state has full competence to lay down the provisions governing its own public service. community legislation cannot prevent italy from amending the provisions governing the status of former lettori and transforming them into linguistic experts, with partly different responsibilities. if the italian legal order is reformed and changed, as has been the case with university staff, we do not think that the commission can intervene as long as every european citizen enjoys equal access to all categories of professions. indeed, any european citizen can become a permanent member of the teaching staff by passing the appropriate competition.
