- mr president, it is difficult to deny that for some years now the social policies of the member states of the union have been conditioned by economic and monetary policies, budgetary compatibility, stability pacts, the flexibility and precariousness of paid employment, in deference to the market and competition, its inseparable companion. the gap between those who have much and those who have little or nothing is widening, while those who have much, in the name of the sacred principles just mentioned, are demanding more and more sacrifices from those who have little or nothing. the charter of fundamental rights, by constantly referring to national legislation and practice for the effective realisation of social rights, tends to make this subordination, this mechanism of unjust appropriation of wealth by a few, this model of liberal-liberal society which is rising with impressive rapidity from the ashes of european social democratic thought, irreversible. this charter of social rights is lagging behind the legislation of many member states and, precisely because of this delay, it will serve as an instrument to change or worsen it. civil and political rights are only formal rights if they are not based on social rights which have been realised and not merely enumerated. it seems that the century that is ending, with all its struggles for the emancipation of the disadvantaged social classes, has passed in vain and has taught us nothing. we cannot be under the illusion that this charter is a first step towards an ever more united union. it is the lowest level of social policy that we will have in the future. i only hope that it will not be incorporated into the treaties and that movements will grow in civil society, in trade unions and in political organisations calling for a fairer and more genuinely supportive europe.
- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, with the debate on the charter of rights our parliament is marking today a new important milestone on the european union's journey towards a more united and, i hope, fairer and more honest europe. i shall vote for this charter, not because i am convinced that it will be applied correctly and effectively, but because we cannot but agree on the principles which inspire it. there are still deep questions, which arise from shared concerns: i am thinking of those countries in the community where the right to life is and remains only and exclusively an assertion of principle, when indiscriminately human life is suppressed from conception; i am thinking of the european consumers who, thanks to the charter, have many new and important rights and who are being given what is left of the mad cow, like that capitalism which is fattening the skin of the poor people. i am thinking of those workers in factories who would have a right to stable employment and who, in the name of the globalisation of markets, are being deprived of their future in order to relocate their work where it is cheaper. i think about students and teachers and the right to education, and i think about the crumbling and outdated structures in so many countries that abdicate this role. i am thinking, ladies and gentlemen, of freedom and the right to express one's opinion, and i am thinking of the many people who are crowding into european prisons simply because they do not think like the others. i am thinking of the right to housing and an affordable quality of life; i think of young people who, in the name of often mafia interests, no longer even have the right to love. i think about all this and more and i am worried, but i will vote for the charter, even if it is a utopia, because we are all called upon to make a revolution which, in order to be realised, needs a grain, a grain of reasoning utopia.
- mr president, the proposal and the adoption of the draft charter of fundamental rights should find a very broad consensus. it seems to me that dissent is justified only by those who are against european union, and we have heard some of them here. i do not understand the disagreement of those who are motivating it because the charter does not contain everything that they would like to see you understand. i think that none of us sees its aspirations fully realised, because the charter cannot be the mirror of one part but must be the common point of reference for all those who consider themselves european citizens, respectful of differences and of the coexistence of different people. could you have done better? i think so, because not everything i have proposed has been accepted. so, it's better not to do anything? do not approve this charter? certainly not! this charter, i repeat, makes the union a community of rights; it is a step in the process of constitutionalising the union, it is the first international document which contains together, in accordance with the principle of the indivisibility of fundamental rights, civil and political rights, economic and social rights, new rights. i don't understand who says it's useless, that it's just generic and fancy words. anyone who says that ignores the history of the institutions: the european parliament has been a great help to the commission in its efforts to bring about a change in the legal system. it is on the basis of formulas like these that our courts have guaranteed our fundamental rights over time. let the cynicism of the reactionaries say that only strength or money counts and that the rest is just words. no, words that embody our principles, our values, our fundamental rights have power and force, if we embrace them as instruments of our civic life. so let us adopt the charter and take its words seriously, let us not allow them to be minimized, devalued, neglected. let us take our rights seriously if we want governments to respect them and the courts to guarantee them!
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the charter we are about to vote on today with a europeanist conviction is certainly a step forward in the construction of the political europe in which we firmly believe. many have pointed out, however, that this text does not have the legal force of a treaty. that is why we must take further steps forward. the final objective is to have a european constitution, the fundamental law of a union which cannot be limited to having a single currency but which must be a political reality, with a truly common foreign and defence policy, an equal partner of the united states and able to face the great challenge of globalisation which will see the countries of the asian continent, starting with china, playing a leading role in the coming years. the charter, therefore, mr president, is only the beginning of a difficult and demanding but at the same time exciting work. the text we are approving today, which, as president poettering has already said, is the result of a compromise and in some respects does not satisfy us, must help to launch a great debate on the future and the future european constitution. the charter must establish the rights and establish the levels of competence of the union, the states and the regions with binding legal force and must bear the seal of the popular will. that is why it must be discussed and approved by this parliament and the national parliaments. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environmentally friendly use of energy.
- mr president, the vote on the charter marks the resumption of the process towards a european constitution. the union is a giant of the world economy, but if it remains soulless, if the free trade area and the democratic deficit grow together, there is a growing risk that competitiveness will come into conflict with solidarity and that a market without rules will feed nostalgia for the past in social and territorial realities that feel their traditions and security threatened. the charter has many supporters but also many enemies; we have heard the criticisms of those who do not want a political europe. this contrast of opinions is part of the rights of freedom recognized by the charter itself. the arguments of the charter's enemies, however, make more evident its political significance and its legal value, which is not in contradiction with the treaties but strengthens their democratic prospects. for some, the charter is too short a step, for others it is too long a step. the people's party, which has christian-democratic roots, is convinced that the appeal to europe's spiritual and moral heritage will strengthen the cohesion of a union which values cultural and political diversity. the method of a transparent and open convention and the work of mr méndez de vigo and other colleagues deserve our strong support. we now expect from nice a strategy to make europe a union of economic, social and political rights.
- madam president, i voted in favour of the paciotti report mainly because this directive aims to protect the identities, data, names, surnames, addresses and characteristics of citizens of the european union. the elderly and the retired, whom i have the pleasure of representing in this parliament, are too often regarded as numbers. but older people don't want to be considered numbers, they want to be considered people in the flesh. this is the main reason why i am voting in favour of this directive, even though, unfortunately, amendment no 65 by mr ferri and mr fiori, which called for a collegium of several persons to make up the body responsible for supervision and controls, was not accepted.
- madam president, i feel it is my duty to stress that with the paciotti report and with other directives and regulations which will be proposed to us, we are called upon to regulate a great power: the computing power. data collection is not painless, databases are of different types; there are confidential ones, the police, the databases of the services: i mean, there's a tremendous amount of power. i would stress that the fact that we have entrusted this great power of control over european databases to a monocratic body - with all the respect and confidence we will certainly have in the guarantor - seems to me to have been a lapse of attention to the very centrality of the human person, who, in the face of computer power, must have a framework of guaranteed rights and freedoms. in my view, the proposal for a collegiate body would have better met this need. however, in future discussions on the power of computers, we must realize that more control is needed and that this means more guarantees for the human person.
- madam president, how could the party of retired persons not vote in favour of the charter? it is the first document of this importance in the world to have an article, number 25, entitled "the rights of the elderly", which reads: 'the union recognises and respects the right of older persons to lead a life of dignity and independence and to participate in social and cultural life.' finally, an important organization of states, the most important organization that exists, which is the organization of the european union, and the most important body, the only one directly elected by the people, the european parliament, recognize that the elderly have a right as such. that is why i was happy to vote in favour of this charter.

- madam president, i voted in favour of the karamanou report, which has another important purpose in the fight against crime, namely the creation of a european police force. i had a doubt, because a pensioner, mrs boroni lucia, the other day said to me: "i was walking down the street and my purse was stolen. so i saw a policeman nearby who had written on his jacket "european policeman" and i said to him: but why don't you run after this thief who stole my purse? and the policeman said to me: but there is the principle of non-interference in national competence, the principle of subsidiarity. the thief was italian, he was supposed to be chased by an italian cop. i'm the future european police. "i hope it remains a doubt and not a reality! i know.
- madam president, i voted in favour of the roure report. this is also a document which aims to combat crime by adapting the penal rules. i should also like to say that last saturday i was in curno, my home town, in front of the bank where pensioners go every month to collect their pensions. i saw a long line of old people and pensioners. one of them, the last one in the line, recognized me and asked me, "why is there such a long line?" i asked her and i gave her the answer: "they're checking for dirty money, given the new rules". "it doesn't matter", the pensioner told me, "dirty or clean, i'll take the pension money anyway". that is what i hope will not happen with the implementation of this document.
- madam president, this is a document - which i voted for - which aims to bring about the establishment of a single european court gradually and little by little. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's legal system is not undermined by the failure of the member states to comply with the obligations imposed on them by the treaty. i would, however, have liked to see a representative of the lawyers in each of the 15 member states in this body, because i believe that when something new has to be introduced in the legal field, it is good to listen not only to the judges who are judging but also to lawyers who have a very long experience in this field. and i'm not just saying this because my daughter just graduated from law school.

that, alas, we have to live with. but we should not forget that the barcelona process has progressed over five years. this has happened despite all the difficulties in the middle east. one thing is abundantly plain. we must not allow the barcelona process to become a hostage to the middle east peace process. barcelona has its own momentum. it has its own objectives which remain wholly valid. we all have an interest in demonstrating both resilience and ambition in marseilles this week. the commission has been encouraged by the generally positive reaction to the proposals that we set out on reinvigorating the barcelona process, both in the european union and among the mediterranean partners. perhaps i can just touch on some of the main elements in the strategic approach we have suggested that i hope will meet some agreement at marseilles. firstly, speeding up negotiation and ratification of the association agreements. first of all with egypt but also algeria, syria and lebanon. we in fact completed our negotiations with egypt almost 18 months ago and i wish that we could now rapidly proceed to initialling the agreement and then in due course to full signature. i would also like to see us commencing more serious negotiations on association agreements with the other countries. we put forward the argument that we should tackle the sensitive issue of agricultural trade. we should review, in our judgment, what needs to be done to ensure that the agreements are fully wto compatible by the end of the transitional period. we argue for enhancing south-south trade by encouraging the signature of free trade agreements between the partners. in this context the commission undertakes to provide technical assistance on crucial items such as rules of origin and customs matters. we want to see the bringing together of policies on single market issues and agreement to introduce cumulation of origin side-by-side with the sub-regional free trade arrangements for all partners entering into free trade with each other and adopting the harmonised protocol on rules of origin. we also want to see an increase in the attractiveness of the region to investors. in addition to economic reforms, the newly created networks of cooperation among investment promotion agencies and among employers' federations will help, as should the introduction of a new regional risk capital facility. reaching agreement on a new regional programme on justice and home affairs covering migration in the widest sense, the fight against organised crime and cooperation on judicial matters is another subject on which we hope we can have a good exchange of views. then there is the issue which i know we had many opportunities of debating in this chamber: that of improving the delivery of meda. the revision of the meda regulation and the reform already announced of the commission's external aid system will help to achieve this and will also lead to more human resources being available. by decentralising the delivery of aid, we shall involve partners much more in all stages of policy formulation and implementation. we all have an interest in ensuring that meda is tightly focused on the right objectives. we intend to do that through a close dialogue with partners at all stages. but there is no escaping the fact that the partners who have faced up to the challenges inherent in the association process are the ones who should get most support. as far as human rights are concerned, we propose a structural approach looking at the performance of countries over time. but here again we should be frank. a country which has serious doubts raised about its record on human rights, democracy and the rule of law and is not prepared to discuss these matters transparently will not find it easy to fit into the new world pattern and it will be less likely to prosper in the longer term. i just want to say one more thing about meda and the reform of our external aid which is relevant to debates which members are having elsewhere. in order to ensure that we deliver more rapidly in the mediterranean and elsewhere in the world, we need – as members accept rationally and intellectually – more resources to actually manage our programmes and the commission has put forward what are sensible proposals for doing that. there are some members who think that we should put those extra resources into the reserve until we have accomplished certain other objectives. i say to members of parliament, in all good faith, that there comes a moment when you have to trust us and when you have to let us try to do the job, because we cannot conceivably implement our plans more effectively if the people we need to manage them are not made amiable until we have actually demonstrated that we can manage things more effectively. it is a crazy situation to put us in so i beg all honourable members who have any influence on these matters to recognise that, if we are to be serious about the reform process, then you have to give us the opportunity to demonstrate whether we can be as good as our word or not. if we cannot we will have to take the consequences, and the commissioner for external affairs will have to take the consequences in due course, but do not put us in a position in which the ends are willed but you do not give us the means until after we have demonstrated that we can achieve the ends. it makes no sort of sense whatsoever. it is an issue which is extremely important to all the mediterranean countries and i hope i will be able to assure them this week that it is our firm intention to do a great deal better in the delivery of our programmes in future. i hope that all the ministers who gather in marseilles will recognise the need to agree on this set of realistic proposals to reinvigorate the barcelona process precisely now that the middle east is suffering serious difficulties. i will be glad to inform parliament about the results of the marseilles meeting at the earliest possible opportunity. we have committed in the past huge resources to this partnership. we have not managed them as well as we should have done but we have committed huge resources and that reflects the priority which parliament, the commission and the council give to strengthening the partnership around our "middle sea". in the next few years the success of that partnership will be even more important than ever and i hope that, at marseilles this week and in subsequent weeks, we manage to ensure that this whole enterprise has even more impulse and energy in it than it has had in the past. commission. – this has been an excellent debate even though, by this time in the evening, the attendance is restricted to the cognoscenti. however, it is good to see some familiar faces in the chamber. i do not intend to traverse the ground that was covered by the minister earlier in his remarks about the zagreb summit. i totally endorse all the objectives which he set out. that summit is taking place in rather happier conditions than we perhaps imagined when the presidency first conceived of it. i want to focus on the regulations. i should like, first of all, to thank the house for its excellent and speedy work during its examination of these two draft regulations. i should like to congratulate the rapporteurs of the relevant committees: firstly, mr westendorp y cabeza, who has considerable on-the-ground experience of these matters in bosnia, and also mr lagendijk, with whom we have a regular dialogue on southeast europe. he is at least one other human being with whom i can share the distinction of having read misha glenny on the balkans. i should also like to thank the following members: mr staes, mr färm and mr gargani for the quality of their reports and opinions. these two proposals respond to two key union priorities: providing assistance to southeastern europe and providing it as rapidly and as efficiently as possible. the european councils of lisbon and feira underlined the importance that the union gives to the integration of this region into the economic and political mainstream of europe. our policy for achieving that is the stabilisation and association process. of course the european union is making a leading contribution through that process to the work of the stability pact. the heads of government have also confirmed the union's determination to back this process with technical and economic assistance. the return of democracy to serbia, thanks to the determination and courage of the serb people and the democratic forces there, offers the chance now of building prosperity across the whole region. more than ever the european union has to live up to the commitments it has made. to do that we must have the right legal instruments, flexible procedures and efficient management. the reform of external assistance which the commission adopted on 16 may demonstrates our determination to improve radically the speed, quality and visibility of external assistance. in southeast europe this determination has already brought concrete results. in kosovo the taskforce which we deployed within days of the end of the conflict and, in the last six months, the european agency for reconstruction have achieved a track record of delivering help on time and efficiently. the figures bear this out: 84% of the funds allocated for reconstruction under obnova – in 1998 to 2000 eur 444.5 million – had been committed by the end of october 2000. seventy percent of the funds committed had been contracted and 43% of the contracted funds had been paid. we have achieved rapid results in serbia too, where the commission, in the space of just over four weeks, has drawn up an emergency assistance programme worth in total eur 200 million. it was agreed by the commission last week and the first trucks of heating fuel started rolling into serbia at the weekend, ahead of schedule and ahead of most other donors. this programme is going to ratchet up every day from now on: a contract for imports of eur 30 million in electricity was signed today with the serbian electricity company and should come on-stream within days. every day counts in this situation. our reforms have started to bring results too in bosnia, where the implementation of assistance, in terms of amounts contracted and disbursed has improved dramatically since our delegation in sarajevo was reinforced last year and authority was delegated to it. the results that have been achieved are extremely encouraging. these are the results of which the european parliament too can be proud. it was the european parliament that sounded the alarm about weak management in bosnia. it was parliament which supported the commission's proposal to create the european agency for reconstruction. it was parliament which insisted on a single regulatory framework for assistance to the region and it was parliament, in its role as budgetary authority, which made sure that funds were made available for emergency assistance for serbia, without delay. this is good progress but we need to build on it. there is still plenty of room for improvement. that is the purpose of these two proposals. members of parliament have tabled a significant number of amendments. i want to comment on them as they relate to our twin proposals on the agency and the regulation. the commission has proposed an assistance regulation which is deliberately simple and clear. it sets out the over-arching objectives for assistance for the main principles governing programming, comitology for programmes, but not for individual projects. and it also proposes simple decision arrangements for programmes run by the european reconstruction agency. let me take up a number of the broad points that have been raised by parliament, first the role of the commission and its financial responsibilities in relation to the running of the agency. the commission takes very seriously its responsibilities for the implementation of the community budget. a number of new amendments underline this responsibility by referring to article 274 of the treaty. but in order to exercise this responsibility we need legal instruments which allow us to act quickly and flexibly. second, parliament wants us to refer more specifically to sectoral priorities. we want, in the light of experience, to retain as much flexibility as possible. but we can accept several of parliament's amendments which urge us to include mention of key sectoral priorities such as assistance for education, vocational training, environment, civil society and ngos, ethnic reconciliation and the return of displaced persons. in the same spirit we can accept the proposal to include a reference to the feira european council conclusions in the preamble to the regulation. parliament's resolution on the commission's communication on the stabilisation and association process also deserves to be mentioned in the preamble. we think it makes more sense to do it there than to build it into the article on conditionality. naturally we can also accept the proposal that the guidelines which the commission will adopt should reflect the search for greater efficiency that underlines our reforms. i just want to add the point that it is important, having put forward a regulation which attempts to simplify things, not to allow the regulations now to be hung about with caveats and qualifications and spectacular quantities of red tape. as mr staes said: we do not want people throwing spanners in the works. if we cannot have a clear and simple regulation then, frankly, we would be better off with no regulation at all. to be clear: we can accept the spirit, provided changes can be made in certain cases to the wording, of amendments nos 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, the first part of 11, the first part of 13, 16 partially, 17, 18, 19 partially and 20, 21, 24, 28 in the first part, 31 and partially 37. the commission's position on the overall sum we estimated was necessary for the region, the so-called financial reference amount and its compatibility with the financial perspectives, is well-known. we do not think, as the house knows, that it is necessary to make an explicit reference to this in the regulation. despite mr lagendijk's eloquence, i do not think it is necessary, but he made one point which is fundamentally true and it was made, in another sense, by mr westendorp when both of them argued that these regulations are all very well but if there is not an adequate budget to cover the political priorities of the european union then we are wasting our time. mr westendorp, said that the council could not – i think this was the implication of his remarks – replicate the new testament and perform miracles with loaves and fishes. that may be regarded by some members of some councils as being a touch brutal in its assessment of the powers of the council but it is entirely true. we have to deal with finite budgets but i very much hope that the budget which is available for the external actions of the european union reflects the political priorities of the european union. that is the discussion which we have been having with the council in recent weeks and months and the commission or parliament do not come badly out of that discussion. i should have thought, in particular, that the experience of the last two months has shown that the commission's proposal on financing was not as eccentric as some people suggested at the time. let me now turn to the second proposal on the table, the european agency for reconstruction and, in doing so, i want to pay warm tribute, as mr lagendijk did during his own remarks, to the excellent job that the board, the director and the staff have done on the ground in kosovo. they are a terrific team and i am not surprised that the results they have achieved are extremely impressive. they have earned their good reputation for delivering results and i know that parliament's own delegation to kosovo in may was as impressed by them as i have been. it clearly makes sense to learn lessons from the past six months of the agency's operations and to see how we can help it to work more effectively. this is essential now that the agency will be responsible for the whole of the fry. our main aim is to clarify the role of the governing board. it has to take on responsibility for the examination and the approval of reconstruction programmes which will be submitted to the commission for decision. we also want to simplify decision-making. according to the new regulation the commission will be permitted to adopt programmes proposed by the agency without having to consult the management committee. let me make it clear that responsibility for the formal adoption of the programmes remains with the commission. it is the commission that decides on the desirability of these programmes; it is the commission which is responsible for the implementation of the budget; it is the commission which adopts the programmes. a number of amendments seek to ensure that the agency acts under the direct and sole responsibility of the commission and thereby to ensure that the commission is solely responsible for the agency's management before the european parliament, the court of auditors and olaf. i want to clarify this. the agency has a certain degree of autonomy, like all european agencies. this is the position under the current institutional set-up and the autonomy, which the agency now has, must be respected unless the institutional structure of the agency is modified. that does not detract from the full responsibility that the commission assumes, as the treaty requires, for the execution of the community budget. i would like to thank parliament for the sensible and pragmatic way it has accepted the current structure of the agency. i know parliament's views on this issue and the commission will take these into account in the design of any future executive agencies. the language regime is a further sensitive issue. i hope that parliament will understand the sense of the proposals that i put forward in may and will continue to work constructively with others on this very difficult issue but i cannot offer to support parliament's amendment to remove the unanimity requirement which would contradict the view of the college. we can accept those amendments which are designed to remove the requirement for a further council decision to extend the mandate of the agency to the whole of the fry. i can accept, too, those amendments which refer to the general affairs decision of 9 october, to cooperation with ngos, to the restoration of civil society and the rule of law, to the payment for services provided by the agency, to third parties, to the possibility of creating further operational centres, to the responsibility of the director for the implementation of the work programme and the structure of the agency's budget. this means that we can accept the spirit, provided changes can be made in certain cases to the wording, of amendment nos 1, 2, 6, 8, 10 in part, 11, 37, 16, 27 and 33. we will look carefully at the desirability of producing an explicit list of issues which the governing board should examine. we will do this in the interest of clarifying its role; that concerns amendments nos 21 and 22. we will also examine the timetable which you propose for the adoption of the agency's budget while respecting the principle of good budgetary programming and compatibility with the community's budgetary procedures. this concerns amendments nos 29 and 30. let me reiterate my thanks to parliament for its hard work on these issues. we have made real headway in south east europe. this proposal should allow us to take advantage of the new opportunity we have, to make a decisive contribution as the european union to lasting peace and prosperity across the whole region. i have to say that the european union did not come frightfully well out of the history of south east europe during the 1990s. i hope we make a better fist of things during the next decade and this regulation will provide us with some of the prosaic means of doing so.
- thank you very much, commissioner. the joint discussion is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at 11.30 a.m.

- report (a5-0275/2000) by mr jové peres, on behalf of the committee on fisheries, on the communication from the commission to the council and the european parliament - participation of the european community in regional fisheries organisations (rff) (com (99) 613 - c5-0108/2000 - 2000/2068 (cos))
the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have to say that i am very pleased with the way the commission has been working. first of all, i would like to thank you for your support of our efforts to promote and also to strengthen the community's activities in the regional fisheries organizations. i agree with all those who say that we need more regional fisheries organisations, and i also agree with mr varela and others that the commission has a role to play in these regional fisheries organisations. we also agree with this house that the control questions in the area of regional fisheries policy must be a cornerstone. i must also reiterate the commission's view that it cannot assume sole responsibility for control in the regional fisheries organisations. it is the member states - and this is our basic structure in the european union - who have the primary responsibility for the controls. in exercising their sovereign rights as flag states, they must provide the necessary human, financial and material resources to enable the community to meet its international obligations. the commission therefore notes its conclusion in the communication that nafo is an exception to the rule but not to be made the rule as regards control activities. the commission should concentrate on its real task, which is to monitor and coordinate the implementation of control measures by the member states in the regional fisheries organisations. the commission also has a lot of negotiating work to do in the context of regional fisheries organisations. it would simply be inappropriate to ignore the existing institutional practice in the community with regard to the control of ships operating on the high seas. i would like to draw attention to two main points. on the one hand, the community must act consistently, whether it is a matter of control activities within community waters or control activities on the high seas. secondly, the positions taken on this subject must be consistent with those taken in the current debate on the so-called core activities of the commission. for these reasons, the discussion of control measures goes beyond the area of regional fisheries organisations. a comprehensive approach must be adopted, taking into account all community fishing activities, both in eu waters and on the high seas. if we want to make a whole new reflection in connection with our tasks as commissioners in relation to control activities inside and outside community waters, i think it is appropriate that we do so in the context of the preparation of the reform of the common fisheries policy. this means that we will have plenty of opportunities to discuss these issues in depth here next year. so much for the core theme of the report. let me make a few brief remarks on a few other points. as regards the duration of the implementation of the decisions of the regional fisheries organisations, i agree with you that the commission's balance sheet can and must be improved. the commission has already made some progress, but it is important to improve timing. on the question of infringements and sanctions: the commission has always been in favour of including sanctions in the control systems. because without sanctions, control is simply toothless. unfortunately, such ideas have not been implemented because the council has always been against them. but we will try to make progress on this issue too, in the context of the ongoing work to create an area of freedom, security and justice, as formulated and decided at the tampere summit. the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. it says that the commission wants to exclude parliament from the process of community participation in the various regional fisheries organisations. i have to tell you that's not true at all, it's the opposite. the commission has always been in favour of the rules governing cooperation between parliament and the commission and has always respected the rules of the interinstitutional agreement.
- this debate is over. the vote will take place tomorrow at 11.30 a.m.
- doc. a5-0305/2000 by mr garot, on behalf of the committee on agriculture and rural development, on the proposal for a council regulation amending regulation (eec) no 2759/75 on the common organization of the market in pigmeat (com (2000) 193 - c5-0225/2000 - 2000/0076 (cns))
the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have just received a letter from the president of the commission. first of all, i should like to thank you, mr garot, as rapporteur, for your excellent report on the introduction of a compensation fund in the common organization of the market in pigmeat. the crisis in the pig sector, which we have now thankfully overcome, was actually the starting point for the commission's proposal. fortunately, we are now in the economically favourable phase of the pig cycle, characterised by a decline in supply and a marked improvement in farmer prices. for several months, producer prices have been at eur 140 to eur 150 per 100 kg, and the outlook continues to be positive from the experts' point of view. the market development thus shows that the pig cycle is still in force and still has its validity and that even after bad times good times follow. we should bear this in mind when we discuss today's proposal. we are discussing an instrument to support producer incomes in times of crisis. we are not talking about a new pig market regulation. the pig market system exists and we should not make the mistake of calling into question the existing pig market system, which is basically working. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very important one. the first is the question of co-financing. this is certainly to some extent the key question in the debate on this proposal, and it is also addressed in amendments nos 11 and 12. i must stress, however, that the main responsibility for the balance of the market and the resulting price level lies with the pig producers themselves. they, the pigmeat producers, decide on the volume of production and thus indirectly and automatically also on future price developments. i think it would be wrong to discharge the producers from their responsibilities. co-financing also carries the risk that the market signals are less clearly received by the producer. i cannot therefore stress the idea that the whole point of the whole thing might be to have an anti-cyclical pricing policy. if we wanted to introduce an anti-cyclical pricing policy, we would simply be agitating the pig cycle. i have learned something else today, and that is that there are supposedly members of parliament who support the idea that we should now introduce co-financing in all market systems. so if we do them in all of them, then we may not rule out the pig question. but that is not really the subject of the debate, as i have understood it so far. the second important question is the voluntary nature of the system. the commission proposal leaves the member states the choice of whether or not to set up a fund, whereas the amendments provide for an obligation for all member states. we should not forget, however, that european pigmeat production has very different forms and is organised differently from one country to another, and that cooperation between the various stages of the production chain is also organised very differently. that is why there are a number of member states, and also pork producers in those member states, who reject a compensation fund in the first place, because they say they do not need it, because they have other forms of income security at a low stage in the cycle. but other countries are very keen to have the compensation fund, and i have to say quite frankly: if we were to propose the compulsory introduction of the compensation fund now, the consequence would be that we could forget the whole thing, because there would never be a majority in the council for this. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the system of quotas is not abused. i think this is extremely problematic because (a) pig production is very heterogeneous and (b) pig farmer support does not necessarily automatically fall into the same cycle phase as farmer support. in addition, the weight of the piglets varies enormously, from 8 to 30 kg. there is also no uniform price quotation system for standard piglets, so to speak, and therefore there is no basis on which to base one's opinion. i believe that the economic balance between the pig price and the pig slaughter price is much better achieved by the market rather than by artificial measures. in particular, we should not forget that in many countries farmers fatten their own pigs and thus have direct access to the compensation fund through the pigs they sell. amendment no 16 is unacceptable to the commission because it would have the effect of drastically encroaching on the freedom of choice of those farmers who do not join the fund in order to retain their freedom. the measures are not yet defined, leaving the decision on the measures to be applied essentially in the hands of the member states. that would be a genuine renationalisation, which i cannot agree to. the proposed reduction in production by member state, depending on previous production, is again very close to a quota system. in addition, this would create an enormous bureaucratic burden, also in connection with controls. the commission considers that it is justified to subject only those farmers who join the compensation fund to discipline, since they receive a certain income guarantee in return, while others who do not join do not receive this income guarantee. in addition to these four key questions which arise in the context of the debate on the report, there are a number of other amendments which are less fundamental in nature but which also deal mainly with details of the regulation, details which in my view should not be included in the council regulation but should be included in the implementing provisions. as regards the staggering of aid according to the number of animals, i would point out that the commission proposal already provides a legal basis for such a procedure. i would like to conclude by briefly addressing a subject which is dealt with in amendment no 6, namely the improvement of statistical information on the development of pig populations and the possibilities for forecasting the development of production. i do not think that a new law or regulation is necessary. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the data on the number of persons employed in the community are not misused. my services have drawn the attention of the colleagues at eurostat who are responsible for carrying out these surveys to the problems that remain and have also urged that the results be improved accordingly. in the last few months there have been several discussions on this subject and it has become quite clear that we are not lacking in rules, but only in the fact that the rules are taken seriously, that the surveys of pig populations are carried out correctly and that the questions put to the member states are answered in good faith. i think that the commission has a duty to ensure that the council of ministers is able to take the necessary steps to ensure that the community's financial interests are not undermined. i am very grateful, however, for the serious debate that has taken place here, and i hope that it will be possible to reach a conclusion in the council on the basis of the commission's proposal, because we still have the problem here - i say this quite openly - of very wide differences of opinion between the member states on this question.
the commission. i have not said that the introduction of this proposal, which the commission has made, will not change the pig market regulation. of course, this is an amendment to the pig market regulation, that is not a question, but in the debate opinions have been put forward as if it were now a question of introducing a pig market regulation, and i took the liberty of pointing out that we already have one.

- mr president, the proposal under consideration was certainly expected. the question we must ask is whether it fully meets the objectives which were envisaged eight years ago or whether it does not create further problems. this is not so much because of the work done by mrs gonzález álvarez, who has done a great deal to improve the legislation in question, as because of the guidelines and some of the contents of the proposal itself. first, in the present case, the commission appears to have been transformed from the primary architect of the legislative process into an administrative authority, without there being any adequate legal framework to provide a legal and transparent framework for this new role, starting with the delineation of its field of research and the control of its decisions based on rapid intervention. moreover, in view of its possible autonomous activation around the start of the emergency measures and the presumably long period before it is possible to ascertain their merits, in the sole concern of the employment aspect, it must be noted that there is no consideration of the damage caused to an undertaking - but more especially to its employees - by a decision which should prove to be wrong. on the other hand, there is the export ban on products classified as dangerous, which certainly attests to the union's high level of civilization, but there is no answer as to whether this ban is consistent with the so-called prior informative concert procedure, which is provided for by international conventions. the concept of liability, which refers both to the definition of a product and to its traceability and assimilation into that concept of services, also appears to be open to interpretation and therefore to be subject to discretionary review. at the same time, consider the possible interpretations as a product of raw materials in the processing processes and the positive effects of this in terms of the search for workers' health, limited however by the lack of a valid european statistical recording system and by the different legal systems for the recognition of an occupational disease. in conclusion, it is desirable that the commission should initiate a 'connection' within existing community legislation and its development in order to make it not only increasingly transparent but also, in view of its certainty, really usable.

in writing. - (it) the european fisheries sector is facing a number of challenges at the moment, due to increased competition brought about by the globalisation of the market for fishery products. in addition, there is a growing need to protect the marine environment and to manage exploitable resources rationally. in this context, it is necessary to strengthen international cooperation and to ensure that the community is more involved in the definition of fisheries regulations. the main instrument for achieving closer cooperation is the regional fisheries organisations (rfos), which play a key role on the international scene but lack sufficient human resources to ensure satisfactory representation of the community. the rdps are a particularly appropriate instrument for achieving the objectives set in the light of regional specificities, but they contribute above all to the rational management of resources while reflecting the specific characteristics of the fishing areas. in this context, given the importance of the rfmos for the future of the common fisheries policy and the different degree of organisation, competences and development of each of them, it is necessary for the community to adapt its participation to their respective characteristics and to harmonise its role within the 30 existing rfmos in order to speed up the transposition into community law of the recommendations adopted by them.
- doc. a5-321/2000 by mr blokland, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection, on the common draft directive of the european parliament and of the council on the incineration of waste (c5-0371/2000 - 1998/0089 (cod)).
commission. – mr president, honourable members, forgive me – especially mr blokland – for being a few minutes late. i could not hear your introduction, but i can guess what was in it. first of all, i want to thank you for your excellent work as rapporteur on this report. the fact that this directive has passed through the legislative procedure so smoothly serves to show how important it is for all concerned. this directive will lead to significant reductions in emissions in several key pollutants across the european union, despite the fact that the volume of waste incineration will increase over the coming years. not only does it contribute to the fight against air pollution but it also covers the release of waste water, as mr lund has said, from exhaust gas cleaning and the quality of waste from the incineration process itself. the conciliation process was demanding, but a well-balanced compromise has been found and the amendments of parliament and the council have produced a better directive. the scope of the directive is much clearer. public access to information has improved. stricter emission-limit values have been introduced for new cement kilns that co-incinerate waste, as mrs evans pointed out. this has been largely due to the excellent work of the european parliament and its rapporteur, mr blokland. i am convinced that the joint text strikes the right balance – a view reflected in your speeches yesterday – incorporating a high level of environmental protection along with the legitimate interests of all stake holders. let me remind you that the directive is only one instrument in the whole waste-management concept of the commission. burning waste is the final stage in the treatment of waste, due to the waste hierarchy, and the commission will make strong efforts to reduce and recycle waste and in its approach to an integrated product policy. of course, the overall objective is to prevent waste in the first place. in conclusion, this directive is a major contribution to the reduction of negative effects on the environment and the risks they pose to human health.

in writing. - (it) i declare that i voted in favour of mrs villiers' report on the capital of banks because it was impossible not to revise and supplement directive 89/299/eec, which was adopted to govern this matter eleven years ago. the increased prudence criteria adopted are justified, but other aspects of the issue must also be considered, in particular the solvency ratio, which is a weighting parameter by type of counterparty that gives an approximation of the actual credit risk in a bank's assets. in italy, it is currently set at 8% (7% for banking groups) of risk-weighted assets both in cash and out of budget. what is absolutely unacceptable is that the supervisory body - the bank of italy - can, under certain conditions, set a higher minimum requirement. you don't change the rules in the middle of the game, you change them before you play. so, yes, a higher weighting factor - say 10% - but one which is absolutely fixed in all cases and circumstances. article 53 (d) of the tulb - the single text of the laws on banking and credit - which deals specifically with this aspect should therefore be deleted, as should all laws of the member states which provide for such amendments a posteriori.

mr president, the opportunity we have today to discuss and then vote on the maaten report at second reading is an important opportunity, a test of parliament's ability to meet the expectations of the citizens who want institutions capable of taking clear decisions. the same applies to their living conditions and their way of life, in which health protection is becoming increasingly important. the work done by the committee on the environment, thanks in particular to the work of our rapporteur, has been very remarkable in this respect. one thing must be clear: we are not launching a framework legislation to combat smoking, which remains the most serious cause of death in the european union. i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. we can and must harmonize national legislation on the production, presentation and marketing of tobacco products to the highest possible level of health protection. the directive has four pillars, as has been mentioned: limitation of the levels of tar, nicotine and carbon monoxide; the prohibition of cigarette labels - labelled as 'light', 'ultralight' - which are universally recognised as misleading; uniform regulation and, where necessary, prohibition of other ingredients and additives which are often responsible for increasing the risks to smokers and, above all, for increasing their dependence; the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens and their metabolites. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens and mutagens is a very good one. in this second reading, our main concerns were two: the first is to reconcile politically the objective of health protection with the legitimate point of view of production and employment. the example of applying the new levels of toxic substances also to cigarettes exported from the union is valid for all. in order to defend this basic principle, we have proposed that the legal basis be extended to article 133 of the treaty, but above all we have postponed the date by which the member states will have to apply it to 1 january 2007. the second concern, which is strictly legal, has led us to make the interdependence between market harmonization and health protection even more strict, following meticulously the indications given in the reasons with which the court of justice recently annulled the advertising directive, reasons which can only be interpreted as a statement of reasons and lead to the conclusion that the two aspects are incompatible. we have therefore done a fruitful and important job, not least because the differences with regard to the council's common position, and even more so with regard to the discussions which took place there after the vote in the committee on the environment, are, as far as we have been able to ascertain, so limited that we can see the real possibility of a rapid and effective compromise. the fact that some people are suggesting that we should scrap all this work and thus the possibility of sending a positive message to the citizens is of course legitimate, but at least we should have the courage to do so in the name of an explicit political motivation and not by hiding behind a formal disregard for the treaties. we have made every effort to ensure that this parliament is as united as possible so that it can, as on other occasions, find the strength to appear to the citizens as a safe and impervious reference point for special interests. if not, at least the responsibilities will be clear and well defined.

chairman of the committee on constitutional affairs. mr president, we shall have to carry out a rigorous and thorough analysis of the conclusions of the intergovernmental conference and the substantive issues arising from it in the coming weeks. i shall not now return to the comments made by several speakers on the subject of method or on other subjects such as those now dealt with by mr brok. the commission's reply the first is that the nice conclusions do not guarantee, at the institutional level, the continuity and development of the process of integration into the wider union that is about to be born. we cannot call them leftovers or relics or leftovers, but the problems which were not adequately resolved in nice will inevitably reappear: i am thinking of the transition to qualitatively essential areas, to majority voting and to the mechanisms for majority decision-making themselves. experience will tell us which problems, whether we like them or not, we shall have to return to. the second fundamental question is political rather than institutional. the atmosphere of the nice council, the spirit of closure that president prodi spoke of, the narrowness of view which has characterized the attitudes of several governments - attitudes of narrow defence of national interests or orientations - tell us unfortunately what the question is: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament. the right answers to both the fundamental, institutional and political questions, which constitute the most negative legacy of the nice council, must be sought in the context of the debate, the verification and elaboration process to be developed under the heading 'the future of the union'. let's think seriously about what happened. the agreement reached in extremis on the treaty avoided an open crisis which would have put enlargement in question, but it is a latent crisis which we must now deal with. the construction of a united europe requires farsightedness and consistency. we are not asking for a rush, i would say to president chirac: we are asking that no one take a step forward and one step back, that the drawing up and proclamation of the charter be promoted and then not even mentioned in the treaty, that the new formula of the convention be happily invented and then not mentioned as a possible procedure for the post-nice period. we ask that the prospect of constitutionalisation be named after him; we are asking for a clear and consistent vision of the future of europe to be given in response to the disappointments and fears that are swirling among the citizens about what the union is or what it can become. that is our commitment, mr prodi, commissioner barnier. we are confident that parliament and the commission will go together in this direction, as they did in this difficult year of 2000.

mr president, i am one of those who have long hoped for the miracle of nice. the european parliament has been a key player in the process of european integration. the miracle did not happen! the most obvious measure of the lack of success is the announcement of the new intergovernmental conference for 2004 and the quality and importance of topics brought to the centre of the debate for the post-nice period, from the division of powers within the union to the value of the charter of fundamental rights. the miracle was not in the details of the decisions to reorganise the institutions. this lack of miracles is due mainly to the weakness of governments and their veto powers and to the lack of involvement of the european parliament; the european parliament is the only instrument of popular legitimacy of the union today. the miracle has not been achieved in terms of the organization of the common heritage of the charter of fundamental rights. parliament and the commission have already declared their intention to comply with it. what is preventing the council from taking a similar decision? there 's only one small satisfaction left: the enlargement. after nice, the institutional obstacle can no longer be invoked. the only winners are the candidate countries, who are seen as paving the way to the european union. only those who have always believed in the strategic value of enlargement can rightly rejoice in them.
- mr president, the nice summit has shown that the intergovernmental conference has had its day. we are on the eve of the enlargement of the union to the east, a development which puts the strategy of small steps in crisis. if the democratic deficit of the european institutions is not addressed, the union cannot count on the support of the people. the list of problems faced in nice is long, but as president prodi has made very clear, there has not been the necessary attention to institutional reforms and the role of parliament. maybe we went to nice with too much ambition. the ambition of parliament is not, however, to lack a sense of responsibility. if we take the realist lesson, we put the bill of rights in a drawer and settle for a free trade area in the hands of big corporations and national interests. there is something wrong, and the young federalists have understood this, and they have asked the heads of government to have more courage, the same courage as the fathers of the european community. we need to start a great debate on the future of europe: this must be the post-nice period if we are to revive europeanism in a reality which has profoundly changed.

commission. – i very much welcome this report and i should like to pay tribute to mr oostlander for producing it. his report has been welcomed by all parts of parliament except, perhaps by those who look back with nostalgia to the not-so-golden days memorialised by a very large number of brave soviet dissidents. but it is an excellent report which, like the common strategy itself, underlines the importance that we attach to the relationship – the strategic partnership – between the european union and russia. the report endorses what is being called our "double track strategy" towards russia, a strategy that combines plain speaking on issues like chechnya – to which i will return in a few moments – with a continuing effort to build an effective relationship based on shared values and cooperation. the common strategy and russia's medium-term strategy for relations with the eu have created a new dynamism. the common strategy identified initiatives in foreign policy, security and the fight against crime. other areas where we seek to bolster european union cooperative efforts towards russia are the rule of law and democracy building, civil society, twinnings as well as regional and cross-border cooperation and, above all, the northern dimension initiative, to which a number of members referred. we strongly support the russian government's economic reform programme which is vital to improve the investment climate. in this context, as parliament will know, at the last summit between the european union and russia, romano prodi launched a far-reaching dialogue on energy. these are all areas in which the commission has a powerful contribution to make, as the report repeatedly makes clear. our technical assistance programme – in particular tacis – already responds to many of the priorities identified by this report. the core tacis programme, worth eur 34 million, focuses on education, the rule of law, democracy and civil society development, including regional media freedom, protection of individual rights and support to self-government. the subsequent action programme – to a value of eur 58 million – focuses on institution-building, on the rule of law in the economic field and on improvements to the business and investment climate. the honourable member's report rightly stresses the need for our moscow delegation to play a bigger part in the management of our financial assistance, and i am determined to see significant progress in this direction as part of our wider reform of european union external aid programmes. the report comments on the northern dimension. we too see this as an important mechanism for regional cooperation for the development of the north-west russian regions as well as kaliningrad. i am anxious to work closely with the incoming swedish presidency to make concrete progress on the northern dimension. this means concentrating our efforts on key areas like the environment – which has been referred to by a number of members – and nuclear safety, on kaliningrad itself and on improving coordination between different sources of funding. we are acutely aware of the urgent need to tackle environmental threats from nuclear storage facilities and rusting decommissioned submarines, especially in the north-west part of russia, for example, around the kola peninsula. this is a formidable task. it requires a combined international and russian effort. the commission has taken a leading role in the negotiation of an international agreement establishing the multilateral nuclear environment programme for russia. those negotiations are now at a key stage and we hope for significant progress by march 2001. there is also a pressing need to raise environmental awareness in russia. this is exactly the objective of the environmental work programme for the russian federation, initialled last june in the framework of our partnership and cooperation agreement. just a word on kaliningrad: the partnership and cooperation agreement already offers an institutional framework for our dialogue with russia on trade, visa and border issues. at the same time the development of the region has already benefited from tacis projects amounting to about eur 30 million since 1991. we are now finalising a communication to the council on kaliningrad. we are in the process of opening an office in kaliningrad. i very much hope to visit kaliningrad myself in the early part of next year, and not just because immanuel kant spent the whole of his life there. it is a serious issue that we need to address as part of the northern dimension. in all of the areas i have outlined we are working closely with russia to our mutual benefit. we are working to strengthen russian democracy, reinforce the rule of law and transform the russian economy. that is all to the good, but there remains one serious impediment to further improvements in the ties between russia and the european union: i refer, of course, to chechnya. at the last european union russian summit in october, president putin acknowledged the urgent need for a political solution to the conflict. i have to say to honourable members – and i will abbreviate what i might have said at much greater length – we are profoundly concerned about the humanitarian situation in chechnya. we are concerned about the continuing reports of human rights abuses, for example from ngos like médecins sans frontières and human rights watch. we hope that we will be able to make a great deal more progress with the russian authorities in addressing those issues in the months ahead. we are profoundly concerned about the likely fate of thousands of refugees in ingushetiya and chechnya this coming winter. it is because we take our relationship with russia so seriously that these issues matter. they cannot just be brushed under the carpet. we have to return to them again and again, but we must also continue, as the honourable gentleman's report wisely recognises, to engage with russia. we must avoid the mistake to which an honourable gentleman referred earlier, which was made at the start of the last century, when russia was effectively excluded from european affairs after the leninist revolution in 1917 with disastrous consequences. we shall therefore persevere with the common strategy to build on the progress achieved to heed many of the points raised in the honourable gentleman's report, and above all to strengthen the hands of the russian federation. just one further word about a point that was raised by a couple of speakers in the debate – and that is the question of georgia and visas. we have already expressed serious concern over the way in which russia unilaterally introduced visa requirements for georgian citizens on 5 december. the entire international community, not excluding russia, is committed to supporting the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the independent states. actions by any country in the region which could have the effect of undermining that sovereignty carry significant implications. if more favourable visa requirements are applied to the inhabitants of secessionist regions or if they are exempted altogether, this would imply support for the legitimacy of their regimes. georgia is a member of the united nations, a member of the osce, a member of the council of europe, and it has a partnership and cooperation agreement with the european union. it deserves our support. we call upon the states of the region to use the osce mechanisms to resolve their disputes quickly before real damage can be caused. i congratulate the honourable gentleman once again on an extremely good report on a very important issue, to which i am sure we will return in this parliament over the next few years again and again. the honourable gentleman has given us a very important and useful political and intellectual infrastructure for our future discussions.

- question no 4 by mr jonas sjöstedt (h-0881/00): subject: strengthening the responsibility of carriers in the fight against illegal immigration at a council meeting, the french presidency proposed, in the context of the fight against illegal immigration, to increase the responsibility of carriers, in particular airlines, when they transport people to the eu without valid identity documents or visas. in many member states the concept of liability means that the carrier concerned is obliged to arrange the return journey at his own expense, an obligation which in some countries is accompanied by financial penalties. the presidency now wants these to be made systematic, arguing that the responsibility of carriers is an effective means of preventing asylum seekers from entering the eu. given that many refugees who can claim asylum do not manage to obtain the passport and visa to enter the eu, the responsibility of the carriers means that their case will not be examined by the eu, as the persons concerned will have been dismissed in advance by employees of airlines, airports and other transport companies. does the council consider that these staff are competent to make a concrete decision on the future of asylum seekers?
the council. - the proposal to which the honourable member refers is an initiative of the french presidency with a view to adopting a council directive on the harmonization of financial penalties imposed on carriers bringing into the territory of the member states third-country nationals who do not have the necessary documents for admission. this text, which was sent to the european parliament for consultation on 6 september 2000, is currently being examined by the competent council bodies. the aim of this initiative is to implement a coherent policy against the real scourge of illegal immigration and human trafficking at european level. the responsibility of carriers is one of the key aspects. the proposal for a directive therefore introduces a minimum common system for all member states in the field of the liability of carriers, by laying down the control obligations incumbent on carriers and by harmonizing the penalties currently provided for by the member states. the aim is not to introduce new sanctions against carriers but to harmonize those already provided for by the provisions of the schengen convention. i would draw the honourable member's attention to the fact that the draft directive states in recital 3 that its application is without prejudice to the obligations arising from the geneva convention of 28 july 1951 relating to the status of refugees, as amended by the new york protocol of 31 january 1967. the european union has repeatedly stated that it fully respects the right to asylum. it must be combined with effective measures to combat illegal immigration and human trafficking. this is an imperative and the council was expressly invited to do so by the feira european council following the dover tragedy.
counsel. - it's more of an opinion than a question. i repeat that we must take effective measures against a scourge that has given rise to a real tragedy and that we must do so in full respect of the right of asylum which the european union attaches to. i insist: absolute respect for the law. one country may have problems, another country may have problems. we're working on it. it's up to him to make them heard. but i think that is a path we must continue on.
counsel. - that was precisely the subject of the question to which i tried to answer and i repeat that this is a matter of extreme gravity, of very great seriousness.

- question no 14 by mr esko olavi seppänen (h-0899/00) subject: mandate of the rapid reaction force the european union is setting up a crisis management force. what are the mandate decisions that allow for the use of force? what purpose will it serve?
the council. - it is for the council to decide on the possible launching of a military operation by the union in the framework of the petersberg missions. in accordance with article 23 of the treaty on european union, the council adopts this decision unanimously, as is the case for any other decision with defence implications. it is also up to each member state to take a national, sovereign decision whether to commit national troops to the operation. the nice european council noted the modalities which could lead the council to take a decision in a crisis situation. thus, in the run-up to the launch of an operation, the political and security committee could address a recommendation to the council based on the opinions of the military committee. the council, whose deliberations are prepared by coreper in accordance with the usual procedures, could decide on this basis. the decision to launch an operation would in principle take the form of a joint action. the psc, which is the backbone of the european security and defence policy and the cfsp, has a central role in defining the union's response to a crisis. in particular, he provides political control and strategic direction of a military crisis management operation. the use of the rapid reaction force could be decided for the full spectrum of crisis management missions, petersberg missions as defined in article 17 (2) of the treaty on european union, humanitarian and evacuation missions, peacekeeping missions, combat forces missions for crisis management, including peacekeeping missions.
counsel. - we have a report which was annexed to the report of the presidency to the european council in nice on european security and defence policy. he will give mr seppänen all the necessary answers. it is very long, but everything is planned in an extremely precise way.
- as the authors are absent, questions 15 to 21 are obsolete. question no 22 by mr lennart sacrédeus (h-0918/00) subject: importance of taxation for the functioning of the internal market the commission president, mr prodi, recently assured in a november financial times article that he did not want tax harmonization or common tax rates within the european union, stating that the tax rate "is a matter for national parliaments and must remain so". the same article also states that, in order for the european union to be dynamic and competitive, decisions on taxation should be taken by majority vote 'where the functioning of the internal market so requires'. what taxes do you think have no influence on the dynamism and competitiveness of the internal market?
the council. - with your permission, mr president, this will be the last question to which i can answer during question time. the honourable member's question concerns the views expressed in an informal capacity by the president of the commission. it is therefore not for the council to decide on this question. i would simply like to point out that the treaty system differentiates between the treatment of taxes and indirect taxes, the harmonization of which is necessary to ensure the establishment and functioning of the internal market - that is article 93 - and the approximation, provided for in article 94, of legislation which has a direct impact on the establishment or functioning of the common market, including those relating to direct taxation. decisions taken by the council on the basis of articles 93 and 94 shall be taken unanimously. after the treaty of nice, they will unfortunately continue to be subject to unanimity.
counsel. - i repeat that i cannot comment on statements made to the president of the commission. but the question of whether decisions in tax matters should be taken by majority voting has been discussed in the context of the intergovernmental conference. as you know, unfortunately, no progress was made in nice in this area.
