the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, it was with great pleasure that i accepted the task of drawing up this important resolution of the european parliament, which deals with one of the most important problems facing our european community: the problem of the environment. the ageing population. in the face of this problem, we must be very sensitive and work to create the intergenerational solidarity that is absolutely necessary to help conclude serious and important policies of a holistic approach and to achieve that social security, that social protection, and above all to ensure that the concept that the elderly are not a burden for society but must be considered as a resource is affirmed in the cultural conception of each country: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. these were the underlying reasons which enabled me and the whole social affairs committee to bring this resolution forward and to conclude it with the consent of all. i would therefore like to thank all the members for their contribution, including during the amendment phase, and the technical staff of the committee for their valuable contribution to the resolution. the european union has been taking up this issue since 1999, when the united nations declared the international year of older persons. we have now come to the commission's communication and we are here today to vote on a resolution. this is a very important step. we believe that a policy which considers the ageing of the population in an active sense, that is to say, which looks at the elderly not as a person who is dying but as a person who wants to stay alive - alive in affection, alive in professional skills, alive in the will to communicate at all levels, not only his feelings but also his professionalism, his experience - is the best way to cultivate and tackle new policies which are intended above all to support social cohesion and intergenerational solidarity. of course, there are complex problems: there is the problem of security, there is the problem of pensions, there is also the problem of care which we have tried to tackle, which i have tried to tackle in this resolution in the most serene and effective way possible, also because we know that care is often borne by families and, in particular, by women who bear this burden often alone and, moreover, without any consideration by the social and labour policies of the member states. member states must therefore do more: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the future may be a day, a minute, a second, but lived in the awareness that it is a whole life and not half a life that awaits the elderly, the worker who has stopped working, the man and woman who are now orientating themselves in the last phase of their lives and who must be able to do so with the necessary serenity and with the consideration, on the part of all of us but above all of the political world and the administrations, that they are people. that is not to be forgotten. this is the basic rationale behind the resolution which deals with various aspects, ranging from leisure to employment; the commission has already taken a number of initiatives to promote the development of the information society, such as the creation of a european information society, the development of a european information society and the development of a european information society. we need a massive upgrading, no discrimination in the workplace and no discrimination even after retirement, when these workers, these people can enjoy all their time with a different wealth and availability and can face life in a more serene way. that is why we are moving in this direction and, above all, towards people who in their third and fourth years unfortunately become disabled. we know that health is not an infinite good. the member states must implement different policies for these people, addressing both the issue of the necessary assistance and the issue of covering the costs, especially for those disabled whose families are not actually able to take on a final and total responsibility.
mr president, i should first like to thank the rapporteur, mrs sbarbati, because, as i have already said in committee, she has prepared a report which i myself would not have been able to compile so perfectly. i would like to congratulate myself and all the elderly and retired people who have helped me to get to seat no 274 in our chamber. i would draw your attention to paragraph 18 of the report. the report calls on the member states to take care of the elderly who are not self-sufficient and are hospitalised, or to reimburse the families who care for them. this was an amendment tabled by me, mr fatuzzo, and approved by the committee on employment and social affairs. i would like to stress the importance of this paragraph. in many of our member states - certainly in italy, but i am sure also in britain, greece and other countries - we work all our lives: the workers work from morning to night, they get up at six in the morning, they come home tired, exhausted at eight, nine at night. the years go by. they get sick at work, they pay contributions for pension, for sickness benefit; they pay taxes, they pay taxes. very often in the last years of our lives, we get very sick, we become totally incapacitated, we need everyone's help. and the state pays nothing, not even to those who are destitute and without income. and the worker, who has given everything to society, must sell his house to take care of himself, must use all his money, must see his family impoverished, just when he expects the state and others to be close to him in the last years of life, when everything is dark and hopes in the light of the help of his neighbor. let us therefore give hope to the elderly citizens of europe by voting in favour of this report and paragraph 18! (applause) i would like to thank
the rapporteur. - mr president, i have accepted mr pronk's amendments nos 2 and 3, in which he argues that the text should be amended and insists on the concept of demographic development rather than demographic ageing. the problem is that, as far as we are concerned as the european union, we cannot talk about development because we have no real demographic development: the birth rate is very low, while the ageing population is increasing. the proposal - which i think mr pronk accepted - is therefore to talk about raising the average age of the population, to avoid a concept which may seem negative and to put the matter in more technical, more correct terms.
- mr president, this is the last statement of vote for the year 2000. i would like to take this opportunity to thank you for your patience, and that of the other presidencies in office, in listening to me during the year. the year 2000 did not start well for mr fatuzzo: in the spring my wallet and credit cards were stolen in barcelona; in the summer my new bicycle was stolen in strasbourg; in the autumn, my diary and phone numbers were stolen in brussels. but today the report by mr sbarbati on behalf of the elderly was approved, which has lifted my heart and given me joy. i would like to conclude by saying to mr flemming, who i see standing next to me, that the fact that people are living longer does not mean - as you rightly said, mr flemming - that they are getting older, it means that they are getting younger. in fact, a person who was forty years old once, years ago, was old; now, he's young. you're young, flemming, and i'd court you if i wasn't married! (laughter and applause)
